SEA IN OCTOBER. Not now, not now, the unfruitful sea be mine, With ever restless tides that ebb and flow Like hopes in a sick heart; nay, I would know How soonest to forget this kindred brine. Show me some ripened land in mellow glow Where heavy hang the clusters of the vine, Where apples drop, where browse full-uddered kine, Where. tilting-topped, the harvest waggons go A-creak across the fields. 0 let me fill My longing eyes with pictures of a land Sloping to sunset, full of twilight peace That seems from plenty's horn to overspill; Let me thus gaze, and gazing, understand Toil's fairest harvest is desire's surcease. ELISABETH FAIRCHILD.
•—Scribner's Ifaya:ine for October.
A NUTTING SONG.

- Hurrah for the clustering nuts that bide 'So high on the hazel-trees, Peeping around on every side, The sport of every breeze! Hurrah for the nuts so brown! Hurrah for the merry hours we spend Picking the nuts so brown! Hurrah when homeward soon we wend, Trudging o'er hill and down, Laden with nuts so brown! Folks Magazine.

Striking Results.—Black eves. A Last. Resort.—The shoemaker's shop. Misplaced Affection.—A lost love letter. Why is the centre of a tree like a dog's tail ?—Because it is farthest from the bark. Life is a quarry, out of which we are to mould and chisel and complete a character. The discovery of what is true and the practice of what is good are the two most important objects of life. HURRYING Tansas.—Customer (in restaurant): " Here, waiter, two boiled eggs—four minutes, and look lively, Pm in a hurry." Waiter (hastily dusting off the table- cloth: "Yes, sah—yes, sah. Have 'em ready fo' yo' in two minutes. sah, two minutes." On the extravagance shown in funerals, Pauli tells this tale. The Emperor Vespasian heard that the funeral of a noble Roman had cost sixty ducats, "And, pray, what will my funeral cost?" asked the Emperor of his chancellor. "Oh, sire ! not less than three hundred ducats." "Then, in pity, hand me the ducats now, and when I am dead chuck me into the Tiber." The Emperor Domitian shut himself tip in his room for some hours a day. The courtiers said—" He is en- gaged on matters of State " ; or, "He is studying philosophy"; or, "He is planning something great for the advantage of the city." Then, one peeped through • a chink in the wall, and saw that he was catching flies. It is so with a good many people whom we suppose to be hard at work at profitable occupations; cultivating their brains, storing their minds, executing great works —they are only catching flies. WIFELY OBEDIENCE.—PauIi gives advice to husbands and wives how to maintain love and concord. One of his stones on this topic is as follows :--A man about to be married visited a wise man, and asked his advice how to make home happy. "Follow me to my house," said the sage, and he led the way to his own dwelling. On reaching the house-door he called out to his wife, who looked forth from an upper window. "Wife," shouted the sage. "pitch out to me my big bottle of tur- pentine." "Certainly," answered the woman, and threw it down. It was smashed on the pavement, and the turpentine spilt. "Never mind," shouted the wise man, "throw down the other." "Certainly," answered the wife, and presently did as ordered. "Now, my friend," said the sage, "this is the secret of household order. Make your wife mind you and obey without arguing."—Cosselrs Magazine. ELIMOROBS AMERICA.—TO be strictly just. we must re- member that a large part of American slang—the raw material of the American language—is ultimately due to the universal mevalence of the faculty of humour in all parts of America. The English. in the lump, are not a humorous people. Our Philistine classes do not see a joke • and, if they see it, they rather resent it, as they would resent a slap on the back, or other unwarrantable interference with their portly persons. The small grocer in England, or the surveyor of taxes, would be incapable of originating a merry jest on his own account; he would be shy of it if originated by his assistant or his shop-boy. But in America the sense of humour is equally distribtited through the whole population. Philistinism, to be sure, is just as rampant as with us; nay, even kore so; New York and Chicago are true modern Goths and Aekelons ; but the American Philistine differs fundamentally from our own variety in possessing, for all that, a spirit of fur., a certain notable quickness of intelligence, and a considerable fund of native geniality. He takes a joke, or, as he himself says, "twigs the racket," with a rekonsive twinklerin the motionless corner of his sympathetic eve. He does not smile: to smile were childish; but he takes it in internally, as Mr. Weller senior took his laughter, swallows and digests it, and chews the cud of his appreciation at leisure.—The Great American Language, in the Cornhill Magazine. • NATURE IN OCTOBER.—The weather in October is often very fine and warm, but the length of the day is rapidly becoming shorter and the early mornings and evenings getting more chilly. A few slight frosts may generally be expected towards the end of the month, reminding us that we must now prepare for the winter and the cold to come. The flowers are fast getting over, and the leaves falling, and Nature everywhere is proclaiming that autumn is at hand. By the end of the month the lime ; trees will be quite destitute of their leaves, and the majestic oak will commence to shed its leaves also. In hedges and woods the hazel nuts will now be fully f pe, and tile cottage children will be quite busy gathering them for the markets. The little beech nuts, the delight of schoolboys, will be found in great numbers on the ground beneath the trees, and the air will he full of the seeds of the sycamore, known as "pigeons," from the peculiar manner in which they spin round and round when tossed up. The "cobblers,' too, the seeds of the horse chest- nut, will be now quite•ripe.and afford much amusement among the country children. The common plantain also ripens its seeds, and a store of the long fruit stalks may be gathered and dried to last throughout the winter for', our little bird pets, if we should have any under our care. The only flowers worthy of notice this month are ' the groundsel, chickweed, and the shepherd's purse, which may be found almost everywhere. In some of the northern countries of Europe the shepherd's purse is largely eaten, being boiled as a vegetable.—Little Folks' Magazine. 4 RESPONSIBILITIES OF RAILROAD PRESIDENTS.—A Ger- man economist has said that the so-called survival of the fittest in modern industry is really a double survival, side by side, of the most talented on the one hand and the most unscrupulous on the other. The truth of this is already apparent in , railroad business. A Vanderbilt on the Central meets a Fisk on the Erie. In spite of his superior power and resources he is virtually beaten in the contest—beaten, as was said at the time, because lie could not afford to co so close to the door of State's prison as his rival. The manager of a large railroad sys- tem has under his control a great deal of property be- sides his own—the property of railroad investors which has been placed in his charge. Two lines of action are open to him. He may make money for the investors, and thereby secure the respect of the community; or he make money out of the investors, and thereby - get rich enough to defy publit opinion. The former course has the advantage of honesty, the latter of rapidity. It is a disgrace to the community that the latter way is made so easy, and so readily condoned. A man has only to give to charitable objects a little of the money obtained by violations of trust, and a large part of the world will extol him as a public benefactor. Nay, more: it seems as if some of our financial operators really mistook the vox impuli for the vo.r Del. and , believed that a hundred thousand dollars given to'a theological seminary meant absolution for the past and plenary indulgence for the future. It is charged that one financier, when lie undertook any large transaction which was mere than usually questionable, made a eovenant that if the Lord prospered him in his under- taking, he would divide the proceeds on favourable terms.—Prof. A. T. Hadlev in Scribotefs.

DESTRFCTIVE_ _FIRE AT PRESCOT.

.42,000 DAMAGES. On Saturday night the town of Prescot was thrown in a state of excitement, by the ringingof the fire bell. It was found that the premises of Mr. Williams, successor of Mr. E. Scaresbrick, watch movement maker, West-st., were on tire. It is supposed the fire originated in the workshop through a lighted match having been thrown on the floor. The tire engine was soon on the spot but the services of the brigade were not required, as the fire had been extinguished by willing 'workers. Great damage was done to the valuable stock of watch materials and jewellery, the 16ss being estimated at over X 2,000. It is stated that the damages are covered by insurance.

' A FATAL ERROR OF JUDGMENT.—Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the St. Helens Town Hall on Monday, on the body of John Kiernan, aged forty years, of Langtree- streetot labourer, who received fatal injuries at the Parr Chemical Works on the previous Monday after- ' noon. Deceased and a number of other men had to push a loaded waggon along a line of rails. On the other side nearest Kiernan a baulk of limber and a boiler were lying, and as the waggon approached the space for him to walk in narrowed. On reaching the timber he stopped in a space of about 14 inches to allow the waggon to pass, but he was caught by a projecting stanchion and crushed between the waggon and the boiler. A cab was procured, and he was taken to the Providence Hospital, where he died.—Thos., Frodsham, . foreman, said he ordered deceased to push the front of • the waggon. and his going to the side was at his own risk .--The Coroner: This seems to have been an error of judgment on the part of the deceased. He should have either stood still sooner and allowed the waggon to pass, or he shcaild have walked back.—Thejury returned a verdict of" Accidental Death." rot all kinds ot domestic sewing,. WHY WE LAUGH
BY " Ruda BErtm." .

You know what Thomas Carlyle says about men that don't laugh; they are arrant rogues, if not out and out villains. I don't want to lead you to believe that Carlyle descends to such language. I only quote his meaning. The fact of the matter is, that I lent "prtor Resartus" to a friend, and if this meets his eye I may possibly be able to give the exact quotation next time I want it. Carlyle says that no man who has once laughed heartily can be utterly bad, but Carlyle and myself fall out very much on this point IR fact I am prepared to swear through a four-inch plank that I have known, and still remember, men who would have taken prizes at any laughing competition, and they had sold their souls to the devil, as the phrase goes. I think Carlyle, in his 'dyspeptic melancholy, must have been so far excom- municated from hearty laughter as to regard it with the gnat sort of eyes as the boy regards the apples when the trunk of the bred . . is )noud his scaling power; _ Carlyle's words cannot be eradicated, howeVer, AO I must content my humble self with the belief that he purposely over-estimated the value of the hearty laugh, thinking that it wasn't appreciated as it ought to be; and there is no doubt that it is a valuable acquisition in a man's general outfit. Not the way in which some of us laugh—as though we earned our living by laughing. We may sometimes laugh in the wrong place, and then the laughter isn't appreciated as it 'Might be if suitably timed. There is a time for everything, and it doesn't do to ruminate over the remnants of some old joke when your f4nd is reciting Hamlet's soliloquy by special request."' Others of us laugh as though we rather enjoyed it, and this is the happt medium (so difficult of attainment in all things) that to. my mind constitutes the genuine hearty laugh; for there is no credit to be taken in having promoted laughter, where laughter is everbubbling up ready to be let free by' the veriest trifles. • Some of us laugh out suddenly, and as suddenly jerk that solemn expression into our features which is sup- posed to be the sole copyright of the gravedigger; as though vie were afraid we 'might have been seen laughing; as Cassius, of whom Car said— Seldom he smiles, and smiles in such a sort, As though he mocked himself, and scorned his spirit That could be moved to smile at anything,— the only difference being that a laugh is only an aggra- vated sort of smile dedicated to blind men. The cachinnatory production, known as the horse laugh, comes under this head, but it might have been better named, as it approaches nearer to the bray of an ale. Heaven preserve us from the horse laugh and from ra'w tomatoes. Now some of us never laugh at all, at least so it is given out. You take a man who has this reputation, and tell him the very driest anecdote you know. You vainly watch his features for an exhibition of the facial contraction known as a smile. The only sign of change you note is a faint scintillation of his eye, and the nearest sound to a laugh is the remark, "Very good." as you conclude your story. You think he hasn't seep the 'humorous side of the affair, and you come away disgusted, tlever thinking for a moment that you have caused more agonising internal spasms in that man than you would suffer if you laughed continuously for a whole day. When anyone tells you that So-and-So never laughs. don't believe them. He may have an abnormal power over the facial muscles, but he laughs unseen, away down in his stomach—" down in him pelly," as the ventriloquist told the youthful Valentine Vox,—and suffers tortures that are unknown to the man with the loud smile. If you know the man that -doesn't laugh, my advice is, don't let him get a bill of sale on your furniture if you can help it The problem is, Why 1:10 any of us laugh? At first sight this question would appear an easy one to answer, but it is not yet settled by the first scientists of the day. You ask some little boy why he laughs, and he will pro- bably say, "Because he wants to." Most of us feel inclined to give little boys' answers to difficult questions at times, but they don t always apply. The answer quoted wouldn't apply to the parson who burst out laughing in the middle of his sermon. He saw through one of the chapel windows a robust woman carrying a tubful of semi-liquid pig meat (commonly known as swillings) on her head, but he didn't laugh. Why Bhou)ri. he? The bottom came out of the tub, and we are given to understand that he laughed; and, personally, I can quite believe it. But, as I remarked above, I don't think he loaded to laugh; on the contrary, he would doubtless have given about two dozen of his old sermons to have been able to resist the tickling sensation. I remember a trivial event that occurred when I was a very little boy which illustrates that even little boys sometimes laugh when they don't want to. It was in chapel—the place above all others where people laugh at things they would frown at if they were outside. A learned minister was in the thick of learned arguments with a learned congregation, and the big words that flowed from his reverend mouth were as full of meaning to me as big pebbles would have been. My legs went to sleep and awoke at intervals, and I wiled away the dreary minutes with wondering how long I should have to sit there before they dropped off altogether (the legs, ncit the minutes). Upon the occasion named I had smuggled in a small story book, in which was a wonder- ful anectode of a boy chasing a fire-fly. The parson and congregation gradually vanished from my sight as I followed the boy and the fly. I read on till he caught it, when he was made to exclaim in disappointment, "Why, it is only a little brown flea." To my youthful imagina- tion there was something so excessively funny in the expression, coupled with the novel termination of the story, that I had to suddenly push both hands against my mouth, and the sounds of smothered mirth seemed to squirt out of both ears. Would the smallest boy in creation tell me that I wanted to laugh when the parental gaze was focussed upon me with the power of a micro- scope? Scarcely! It seems incongruous that the subject of laughter should lead on to that most solemn and impressive subject the church; for of all places in which a person ought to laugh this is certainly the last. But what are people of a mirthful temperament to do? Stay away ? Hardly! Take an example. Only a few weeks ago the minister of our chapel was describing the amphitheatre at Ephesus. He spoke thus :—" The theatre at Ephesus contained 127 pillars, said to be the gift of 127 kings, many of them beautifully carved and ornamented." It might have been my imagination, but I fancied I could trace a connection between the sounds of combined coughs and sneezes, and the mental picture of 127 beautifully carved and ornamented kings all in a row. Even the minister seemed to be struck with the idea that his congregation were all awake for once, and I have no doubt he has made a note of the circumstance. I have repeatedly asked myself the question, "Why do we laugh ?" But I have had to give it up in despair. I mentally draw a life portrait of a very fat man who has just evacuated himself from a 'bus, and has un- ceremoniously sat down in the middle of the road, and I ask why evdryt spectator laughs. It is evident to all that it is a misfortune to the fat man, and yet they laugh. Why doesn't the fat man laugh? And why do the people laugh more at him that they would at a lean man under the same circumstances ? Is it simply because the fat man makes the worse acrobat of the two? A hearty laugh is a pleasant thing to hear—sometimes— when you have told a comic story, for instance. But step on a piece of orange peel, and let your hat fly one way, your umbrella another, and yourself a third, and you require a different standard of measurement for the laughter you hear, and still it might be.exactly the same sort of laughter that led you to think your story a good one. Some men profess to judge the character by laughter, but on the principle that circumstances alter cases, I don't see how it can work successfully. There is no doubt that you can tell the laugh of a fool from that of a sensible man; but when you say that such a kind of laughter indicates such a characteristic, please to state in what,relation the laughist stands to the laughter. I could write a volume on this subject, but space—no, I may as well be candid, I should be at a dead loss what to write.

The Bank rate of discount was raised on Thursday from fclur to five per cent. A scaffold fell on Thursday in the yard of the Naval Construction and Armaments Company at Barrow, and five men were injured, three somewhat seriously. GOVT.-Rightly or wrongly the Medical Profession seem to be pretty well agreed that where stimulants are necessary the best drink for those who suffer from, or are threatened with gout, is good Whisky, thoroughly matured and plentifully diluted with some reliabie mineral or potass water. This will go a long way to 'explain not only the popularity of the article named, and its increased consumption, but also the great competition which exists amongst the principal Wine Merchants in the sale of Whisky. As an illustration of the keenness of this competition, we may state that one of the largest and best-known firms—W. & A. Gilbey—lately purchased one of the celebrated Scotch Distilleries in the Glenlivet dis- trict named Glen-Spey, so as to acquire the exclusive distillation and sale of this article direct from the distillery through their various depots. Fortunately, the public, as usual, are the gainers by this " race" for trade, for certainly none but reliable brands now find purchasers. Out attention has been called this fact on the ground that medical men are particularly interested in knowing what brands to _ recommend to their patient 4 as supplying an alcoholic beverage which fulfils the above necessary conditions under the guarantee of a reliable house. Whisky and Potass' however, although they may constitute the best drink for the gouty will not cure gout, and it vet remains for science to find a remedy for that once fashionable but now very unimer- sal malady—indeed acidity of the blood is beyond all doubt the illness of the _present generation, and must result in some walflom our present me-de of • living.— Medical Pros, Sept. 26th, 1888. i/QTEMPERANCE Cintan.—A wealthy American Lady whose only son was for years a slave to intemperance, after seeking in lain "or a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last foul dB, imple means that cured and save him from a drun- kard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy cause, by sending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hart-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1888.
HER BROTHER'S KEEPER.
By Mns. J. K. SPENDER, Author of "Mr. Nobody," "Parted Lives," "Both in the Wrong," "Recollections of a Country Doctor," "Trust Me,' &v. CHAPTER XIIL A NEW ANXIETY. 4

"Whatever may be said of the landowning classes, it must be admitted that they shpuld shew full recognition of the great responsibilities attached to their position," said the doctor, in apokigy for some of Ursula's talk.

"One would think that she verily believed we were the sworn enemies of the working man,—hunting him to death," fumed Sir Thomas, "instead of doing all for him that we possibly can. All this windy declaration going on in the country now is to prepare lis fel' the Urn.; when every man will think he has rigti to put his hands in his neighbour's breeches pocket," rOated the irate landowner. The doctor did not answer the old baronet, who had good reasons for being irascible. Dr. Havard had ideas of his own that it was better to allow the fotiV mind to expand in its own direction than to lay down rigid tamers which may afterwards be rudely thrown down. According to Sir Thomas there were few questions open to argument even for the pro- perly-trained masculine intellect, but still fewer for the female Rasselas, who, if she tried to soar, would be sure to come to miserable gllef. "Better," said the doctor, to have a few fells than never to try one's wings at all. Was it not natural, he asked himself, that one so young, so de- fiant, so merrily full of life should shew a little op- position to,old established opinions? Ursula was no Corrinne, but it was the doctor's private opinion that she had a wonderful head on her shoulders, and belonged to the minority upon whom is laid the inexorable necessity of thinking out cer- tain questions and being unable to escape from them, while others never even tried to get to the bottom of them.

" I don't like new schemes. They so often come to nothing," said Sir Thomas, severely. "I wonder a young girl has pluck enough to think of facing the blackguards who made so free with her preserves." He ventured on black prophecies the first 'Hine he met her.

"Oh, I have nerve , enough for anything," an- swered Ursula, bracing herself for utterance, and be- ginning to enlarge upon ideas which jarred upon Sir Thomas, making no secret of her new theory that great possessions were accumulated wrongs, and that money should be utilised for fertilising all the soil instead of being confined as it was at present to a few. "1 can tell you," she cried, "that there is a good deal ia your free England that is superstitious, de- graded, and enslaved; yet you have your workhouses. Louise Michel thought a good deal when she came to England of your providing a shelter for the poor in their old age, but she did not know that the deserving poor avoided it and hated it as much as they hate a prison." It was too much for Sir Thomas. He turned 'c'n his heel and left her with a freezing bow. It was bsd enough to have suspicions that M;ss Cam 'ion had refused the suit of his own son, who was a hundred times too good for her; but that a young girl should mention glibly such a name as that of Louise Michel, and should not know it was revolting as coming-from her lips, was only a little worse than'that she should regard her own childish acts of interference with per- fect complacency as achievements of importance. "Talk J yes, she'll talk till she makes your brain reel, and would persuade you that the Moon is the sun, that black is white, or that Tyndale and Car- dinal Manning are agreed," groaned Sir Thomas afterwards to the doctor. Ursula's private opinion was that her neighbourwas one of the Philistines, who dwelt, as her father used to say, in a dull and stuffy atmosphere of logic. My dear, you must do something," said Miss Havard, in a despairing way, to her brother ; "it will never do for people whose estates join each other to begin quarrelling like this." • Do you know what the folks in the neigh- bourhood are beginning to say about you?" asked the doctor one morning, when there was a sudden spell of finer weather, and when he surprised Ursula, busied with a freak oegardening, her face as fresh as the :rich-coloured chrysanthemums which she was still stooping to tie up, just as if there were not gardeners enough for the work. "They hint that I should get one of my brethren to help me to sign a certain certificate. A little judicial restraint, you know! I believe that one or two of the dowagers would gladly help me to put a strait. waistcoat on you, or at least conhne you to yourown grounds." . "Do you think I care a hang what they say?" said the girl, looking pertly up in his face with one of her brightest smiles. She was certainly proving, herself an adept at picking up English slang. But much as he disliked this horrible habit of hers, the brightness of her ap- pearance had its usual effect upon him. He was inclined to be tolerant He put on his spectacles solemnly and inspected her with a humorous look. "I was trying to imagine you one of the young. women who have a fancy for cotton or merino gloves, hhir cut short, eye glasses, and a predilection for waterproofs—views as to their rights' on this side the grave, and who profess themselves sceptical about the next." _ .

"Well," she said, "and I think that is one of the right sort. Somebody must be reviled at Smithfield —ready for the burning by orthodox people." "But I don't see why it need be you, some of us value you too much," sp,id the doctor in his quizzical way. , He had been coached up by Margaret to give a lecture to this child, but had been telling himself throughout his drive that it was of no • use to use the curb with some women ever so lightly. The free laxity of lief speech meant nothing really shock. ing. It was queer, it was even flippant from his old- fashioned point of view, but it had no taint of 'wiekedness.

There 'were some people laughing at Ursula a good deal-just then, but Ile thought it was shame- ful of them to laugh: It might be that she had been guilty of giflish imprudence in misleading some of the poorer folks, but her private motive had been a good one. Her rectitude and her determination to stand up foi what was good and true had influenced the doctor as much as her grace and boldness. "I wouldn't hide myeyes with those horrid nippers, and I don't like hair cat short," she answered, look- ing up at him and leaning on her spade, as she found that the conversation flagged; "but if you think that I make unfortunate 'remarks to the poor people I will try to be a little more particular in what I say. We never thought of what we said in Paris, but now I come to think of it perhaps it is stupid to be always dropping one's vague thoughts about to the annoyance of one's neighbours—one should wait till they are properly marshalled." Yes, vague surmises are best kept to yourself," d the doctor, who was not pessimist enough to Snalyse the girl severely', bat liked simply to look at her bright face. The pagan instinct, strong in so many natures for simple enjoyment of this sunshiny world, was uppermost in both of them just at this moment. The doctor, in his youth, had never seen anyone as free and independent as Ursula, with that air-of cheerful alacrity and of being always on the alert, which prompted her to say, "I could not be offended !" when he told her that all this meddlinr, with the people in the village was not likely to snake them a hair's breadth happier; that her crops would come up without her at- tending to them, and that it would better if she hid herself less at St. Agatha's. "You should think of your brother as well as of yourself; you will make enemies, by refusing all your invitations." ' • "If—you—are sure it is the riglit thing to do," said the girl for the first time, a little dejectedly, "I suppose I must go through with it" She spoke with some unwillingness, having an exhilarating sense of freedom in the pure sunshine of those autumn days and believing la her secret heart that it was a nuisance to be interviewed as a sort of strange product, and to be obliged to accept all sorts of invitations. Such social regulations, she had hitherto determined in her downright way; were I better obeyed in the spirit than in the letter. But the sweetness of her nature prevailed. Had not her mother with her last breath commended her to the kind help of • this benevolent friend, and had he not evidently made an effort to stave off awkward. subjects as long as he could? So, with one of her many jokes about the, special paradise which ought to be prepared for all good doctors, where there would be no more hyponchondriacs or fidgety lady patients, she sent him home with-a happier heart, having formed the determination of taloing upon herself once more that burden of provincial society which in her heart she hated.

Her very education had unfitted her for the task. It was hard to help having a, scorn • for that local imagination which coloured every foreign landscape with its own surroundings. The excitetuW; ra• duced by a birth, or still, more by a death a ,the neighbourhood, with all the little incidents and the details of the last hours, were only lass than the stir

and gossip produced by a marriage.. Every littlg event which occurred to somebody they .had knowili furnished the women with days and weeks of talk. The windings and he circumlocutions in these women's minds, when a man would have gone straightforwardly to a conclusion, and the fine reasonings which never seemed to 'lead to fine issues, were exasperating to Ursula. The strict account which Miss Havard kept of every social slight, and the manner in which she mourned over the hiatuses and shortcomings of her much-conned visiting list, seemed to Ursula inconsistent with a profession of unworldliness. The way in which people yearned to belong to the hierarchy of a pro. vincial city, and to lae called with bated breath "the leaders of society," tickled her risibilities. let she remembered the doctor's; lectures, and kept herself well in hand, so that when she shewed herself a little incase, the few people in Abbeyford and the neighbourhood of St. Agatha's who looked forward to Miss Campion's racy descriptions, and who de- clared it was really refreshing to meet somebody of a different pattern, were doomed to be disap- pointed. Ursula made no daring speeches and said few amusing things. She tried hard to accommodate her- self to.the general flatness of her surroundings, but it was a monotony which made her yawn and which contrasted strangely with her love for incessant activity. Whenever it was possible she draggect kayinand with her. But as he, too, contisased to the same sort of shapeless feeling which she had herself of wanting something or seeking for something else in life, and as his sister bore with his caprices and his changes of mood more readily than with her own, Ray was more often left at St. Agatha's reclin- ing in an armchair reading a Fressch novel. "It was a sleepy sort of a place, and there was no good in trying to hold out against it," Raymond de- clared speaking in a sleepy way, as if he were quite satisfied with his own laziness. His love of bright conversation seemed to havd forsaken him: There were days ' when he said very little to Ursula, and then she accused him of being, as the Germans would express it, " damni and toll." But he took her jokes in such a serious way that she found it necessary to alter her jocose tone. Even then it never troubled her that the ill. natured gossip which she was managing to divert from herself was being indulged in with a vengeance in the case of her brother. She contented, ' herself with saying it was a "Shame ! " in capital letters. Anything, she thought, would be better than to degrade herself with worries like midge-bites. Hitherto she had lived in such an indepandent at- mosphere as to be able to avoid that discord about small things which is jarring to most women, if not fatal to their goodness. "I always stand on my guard against people who are popular with everyone," she said one day to Miss Havard, when that lady hinted that people were saying hard things about Raymond. "If you think, you will see how Tittle it signifies." It seemed to her that Margaret Havard never half thought, it was difficult for her to fix her mind on anything. "I wonder you take it so in deadly earnest. Its, all very tunusing," she said, with a toss of her head. "I tic, ndt see any cause for hilarity." "Not when you have a lot of old people thinking themselves very good, and solemnly playing at nine- pins with the reputations of others." "If you knew ! " "Why should I care to know? they bowled me over yesterday—they are bowling Ray over to-day. Little things amuse little minds. What's the harm of their having Some fun out of us? You say they talk of the undesirability of a man indulging in numerous flirtations. Ray is not a man, he's only a boy, and as to flirting, why he spends most of his time either in the stables or else over a novel." • . "That is speaking coarsely," said Miss Havard, drawing herself up, and doubtful whether Ursula was in irony or not. It will be owing to your example if things go wrceig with your brother." "Girls do odd things nowadays as well as men," she, complained afterwards, though Ursula did her best to repress her spasm of disrespectful laughter. "I should not have tried to speak to her if I was not pro- perly sure of what I am saying;. I am always certain of what I say," she added tardy, "some one must tell her the truth." It fell to the doctor's lot much as he disliked it. He hated interfering and saying unpleasant things, espe- cially to this girl, who had a tenancy to take her affairs in her own hands. Towards the close of a dull day inthe beginning of October, when the Campions had been speculating as to whether they would be left in peace, the doetor appeared in unwonted guise. Ile rode over to tempt Ursula to accompany him on horseback through the country lanes. "You are a sight for sair e'en. We were get- ting bored by ourselves, and did not think anybody was likely to turn up; but I think the change id rather pledsant after the misty wean er,and a ride will be delightful now it has cleared up," said the girl, ; rattling on as slid/often did when she pleased. and assnt on hiding her astonishment that the doctor had chosen that spebial evening for a ride. It took her but a minute or two to be equipped In icr.habit. Then she could not help noticing that the doctor was rather thoughtful, and she kept on a continual trickle of innocent chatter to cheer him up, and rouse him from his uninual fit of low spirits. " Don't you associate me with unpleasant things ever since the days of rhubarb ?" he asked her, after a time, as they both slackened rein, letting their horses go quietly, that they might watch the effects of the sunset and the lengthened shadows On the fields. "Oh, you doctors are wiser now. You have found mit that even the rhubarb is not necessary," she said, in her eager way, looking up in his face. "There is . nothing of the bogey kind about you anymore- than my father,"' she continued 'merrily. "Of course he knew that I as well as he, had a strong will inherited from him; but he let me go my way while he. went his. It's nice to have fathers who jet you do pretty much what you like." There was a stone in her horse's fore foot. He stooped down and took it out. He was conscious of a change of complexion, even at this age, whichanade itself evident in a pikwoking way in his cheeks and nose, when she coupled his name in that cool way with that of a blackguard like Campion. He hated wounding others, or tearing open their wounds, simply from a want of tact or thought—he would not willingly have inflicted pain on the smallest thing which breathed, and yet he had to conic to the point and did not help himself by a long Preamble about English straight forwardness and English in- tegrity, while Ursula stared., at him with widely doened eyes. He did not see the vague foreshadow- ing of something *mat like terror in these eyes, when she began to understand the gist of .Dr. Havard's remarks. • ," Oh, I do not ,believe the world is half so bad as they make out. I thought yo7c. would not be taken in, whoever else might be. But I can't help knowing what you are going to say. You believe all those horrid things they olake up about Ray," she cried indignantly,. whi!e her heart thumped, and there was a noise like a cannonade in her ears. "Men always say such hard things of each other." My information omie mostly from . women'," he answered quietly. " Oh, and womersare so unreasonable ! I hate these- back-biting womea." "Have you aos noticed for yourself ?" Then she • began to redem her how the bright Less had gone from Raymond's eyes and the colour from his face, and how he had 1134 his appetite, especially at breakfast. She had thought of him as unwordlly,shrinking, indolent, with plenty of genius but no power of energetic ex- ecution. She had. lamented these things in liiin, but that he should be blamed .for those terrible things, which she vaguely remembered in her childhood, and which she could not quite put out of 'her remembratice, however she might try to ignore thernin the case of her own father, was more than she could bear. Oh no, it was net possible! Ray- -mond, was weak, terribly weak, but he could not be wicked or brutal. "-Do not take it so seriouSly to heart.. How will you bear a dagger-thrust in your future We if you can't even put up with a scratch nova?". askest the, doctor pityingly. She heard his voice speaking to her as if from a .diatance. The weather Mull cleared, and she ever afterwards remeniberel haw beautifal the Pale faint sickle of the young moon looked in the evening: sky and how tenderly the broad shadows of the trees tested on the soft green grass! It was as if her physieal eyes teak in all these beauties of the prospect mind sume, other eyes which were not physical were, staring straight in front a her perplexed by somas exasperating point of eternal law which she could not fathcan.a. " If it is a. scratch," she said, after a little interval, "it is one which hurts right down to , the quick."

"Well, it is a question of will," he answered, rather irrelevantly,. -44 educated will you know. I use the word advisedly, you can do so uiuch to influence him." It seemed to the old man as if his blood ran cold, when the, girl who but a short time before had been breaking- upon the silence with childish re- marks, burst into a fit of harsh, hysterical laughter. "i influence him, when all the powers of what you call Hell may be tugging in the opposite direction I You know how willingly I would influence him. I would give my life for him, but when people talk

about inherited instincts and the curse of genera tions, though we did not make ourselves, and can't be different from what we are, what good do you expect my influence to do?" You must not reason in that way. You must marry the thought to quite another set of consi- derations," said the good doctor, shocked. "I heard them talk about heredity even in Paris," she added, in a voice which was so low as to be barely distinguishable. " Humbug ; I don't care a rap for what you heard. We have all a mongrel ancestry of saints and sinners,' reverting after generations to a normal type. Exaggerations can be lessened, defects re- medied, wants supplemented—l speak to you as I would speak to one of my own sex—there is no occasion to despair of anyone, on account of inherited tendencies. Think of the close kinship of all man- kind; think of the wild irregular thoughts which sometimes take posaession of the best of us, perhaps coming down from some remote ancestor. Take heart, my child, we are all of us composed of iicon- gruous metals which have to be fused in one crucible, and passed through one alembic." Ile was wasting his breath, Ursula did not eveu hear him., Oh,if I had a mother I could consult her about it !' The burden is too great for one as young as I am,"was the cry of her heart as they rode back through the dusky lanes, the doctor talking all the time out of the Sheer goodness of his heart—a very queer hodge-podge of philosophy, quite unworthy of an M.D. who had passed his examination in logic. The first thing she did hear in the state of tension which caused exhaustion of body as well as of mind, was the feeble tinkling of a little bell which had a cracked tongue. It did its duty valiantly, though the effect was that of a dismal wagging which reminded her suddenly how good Mr. Bond had carried out his whim ; how, to please him, she had let the little chapel in her grounds, so long used by the family, he opened once more, and how this was a Friday, when the few people in the village whom she allowed to mix with the devout of her own household, were dribbling in for an evening service. Mr. Bond had introduced a modern ritual in the little chapel. It seemed to Ursula to have a comical effect; but if the pageantry ' helped anyone she would not oppose it. Hitherto she had never thought of propos- ing to attend it herself even on Sunday. Neither she, nor Raymond had seen the need of it. He had been content with tlie temple of his own self-consciousness in which some of us worship pretty freely, and she had never dreamt of forcing herself out of the fresh air or sunshine, and obliging herself to attempt devo- tions which were distasteful to her.

It occurred to her just then that religion might effect a diversion, and that it was well for her, as the mistress, to see what was going on. This evening for the first time, as some relief from the thoughts which were coursing through her brain, she crept, when the service was nearly ended, into a corner of the little chapel, listening to the jubilant tone of the hymns. Did they mean it, those simple. hearted villagers, who stood shouting enthusias- tically about Paradise? Would some such aid as this be of any assistance to her in trying to make Ray- mond perceive the eternal distinction between right and wrong which she thought she saw so plainly herself 7

• DOWN THE WYE, AND ON TO ILFRACOMBE. A HOLIDAY RHYME. EY THE EDITOR. My dear old fellow,—And so you think, Since I've hitherto failed to tip you the wink. That the direful cause of my not having written Will be found in the phrase—' They were water bitten.' Well, you might be right, but you're certainly wrong, And that you'll see as I jog along. The simple fact is I'm out of practice In spinning a yarn : when you've had a holiday, And it's proved, as it should do, a regular jolly day, . Ideas are hazy The mind's a bit Mazy— Yourre happy-go-lucky and healthfully lazy. Oh! ' the rain it raineth every day ; ' As somebody sometthere once did say. . That was years ago, When things were slow, When,they counted the drops as they fell in a row, When they'd nothing to do, and nowhere to go. But it might have been said of this year of grace When the sun was ashamed to show his Pane For as summer weather it proved a bad lot— Humph!Some are summers and some are not. But we, Ivy boy, why we were in clover When we made our start, it had just given over.' And there's nothing to one who has half an eye Like seeing the land, sea, river and sky, The frownrng cliff, or the smiling plain— There's nothing like seeing them after rain • For it's thenithat Nature, kind mother of ail, Puta on, as it were, her loveliest shawl, And decks herself in her very best • See the starry gleam on her jewelled breast; The delicate sheen Of her robe of green; And' the flowers in her hair— Oh ! she's wondrous fair, -And beauty flows from her everywhere. But, really, 'Where are we working now This sort of letter you'll not allow,

So to seem more exact, And to edge in a fact, Let me tell you the better half and I Set our hearts on seeing the winding Wye.. ('Why not? 'you'd say, But don't, I pray, For alLsuch jokes on the Wye, and the 'wherefore.' . Have Men done-to death and are used up therefore.) We took in Shrewsbury, or, shall I say? S. took in us while on the way. It's a rare old town, Castle seems to frown, , With houses looking uncommonly brown, And wrinkled, and aged; They are penned and caged * In so many queer ways, and so many queer places, That you somehow expect to see old-fashioned faces; But the people are modern enough, and—well, Their modernity seems a bit of a sell. We-'clid' everything, of course, worth doing— The newest church and the oldest ruin ; Market House, Council, and other things' That have known the tread of a race of 'kings ; The Abbey Church, and the ancient wall, And Lord Hill's column so very tall ; We went through Wyle Cop, and had a go At Dogpole, Shoplatch, and Butchers Row; Strolled by river and bridges, and through theDiagie_ A sight to sat one's blood a-tingle t The Salopian folk sing its praises loud, And they're right—they have very good cause to be proud. Now„, as for their cakes They're no great shakes; I've eaten as good at fairs and wakes ;; But I whisper this as a word in haste,: For, I need hardly add, it's a matter of '`.taste.' They may "take the cake ; ' it's a sweeter thing To know that, when Edward (Longshanks) was king, The very first (And by no means the worst) Parliament' ever held in the nation, With Lords and Commons—a new situation— Assembled at Shrewsbury;: call it of news very Good, though it is not the 'latest 'May be— (Year tweite hundred and eighty-three). The Lords-in the Castle met—that was the plan; 'Twas a barn for the Commons with-91)o as you can.' Ah ! but isn't strange To notice the cl4ange ? The Commons are now to the front,,l dieclare The Lord§ take a back seat with--"Do, if you dare.' But we're off to Church Stretton we make a short stay*, And pieasantly pass the hours-a.way. We stroll by a rill,. Then climb up a hill; : AAi'eorgazinv., why, we can take our fill. Thens'S nothing to pay, and tirere'k,plenty of room' Thereat/le heather aglow, and the gorse abloom. No-wonder that Linnieus,the fine,old fellow, Went down on his knees when he first saw its yellow.. a hope that he didn't kneel whets it was planted— He might get a touch of it more than he wanted.) Church Stretton you'd like ; it's a charming nook; It has such a quiet aril happyclbok. One could go-to sleep there With no thought or care Of the rush of the world and its wear and tear; a world in,itself which is ever the same ; 'Pis a picture, too, with the hills for a frame. Buthere is Hereford; more of history, And that means, mostly, a guess at mystery. The Cathedral pile is certainly there ; This, too, may be said it is certainly fair; There is chapel, and cloister, and tomb, and nave, But everything has a look of the grave, Excepting this—some would say it-was best of all—. Preparations are on for the Musical Festival. It is hammer and tongs—a terrible din— Enough to awaken tht-elead within. So we turn aside to the Castle Green, Where ea older but fresher and fairer scene both greet the eye In the river Wye ; For, unlike church lore, It is now as of yore--. 1 It is always lovely and never 'dry.' Q 4 those liereford men, they were dry of old,

For they used to have ale-conners bold. Used to have '—why, they have them still, And they con ' the ale with a right good will. Nell Gweeme was born here in a aingy court, Where she'd better have stayed than have been the 01Ort Of that merrie monarch whose bastard set Still cling to us like the National Debt. But bye-bye Hereford ; Ross is reached, fef,' And who hasn't heard his virtues preached— r That Man of Ross who guarded the poor; A Guardian he whose fame shall endure • - (The fame of others is not so sure.) . 0, its nice at Ross to rest your head, t e 4 , (While the lordly Wye 4-eee• Goes grandly by,) 4 - '‘ • --, But it it isn't to pay six shillings for a bed. (N.B —llhen you roam Away from home, You cannot always do as you would, And one must bleed' for his country's good.) But he, ho! our friend tome—one, two three; There's that other old chum and his wife, you see; And H. tee, all from the town of B. They are here to time, Like a well-turned rhyme; And we take ourselves at once to the water, With better luck than Lord Ullin's daughter. What a day we had ! To say we ever° glad Is scarcely In It' ; not so much gladness, - As what Shelley Would call harmonious madness.' You're all afloat Ina well-trimmed boat.; You go with the s ream at a lively speed; ' Each reach of the river, Gives life to the liver'— Take it as you will—it is charming indeed. That is Goodrich Castle, there on the right, Embosomed in trees: it's a pretty sight. Twee here that Wordsworth, so it is said, Had his famous chat with that 'little maid,' Who, counting the family (two though in heaven), Still stuck to her number—' Nay, we are seven.' Away we go till we reach Joy's Green— As pretty a view as ever was seen, Though it's only fair As to scenes so ra,re To sae, 'green' is a ' joy' to us everywhere. Coldwell Rocks, for instance, at Symond's Yat, Seven Sisters, the gorgeous gorge, and all that— They are all of them green, and the boatman sly He looks to see if there's green in yohr eye. But let us wish luck to his strong right arm: He has beached us at Monmouth free from harm. For twenty miles, and a mile or two more, He has steadily bent his back to the oar, And that's a task when a man's threescore. But his work is done, His supper is won, ' Arfd egad! he's as fresh as when he begun. We find Monmouth fusty, It smacks of the musty; It is ancient enough, but decidedly rusty, So we on to Redbrook which isn't so dusty.' We put up for the night at the sign of the Bell, And are ta'en in and done for—uncommonly well. Still down the Wye, with .a lift by rail (Great Western is never known to fail, And here 'tis rush through one mass of greenery— 'What a line it is for deliehtful scenery!) We foot it the greater part of the day, And are tempted to stop every mile of the way e For the latest scene seems always the best, And a good excuse is good for a rest. Ah ! there is Tintern—a noble pile, 'With broken column and grass-grown aisle ; A ruin, and yet who fails to trace That its form is that of beauty and grace? A ruin lifting itself in air— Aspiration embodied—a perfect prayer. The architect planned At God's command. He had a dream which was not his own; lie awoke and found that his dream had grown Into Tintern Abbey—a dream in stone. But on and on, for we musn't miss The Windcliff view, since it is for this, If not this alone, that we climb and climb— The path is toilsome to the sublime. Now we're on the cliff of a thousand feet— Is that where the Wye and the Severn meet? Are those the three counties' we see—' over there; And is this the landscape so rich and rare ? ' What is it we see? Are these visions about ? ' Have the cliffs tumbled in, and the heavens' fallen ou"' ' • Sad case' you bet, After all this sweat ; We are on the Windcliff, and it's awfully wet; We have climbed the Windcliff amid mist and rake: It is plain as can be, • There is nothing to see And there's nothing to do but climb down again. ' Well, the rain you must know, Had ceased at Chepstow; So we got a peep, At castle and keep. ' Then by rail to Cardiff for supper and sleep. The morn breaks bright ; we are off to 'Combo; Good weather, good boat, and a good cleat of room - How the laughing waters merrily Play— They, too, are having a holiday; There is music and song As we dance along; There isleliff upon cliff and bay after bay.. Oh there's nothing Else sailing With hear unfailing— But what's this? Bless us! The ladies are ailing ! Alas, all is o'er, And so, say no more; There is no 'bought now but of getting ashore. You've not been to Ilfracombe? Why, then go; It is one of the bonniest spots I know. It is by th sea, yet among the hills : There are cliffs and bays, and valleys and rills, You cannot go wrong for a walk or drive, For flowers of all kinds live and thrive; And by day and night the place is alive.* But then understand, Though it really is grand, There is not such a thing as a yard of sand ; So have it in mind, when you this way roam, It is better to leave thq young uns ' at borne. Need I tell you of walks by The Tors to Lee, A nest in a tiny vale by the sea ? Of Morthoe, Watermouth, Lenton, too ? All these are places you ought to do; But finest, or anyhow quaintest of all, Clovelly will held your heart in thrall. A two-hours' sail and it greets your eye ; A village perched between sea and sky ; One in-and-ou, street on the face of a crag ; A most higgeldy-piggledy, double zigzag; Each house like a roy-box, and yet weather-proof, With creepers and flowers right on to the roof; There stands Clovelly—' all of a rook '— A queer little place in a queer little nook. We roamed, through the Hobby Drive whilst eve there, And seldom have seen a scene so fair. Headlands and glens and ferns and trees ; A brilliant sun and a:kindly breeze ; A babble of brooks and a ripple of talk, All went to make it a wonderful walk, WhEst ever before us gleaming lay The glorious sweep of Bideford Bay. Here let ins finish, for further addition Would be in the nature of repetition; And so, my friend, good-bye for the present, And may every holiday be as pleasant.

Leo XIII. entered the basilica at half-past nine, •tand on his appearance irrepressible cheers broke out, and rolled from end to end of the church. A REPORTER'S EXPERIENCE. The Whitehall Beans contains the followingYrela- ' tive to a Matter which has been made the sUbject 'of considerable comment and investigation on the Part of various newspapers A representative of this journal was commissioned to investigate the Mabject by personal interview with the parties,Who COuld speak from actual experience. From rthe results as given below•itanay well be claimed that the general adoption ot ,this remarkable anent will cause a revolution in certain quarters. "The 'first gentleman interviewed was 'Mr. William Howes, civil engineer,No. 68 Red -Lion-street, High Holborn, W.C. Mr. Howes stated that for over twenty years he ,had been constantly and eeverelyartlicted with rheumatism. At times his hands had been swollen to twice their natural size. Again. his jointsbecame so stiff and pain- ful that he could not walk, and his feet so sore that 'he could not bear his weight on them. He had at different , times tried physicians and many remedies which .hati been aecommended to him as-a.cure for his complaints,' but derived no benefit Whatever. An acquaintance, who had himself been cured.of a severe rheumatic trouble, gave him a bottle of St. Jacobs: Oil, which ho- applied once, with such unexpected and marked benefit that he procured another, which, to use his own language, settled the business, by removing-the pain which he had not been tree from for twenty years. Mr. Howes said that ha&iie not used St. Jacobs Oil he would now be in bed, instead of attending to his•business. Be added, 'lts effects were simply magical: ;It produced a com- plete cure. I will also add that numerious friends arnd acquaintances, suffering from rheumatic and neuralgic affections to whom I recommended the Oil, speak of it as wonderful. It seems to effect a cure in every case." "The name of Mr. C. H. Palmer, Secretary of the • Conservative Defence Association. and Overseer of the District of I.slingtort, having been 'mentioned to the • reporter, this gentleman's opinion was sought, and Cheerfully given in the following language; For a long time I have been a great sufferer from neuralgia in my lace and head, and rheumatism in my limbs. After , trying various ,remedies without obtaining relief, and having learned of the signal benefit which several ' • friends, who had been suffering from severe rheumatism, , derived from the Oil, I procured a bottle, the use of 1 Which completely removed every trace of,pain: It may 7be added that in its current number the Magazine of .Pharmacy, Chemietry, and Medicine devos considerable 'Space to a discussion of the extraordinary power of St. .Jacobs Oil, and cites some astonishingcuree• :It appears 'also that this remedy received no less than six gold Medals during the _past year at the International and Other expositions. Judging from the foregoing, St. Jacobs Oil will prove of incalculable value to the army of sufferers from such diseases as those enumerated, and the public will be indebted to the press for ,calling-attefl. tion-1.3 its efficacy."

LORD lIARTINGTON IN SCOTJAND.—On Wednesday Lord Partingtou, addressing a meeting in Inverness at which 'le received addresses from numerous Liberal Unionist Associationa in the north of Scotland, replied to Mr.. Gladstone. He asserted the right and intention of him- self and followers to sit 'behind the front Opposition ""ch, and repelled the insinuation that they had been gudlty of any treachery to Liberal principles. As to the 9.arge that there was no difference between Liberal . Monists and Conservatives, he said the change was not the Liberal Unionists, but in the Conservatives, who bad seen the necessity of abandoning some ancient pre- Judices and adapting themselves to the time. The ,country was, he added, a gainer by that alliance. He ..I'3serted that he had no right to break up Parliament and spbstitute Federal and Imperial government without con- Vdering the consequences to the three kingdoms. The Ldberal Unionists were returned, he said, pledged to Maintain inviolate legislative unity, and neither bland- ishments nor menaces would make them abandon their Pledges. He expressed surprise at Mr. Gladstone's alli- -..nee. with a party which had been in rebellion against .art lamentary institutions and had encoura'ged intimida- b,oycotting, outrage, resistance to the officers of the they and had only stopped short of insurrection becAnso wanted the Power to make It successful.

MUTILATION OF WOMEN IN LONDON. TWO MORE MURDERS. The Metropolis was on Sunday morning thrown into a state 61 renewed consternation by the announcement that The bodies of two more murdered women had been disoovered in the East End. This report unhappily proved too true, and the terrible`character of the crimes is intensified by the circumstances that the locality and manner in which the mutters were committed point 'very strongly to the concision that the same miscreant, who was responsible for at learn two of the previous murders, is also guilty of the present crimes. It Will be remembered that the 'first of the series of muniers was committed 90 far hack as last Christmas, when a awoman, whose identity was never discovered, was found murdered in or contiguous to the district known as Whitechapei There were circumstances of peculiar barbarity about the mode it which the body was treated. This fact did not attract so much attention at the timo as it did when, on the 7th of August last, a woman, named Martha Turner, aged 38, was found dead on the first-floor landing-of some model dwellings in Spitalfields, with 39 bayonet or dagger wounds on the body. On the 31st otthe same month , the woman -Nichols, an "unfotturtate;' 'was found dead ' in RuCkshroad, Whitechapel. With this probably begins' a series Of crimes which have latelyditerrified and terri-' fral the' public; for the mutilation of the body was done with somuch technical skill and 'audacity as to suggest a definite but extraordinary—ernd est that time unex- plained—purpose. What that object was the coroner recently suggested in the summing-up at the inqueet on the woman Chapman, who was 'murdered in the settle 'district, and under similar ojecumetances, on September Bth. That crime crested almost a panic which bad -scarcely died 'away when it became known on Sunday that two more murders of apparently the same kind had'been committed under ciretrinstances detailehere- under. MURDER TN 13ERR-STREET. 'The scene of the first ,of Sunday morning's outrages is a narrow court in Berner-street, a quiet thoroughfare -running from Comm-reed-road down to the 'London, Tilbury, and Southend Itailvrey. At the entrance to the • court are a pair of large wooden gates, in one of which is a small wicket for use When the gates are eloied. For it distance of 18 or 20 feet:from the street there is a dead wall on each side of the court, the effect of Which is to enshroud the intervening space in nbsolate darkness 'after sunset. At the tinieewhen the munder was com- mitted, the lights in all the dwelling-houses in the court had been extinguished. From the positionin which the body was found it is 'believed that the moment the mur- derer had got his victim 'in the dark shadow near the entrance to the court 'he "threw her to the ground, and with one gash severed "her throat from ear to ear. When discoveredothe' hely was lying as If the woman had fallen forward, her feet being about a couple of yards from the streetoand her heed in a gutter which runs down the right hand side of the court close to the wall. The condition (Irttite corpse and several other cir- cumstances whiclecatne to tight during the day prove pretty conclusivelythat no considerable period elapsed between the cammittelbf the murder and the discovery of the body. Inlachinis pretty generally conjectured that the assassin -was:disturbed while at his ghastly work, and made oft hefere he had completed his designs. All the features of the rase go to conneet the tragedy with that which Coale. place three quarters of an hour later a few streets dietant. The obvions Poverty of the woman, her totellaCk of jewelry or ornaments, and the soiled condition of her clothing 'are entirely op- posed to the'theory that. robbery could have been the 'motive, and the secrecy and des- patch with which the crime was effected were equally good evidence' that the murder was not the re= : 6ult of an ordinary street brawl. No one in the locality heard anything intim nature of a scream or a woman's cry of distress. 'news Diemshitz, ste ward of a work- men's club overlooking the court, -found the body. Without waiting to see whether the-woman was drunk or dead. Diemshitz-entered the clith by the side door higher up the 'court, and informed those in the room upstairs, where a concert was going -en, that somethine had happened in the yard. constables were quickly an the spot, and the gates at the entrance to the court having been ielosed, and a guard set, rrn all the exits of the club and the cettages, the superintendent of the dis- trict and. the divisional sureeons were sent for. In e few minutes r:Phillips was on the-scene of the miir&r, and a brief examination sufficed to show that life had been extinct some minutes. Careful note having been taken of the position of the body, was removed to the parish mortuary of St. George's-inahe-East, to await identification. The features are eharp and somewhat pinched, as though the woman had endured considerable privations. In-her right hand were tightly clasped some grapes, and in'her left' she held a "number of sweet- 'meats. Herienket and bodice were open towards the top, but in other respects the clothed were not disar- ranged. 'The linen was clean and in tolerably good repair, but aomeiarticles ,were missing. The out in the woman's throat, which was the cause of death, was evi- dently effected-with a yen- sharp instrument, and was made with onecrapid incision. 1110 weapon was appa- rently drawn across the throat rather obliquely from left t.o right, the gash being a cut three inches long, and nearly the Fame 'depth. Oh the arrival of the shperin- tendent from 'Leman-street, Police station, steps were taken to ascertain' whether the members of the club were in any way connected with the murder. The names and addresses of all the men present were taken, and a rigorous search Of persons and premises was instituted, much to the annoyance of the member-s. The residents in the court had to submit to a similar scrutiny. In neither ense, "however. wes any incriminating:evi- dence discovered. •1,-.rng before daybreak the usualle- quiet thoroughfare was the scene of great excitement. Several matters have. transpired which tend to fix pre- cisely the thee at, which the unfortunate woman was murdered. Morris Eagle, one of the members of the club, left, Iterner-etreet about twelve O'clock, and after taking his sweetheart. home, retnrited to the club at shout twenty minutes to one, with therintention of hav- ing supper. Ile walked up the yard and entered the club by the. gief., entrance, but neither saw nor heard anything to make. lint suspect foul plaT was going on. He !nicht have passed- the hotly in the darkness, but, the probability is that 'he would have stumbled over it if the murder had 'been committed before that time. Another member -of -the • club. a Russianenamed Joseph' Lave,,feeline operesseti by the smoke iruthe large room, went down into the court about twenty-minutes before the body was diseevered, and walked about in the Open, and for five minutes or•inore he strolled in the street, which was very quietiat the time, and returned to the concert-room without quieting encountered anything unusual. THE INQUEST. The inquest ma the hOdy of Elizabeth Stride was opened on Monday, lv Mr. 117.-ntre-Badt_ter, at the Vestry Hall, Cable-street, Commercial-road. William West weidlio lived at the International Work- ing Men's Institute and Club, Berner-street. ,at the side of which is a passage leadieg to the yard. 'Two large wooden gates protected the entrance to the' yard, and these were sometimes *pen at night. In the yard there are two or three small tenements:. The club 'was a Socialist, one., and persons of all nationdlities weri eligible. Witness wee at' the club on Saturday night 'from about 10 30 or I:l..whert me members WW2 discuss- bug. The bulk of themenabers left, the club by the front door before 12. Witness liwel at 2. William-stneet, Com- mercial-road, whitherthe went at 12 30. Before leaving he noticed that the gates were opened, but there was inething on the ground. Morris Eagle, travollitre••jeweller, and a member of the club, said he was at theiclub on Saturday, and left about '1145. He returned about, 1240, and as the fronedoor was-closed he went, in threneli the gatewayand side door. He saw nothing in the /hied, butethont tweney minutes later .a member announced t,130 discovery of thabody. Louis Diemshitz, steward ,of -the .club, deposed that tie returned to his home at. elle club -tit one o'clock, riding in a 'kind of barrow, drawn 'by • a pony. He drove through the gates of the yard when the pony allied -at something on the ground.. He 'felt it with his whip. handle And tried to move it, but failed, and jumped down at once. He struck aught. He then saw it was a woman. He called his wife. and .got a candle, And then saw blood. He sent for the police, and just before they arrived a man, when tie <lid .not know, took hold of the deceased's head arid howed et wound in the throat. Millie people in the club were searched before they left, and their mines and 'addresses taken. , In reply tothe Coroner, Inspector Reid said the body has not yet been identified. The Foremanot the jury: But we hays been told her name is Stride: how is that? The Coroner: Something is known .of her' she has been partially identified. Inspector Reid said he poula be prepared with further evidence to-morrow, milli the inquiry was accordingly adjourned. The inquest waa Asumed on Tuesday afternoon. The first witness called was P.C. Henry Lamb, who said that about one o'clock on Sunday moraine he was on duty in Commercial-road, when two men Caine to him. They were shouting "Come on there's been another murder." As they got to the corner of Berner- street they pointed Clown it. He ran down Bernec-street, followed by another constable, and went into the gate- way of 40, ilernenstreet, and saw something lying on the right hand side, close to the gate.'Be turned his light on, and found it was a woman, with her throat nut. He sent time other constable for a doctor, and a man to the station for the inspector. There were about 30 people in the yard when he arrived, He put his hand on the face, which was warm. The woman was lying on her left side, with the right arm across her breast. The clothes were not disturbed. Some of the blood was liquid, and seine congealed. Dr. Blackwell arrived about ten 'minutes after, and 'examined the body. The gatekewere closed while the exa tni It at jell was going on, and no person was allowed to enter or go out. He ex- amined the club premises, and also the hands of the people present, but found tin traces of blood. He then went into the yard, and examined the cottages and closets. All the cottegers were in bed. He had passed the Commercial-road end of Berner-street about six minutes before he weg called to the yard, bat noticed nothing suspicious,

Edward Spooner, a horsekeeeer, said that about 12 30 on Sunday morning, he was standing outside the Bee- hive public-house, at the corner of Christian-street, when the alarm was given. He went into the yard at Berner-street, and a man struck a light, and witness lifted up a woman's Aim which was quite warm. Blood was coming from the throat. He could not say if any- one left the yard. He thought it was about 12 35 when he arrived at the "yard. Witness was searched, and gave his name and address before he left the place. Mary Malcolm, Eagle-street, stated that she had seen the body in the mortuary, and recognised it as her sister's, Elizabeth Watts. She was satisfied it was het sister. She 'last saw her alive on Thursday last. She came to 'witness to ask for assistance. Witness gave her a shilling and a *ltch She did not know Where the deceased need, but thought it, was somewhere in the East 'End. The decease 3 was given to drink. Her age was 38. Her husband was alive, and his father was a wine And spirit merchant at Beth. The deceased left her headland about eight years ago. She had two children—a boy and a girl. Her hutehtmd left her because he caught her with a porter, and sent her home to her mother, who died five years ago. Witness believed that the deceased had been charged with drunkenness, and let off on , the ground of epileptic fits. The deceased had jived With a man who kept a coffee house at Poplar. He went to sea, and was wrecked at the Isle of St. Paul, edema `three years ago. Since then witness did not think the deceased had lived with anyone. Witness never. visited the deceased, whose nickname was "Long 'Liz." Witness had never heard the name of Stride before. Deceased used to eerie 'to witness every Saturday for two shillings which she itiowed her. Deceased did not come last Saturday. She used to meet witness at the corner of Chancery-lane. Witnss did not recognise the deceased at first, 'hut did so afterwards. Witness had a presentiment„thet the deceased had come to harm on Sunday learning. At 120 she was in bed, and woke up, and heard a noise like a fall; and also a sound as of kisses. Her husband 'also heard the noise. She was much depressed, end when she saw the papers went to the mortuary. Witness knew the decased by a mall made by eh 'adder's 'bite when they were Children. He did not think the deceased had ever broken any limb. Witness had a brother and sister, het they had not seen the deceased for years. The deceased had a hollow under one of her feet, caused by an accident about three years ago. 'Witness could not recognise any clothing worn by 'the deceased. The deceased once left a nakai baby outside her door. She believed the deceased after- wards took it to Bath, where it died. The Coroner advised the wit,nes to go'to the usual meeting place pn Saturday next, as there was some doubt as to thhileceased being her sister, and witness promised to do this. Dr. 'Blackwell, 'lOO, Commercial-roaa, -said he was eatiedam Sunday morning. at 1 10, to Beruer-street. fie detailed the injuries to the body, and stated that the post-mortem evidence would be given later.. The inquest was adjourned Mr. Wynne Batter resumed the inqUiry on Wednes- day afternoon in Whitechapel on :the body of the woman murdered in Berner-st.' and identified as Elizabeth Watts by one witness, though she was said by some persons to be Elizabeth Stride.—Elizabeth Tanner, Livingin Flower and Dean-st., said -she recognized de- ceased as "Long Liz." Last saw :her alive On Sent- ' dey afternoon:in the Queen's Head, Commercial-street. The deceased was a Swede.—Catherine Lane, living with the last:witness, also recognized the deceased as 4' Long Liz:" • Deceased told her on Saturday that she had quarrelledwith the man shehad left on Thursday.— Michael Kidney, Dorset-st., a waterside labourer, said the deceased was Elizabeth Stride. She was a Swede, ad lived with witness nearly :three years. Her hus- ' hand was a:ship's carpenter, and 'was drowned irethe Princess Alice disaster. He had not seen her since • the Tuesday before her death. Witness had never neg- lected her,lut had treated her as a wife.—Thomas Comm, a lad of 18, produced a knife about 12in. long, which he found on a doorstep of :No. 253, Whitechapel, twenty-four. .hours after the murder.—Police-constable Drage said that when the boy found the knife the blade and handle-were stained with blood.—Dr. Phillips gave the result of the post-mortem examination. , He said the nut in the throat was 6in, long, and severed the principal ' .arteries. The cause of death was loss of blood and , division of the windpipe.—The :inquiry was adjourned until Friday. a•• . . .

It is apparently established by Wednesday's evidenoe at the inquiry, on the Berner-st vicdm that the woman murdered is Elizabeth Stride, land that Mrs. Malcolm was mistaken in stating that the deceased was her sister. The clue afforded by the discovery of the blood- stainedlnife on a doorstep will be followed up, although it seems certain that the knife was not in the place an hour before it was picked up, and the object of the person who put it there is unknown. Michael Kidney will probably be examined 4gain respecting his pre- tended epecaaLinforrnation. MURDER J'N ALDGATE.

Shortly before two o'clock :on Sunday morning—or ; about three-quarters of an hour after the crime described above—it was discovered that a second woman had been horribly murdered and mutilated, this being in Mitre- square, Maple,' within the city boundaries, but on the corifines••of the now notorious district. P.C. Watkins,: of 'the•city police, was going round his beat, when, tarr- ing- his lantern upon the darkest corner of Mitre-street, he saw the ,bocly of a woman, apparently lifeless, in.*, pool of blood. The scene then dire elosed was a most IMrrible one: The woman, who CV71.9 -epparently about 40 years of age, was lying on her beek quite deed, :hitt-email the toddy was- still w ~rm. The !hroat was -cut half-way round, -revealing a dreadful wound; from which blood harbfilowed in great quantity, !! stainine the pavement for some,alistauce round. Following the plan !in • the'Whitechapel •murders, the, miscreant was not con- rent with merely-killing his vietim. The poor woman's clothes had been piffled up over her chest, the abdomen . . ripped completely open, and part of the intestines laid '. oniher•neck. -After careful notice had been taken of the position the- body when found, it was conveyed to the Citte:Mortuary in Golden-lane. Here a more ex- •tended examinatiart was made. 'The murdered woman , evidently • belonged to the "unfortunate" class. The : policeefound !upon the body a white pocket handkerchief, Preunt• hone-handled table knite,,a short • clay pipe, and • a red ecigarette ease with whiteemetal fittings. The . knife bore no traces of blood. When - the news-of - this additional murder became known.the4txcitement in the crowded district of Aldgate was 'intense. The scene of ths murder; Mitre-square: is an -enclosed place, the rear Of St. Kathrine's Free ChurcheLeadenhall-street. It has three entrances, the principal °mould the onlv one having a carriage way, being et' the southern end leading to iv:litre-street. Mitre- square ,coritains but, two dwelling-houses, in one of which. singularly enough. a 'ity pelioeman lives, whilst , the other-is-uninhabited. 'File other buildings, of'which there !are,only! three: are large wa.rehouses. in the south- east corner, -and, near to the ent ranee iirom Mitre-street. E is the baekyard of some premises, but,- the rulings are closely boarded. iit--was just under thesp that the woman was foundequite hidden from sight by Ihe shadow cast by the corner of the:a.djoinieg house. :The officer who found the 'body ,is • positive that it could, not have been' there more -than quarter of au hem- before he dis- covered it. :He 'is timed to "work hie beat," as it is called, its tten -to :fifteen minutes. and is spoken of by his Ismerior officer as a most trustworthy man; The 1 wounds do lint appear tel have been caused so skilfully and deliberatelyess.in • theeiase of the mu-der of Annie Chapman in !Haelurry-street. Five minutee, some of the doctors think, would have S m eed for the CCJrimletion • the murderer's work, .and he was then onakeed to leave the ground before .11 le! ret urn. of rite policeman on duty. The murderer probably nonid,,d much blood-staining on account of also -woman being out ier back at-the time of the outrage, and leaving the ,square by either of the courts he would he Able to .pas quiekly away through the many narrow thoteeigl witlieut exciting obser- vation. Not the slighfast scream or noise was heard. The effect of ire murder upon -Ike residents in the east of London is ext raord iniiry. All day crowds thronged the streets leading to me re-senare, discussing the crime; and the police Mille iieiehthierhoodof the square were fully occupied iii kecring back the excited and curious people.

In connection vita the Mitre 609.uare murdeK, the ,principal incident has been the positive identification of the woman by John. Kelly, with whom she had lived .f or seven years.
