div.head: EXTRAORDINA RY LETTEItS.
div.p: EXTRAORDINA RY LETTEItS.
On Thursday last the following letter, bearing the " RC" postmark, and directed iv. red ink, was sent to the Central News
.25th September, 1888..

Dear Bose,—l keep on hearing that the police giave caught me, but. they won't fix me just yet. I have laughed when they took so .elever..and talk about, being on the right track. That joke about Leather Apron gr.ve me real fits. lam down On--. and attan't nnit ripping them till Ido get. buckled. Grand work the last job was. I gave the lady no time to squeal. How eau thcy retch me now ? 1. love my work, and want to start agaits. Yon will soon bear of use with my funny little games. I saved some of the ;wooer red stun' in a ginger' beer bottle over this last job to write with, but it went thick, and can't use 4., Red ink is fit enough. I hope, ha! ha! The next job I do I shall 'clip the Mies' ears oft and send to • the police officers limit for folly, wouldn't. you? Keep this letter back till Tie shit inore work, then give It ant straight. My knife's so nice awl sharp I went to get it chance. Goon luck.—Yours truly. &ker.,: P. RierFit. Don't mind Inc 'giving the trado Fume. Wasn't good enough to post Lida before I got all the Ted ir.k off Illy hands, curse it No lack yet. They say I ant,* tioctir,r uow. Ha! ha! •
The whole of this extraordinary epistle is written in red ink in a free bad clerkly tlatni. It was of course treated to the work of a Pauti4.4 joker. but it is singular

to note that the latest murders nave been committen within a few days of the receipt of the letter, that apparently in the Case 1/f. his last victim the inurrer made an attempt to cot off the ears, and that he actually did mutilate the face in a Manner which he has never before attempted. The letter is now in the hands of the Scotland Yard authorities. The• Central News sacs: A postcard, bearing the stamp "London, E., Oct. 1," was received this mornina,addressea to filf! Central News office; the address and subject - 'matter being written in red, and undoubtedly by the same person from whom the sensational letter already published was received on Thursday last. Like the previous missive, this also has reference to the horrible tragedies in East Landon--forming, indeed, a sequel to the first leltter. It runs as follows:

"1 was not coding, dear old boss, when I gave you he tip. You'll hear about "Saucy Jaoky's work to- morrow. Double event this time. !Cumber 1 squealed a bit. Couldn't finish straight off. Had not time to get ears 'for police. Thanks for keeping last, letter back till got to work again.—JACK THE RIPPER."

LAThe card is smeared on both sides with blood, which has 'evidently been impressed thereon by the thumb or 'firmer of the writer, the corrugated surface of the skin being,plainly shown upon the back of the card. Some words are nearly obliterated by a bloody, smear. It is not necessarily assumed that this has been the work of the murderer; the idea that naturally occurs being that the whole thing is a practical joke. At the same time, the writing of the previous letter, immediately before , the commission of the murders of yesterday was so singular a coincidence that it does not seem unreasonable to suppose that pie cool, calculating villain who is responsible for the crimes has chosen to make the post a medium through whillk to convey to the Press his grimly diabolical humour.

div.head: POLICE UV/ELOPING ACTIVITY.
div.p: POLICE UV/ELOPING ACTIVITY.

Hitherto the murderer, assuming that there is but one, confined his operations to the metropoli- tan police district:; but by pursuing his career ' near the city. he has brought upon his track some 900 additional officers. Both the metropolitan and the city authorities have greatly augmented the force on duty, and there can be no doubt that augmentation was neces- sary. Since Sunday morning, a remarkakable change has come over the attitude of the police authorities; and information wlriob was hitherto denied is now cheerfully imparted. it would seem that both Sir Charles Warren and Colonel Fraser are bending to the conviction that the public is the best detective. Sir Charles Warren has ordered constables to the Cominercittl-street station from the T, A. and B divisions; while Colonel Fraser has drawn men from every available district in the city to that portion Of the area nearest Whiteehapel which is considered dangerous. The neighbourhood of Mitre- square, where the mutilated remains of the victim not yet identified were found, is respectable. There is only one occupied house in it, the tenant being Constable Pearce. The police have made an important discovery, throwing light on the direction in which the murderer made his escape. A portion of an apron was found in Goldston-street, and when the body of the woman found in Mitre-square was examined, it was found that she was weuing a portion of the salmi' apron. It is therefore inferred that the murderer :F..aped through Whitechapel. A man who passed through Church-lane, Aldgate, at 130 on Sunday morning, says he saw a man sitting on a doorstep, wiping his hands. The man, who is described as wearing a short. jacket and sailor's hat, tried•to conceal his face. At intervals several men have been arrested on sus- picion, but on Monday night all had been released, having given satisfactory accounts of themselves.

div.head: GOVERNMENT REWARD REFUSED,
div.p: GOVERNMENT REWARD REFUSED,

The feeling of indignation against the Rome Secretary for not offering a reward has immensely increased since the discovery of the last two murders, and the following Practical letter was forwarded to the Home Office : " Sir,—ln view of your refusing to offer a reward out of• Government funds for the discovery of the perpe- tr+r, or perpetrators, of the recent murders in the East End of London, I am instructed, on behalf of several readers of the Financial News, _

whose names and addresses I enclose, to forward you the accompanying cheque for £3OO, and to request you to offer ,that sum for this purpose in the name of the Government.—Awaiting the favour xv your reply, I have the honour to be, your obedient servant (signed), HARRY 'H. MARKS."

A letter was received on Mondly evening 'by the editor of the Financial Nava :—Mr. Matthews' secretar7. ac- knowledged the receipt of the letter containing a cheque for £3OO to be offered as a reward for the dis- covery of the recent murders. If Mr. Matthews had been of opinion that the offer of a reward in these cases would have been attended by any useful result he would himself have at mice made such an offer, but he is not of that opinion. Under these 'circumstances he returns the cheque. A member of the London Common Council had aiven notice of motion for their meeting, on Tuosday, that the Corporation should offer £250 reward for the detection of the murderer of the woman in Mitre-court. This has, howevr. been anticipated by the Lord Mayor, wholes on behalf of the Corporation issued an offer ot 2500 reward for the apprehension of the criminal. Another meeting of the Whitechapel Vigilance Com- mittee was held on Monday, when a resolution was passed that a further letter should be sent to the Homo . .
Secretary, insisting upon an affer of a large Government reward immediately. A letter was at once despatched. _ .

• _ ... Bills offering 2500 reward on behalf of 'the city authorities were widely circulated on Tuesday morning . Several arrests were made on Weemeedayin connection with the recent murders in London, but so far .there is nothing to justify the hope that the police .have, the i .culprit n their hands.

ANOTHER MUTILATION OF A BODY IN LONDON. At 320 p.m. on Tuesday, a carpenter, named Frederick Wildborn, while searching for timber on the foundation of the new police head-quarters, on the Thames Em- bankment, London, found in one of the newly-constrimted

- . cellars, a parcel wrapped in some kind of ,Cloth, anoi fightly, hound with cord. On being opened, thelrunk of a woman, much decomposed, minus the head, arms; and legs, was found, wrapped in an old black petticoat. Or Bond wag called, and he 'examined the trunk, which i, supposed to be that of a woman whose arms ,had 'beet ' found' in Pimlico and Lam4eth.
The Central News says the discovery was made 'by

man- in the employ of the builder who has secured tie contract for the erection of the new popfico'headquarterr upon the site of the abortive National 'Opera flous, speculation. The man had occasion to go into a vatilted cellar which was built, by the eontractor for thmOper, Rouse some years ago. Re ;was first startled by'llt horrible stench which filled the place, and Which cause,' him to look around to see whence it came. To hi horror, he saw a large mass of decomposed 'flesh, which. on.closer observation, proved to he the headless, legless. trunk of a female. The workman rushed into the open ail', -called loudly for assistance, and then hurried for 'al pdlicema,n, who arrived almost immediately. 'Word was At once sent to Scotland Yard. and Dr. 'Bond, divi- sional surgeon, and sever,' leading officials, were qUiCkly erythe sprit. The remains were conveyed on an etribulanco stretcher to the Millbank-siteet Mortuary, 'Westminster. after which the vault was very carefully searched. At , themortuary Dr. Bond made a cursory examination of the 'remains. He found that cords had been lightlr hound .round the body, apparently with the idea ,o' keeping.it together. when decomposition had -ftifly ,s 0 in; The trunk was wraepecl in a coarse kind of ,cloth. , which .has, of course, been carefully preserved, And which mac prove of the createst importance in the Oral of solving the mystory of this, the latest. and Ter- haps,notthe least, horrible., of the crimes of the metro, iL The site et the new pelieu, offices in course of erectim extends'from the Embankment right through to Can

non-row. 'Westminater. The contractor for the ewten- sive 'buildings are Messrs. 'Grover and Sons, builders, wnton ,iWorks. Islincton, voti:n are employing a hire, nuttber of hands on the work_ It seems that the mar who went into.the vault was induced to do so by hi, fellow-workmen, who bad been .annoyed by the steriel, arising from it, and the MLIRC of which it wa, intended to ,remOvr. if prssible. The vault i- on the Cannon-row side of the hoilding„ and the trunl: was lying on its hack in the basement. It rested upon , what loGiked like a piece of black linen, which, however. has since been proved to he cloth. There was not a scrap of •clothing ,an tip trunk, and it was tied with ropes lengthways and crossways, 'lust as one would tie , up a nareel. The,vault is shout alft. by 30ft. in sire. and 12ft. or llft. deep, and it is rnearly covered over with loose planks, .the ground showing only a small space at each' end of the place. The trunk mug* have been carried either from the Embankment, or from 'Cannon-roW. -certainly could not have been throort, over to where it -larcrom either roadway. Its genera, appearance, hvieed, 'indicated rather that it had been carefully planed where t was subsequently found. 11 is simply astounding that' any man could have carried such an 'offensive burden through the public street erfhout -attracting attention, arid it in still more extraordinary how it could have been taken into the vault, -withont diseovery. The route from tlannon-row to the vault is *1 difficult one. A. boarding, .ome 7ft. or Bft. would tlave to be climbed, and the _ _
ground is of a very broken .character. From Om Em- bankment side the hoardim, lo about the same iwight,

and to reach the vault one-,mnist actually pass thfo-ugh the building in course of erocrion, around which several nolicemen a reconsta ntly patrotti n 'lt is more reasonable To asquEnetliat the vault was gained from Can n ()worn w,,,and in that case it seems pretty .aertaist that more than .one person was concerned in the disposal of the ghastly parcel. One man probably clitaibed to the top .01 the hoarding. with the assistance of his accom- plice, from whom he tli9n received the parcel, dropped it on the inner side, and then let himself down after it. The other man pre- sumably kept swatch while his confederate dispowl of the remains. Row the men could have known of the existence of the vault is not clear, for streeaers are not admitted to the works except on business. Possibly the original intention was to place the remains n some out of the way corner in the works, and that they were only taken to the vault finer that obviously desiratrle place ,g concealment had bag aividentally diococerid,

Dr. Bond, divisional police surgeon, and Dr. Hibbert, his assistant, on Wednesday made an examination of the trunk of the woman. The arm found in the Thames was produced, and found to belong to the same trunk. Detectives continued the search in the vaults of the works on Wednesday for the missing- portions of the body. LIST OF THE EAST-END MURDERS. -

Six women babe now been murdered in the East-end under mysterious circumstances, five of them within a Period of eight weeks. The following are the dates of the crimes and names of the victims so far as known:- 1. Last Christmas week.—An unknown woman found murdered near Osborne and Wentworth-streets, White Zibapel. 2. August 7.—Martha. Turner, found stabbed in 39 places on a landing in model dwellings, known as George- yard Buildings, Commercial-street, Soitalfielos. 3. August 31.—Mrs. Nicholls, murdered and mutilated in Bucks-row. Whitechapel. 4. September 7.—Mrs. Chapman, murdered and muti- lated in Hanburv.street, Whitechapel. 6. September .30.—Elizaheth Stride, found with her throat cut in Berner-street, Whitechapel. ,
6. September 30.—Woman unknown murdered and mutilated in Mitre-square, Aldgate.

div.head: PARALLEL IN TEXAS.
div.p: A PARALLEL IN TEXAS.

Not a great many months ago a series of remarkably brutal murders of women occurred in Texas. The mat- ter caused great local excitement, but aroused less interest than would otherwise have been the case, be- cause the victims were chiefly negro women. The crimes were characterised by the same brutal methods as those of the Whitechapel mill-dirs. The theory has been suggested that.the perpetrator of the latter may be the Texas criminal, who was never discovered. The Atlanta Constitution, a leading Southern newspaper, thus puts the argument :—ln our recent annals of crime there has been no other man capable of committing such deeds. The mysterious crimes in Texas have ceased. They have just commenced in London. Is the man from Texas at the bottom of them all? If he is the monster or lunatic he may be expected to appear any- where. The fact that be is no longer at work in Texas argues his presence somewhere else. His peculiar work was executed in precisely the same manner as is now going on in London. Why should he not be there?

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The death is announced of Mr. W. Gifford Pa!grave, British Minister at Monte Video. . Lord Sackville died at his residence. Knole House, Seven Oaks, at 10 40 on Monday morning. Sixteen thousand men of the South Staffordshire and Carmock Chase coalfields on Saturday gave notice of a claim for an advance in wages.

The colliery owners in the Manchester district, who advance the price of coal on Monday, have decided to grant the miners an advance of 5- per cent. The men had asked for 10 per cent. Pheasant shooting commenced on Monday, under dis- advantageous circumstances so far as the Northern dis- tricts were concerned, but in the Midlands and the South finer weather is reported to have prevailed, and some good bags were made, the birds being numerous and in excellent condition. Ovaawona ON RAILWAYS.—The Board of Trade is seeking returns 'from the home railway companies as to the periods servants working the traffic are kept con- tinuously on duty: It is believed that the Government intend introducing a measure next session dealing with the question of overwork on railways.

SENSATIONAL ELOPEMENT FROM BOLTON. —The dis- appearance of a well-known Bolton estate agent and accountant, along with a young and pretty barmaid, is causing much comment in that town. The gentleman's name is Peter Budge. and he had a most extensive estate agency business; keeping a couple of horses and traps. The girl is the daughter of a Stonecloug,h farmer, and was engaged at one of the principal hotels in the town.

. _ - THE DEFAULTING TOWN CLERK OF SALFORD.—WARRANT Issum—The public examination of John Graves, late Town Clerk of Salford, should have taken place at the District County Court, on Monday. The Official Receiver in Bankruptcy was present, by. Graves did not put in an ap- pearance. The Official Receiver thereupon applied for a warrant to issue for his arrest, and the Registrar acceded to the application. It is stated that the defalcations amount to a very large sum. THE SALT SYNDICATE.—THe promoters of the Cheshire Salt Syndicate definitely announced on Monday that they had been successful in securing the extensive works of the Droitwich Salt Company. It was only after much difficulty that an arrangement was come to. The "corner" in salt is now practically complete, for the syndicate have secured the Irish salt mines in county Antrim, the Middlesbrough saltworks, the Fleetwood saltworks, and every manufactory in Cheshire. As a consequence of the early prospect of a considerable rise in the price of salt, the shares of salt companies had jumped up 50 per cent., but the reaction will be speedy.

TERRIBLE BOILER EXPLOSION: FOUR. MEN KILLED. On Saturday morning, one of four large boilers, 30? t. by sft, at the flour mills of Messrs. Watson, Todd, and Watson, Vincent-street, Birmingham, exploded, and be- sides doing very great. damage to property, killed three men and seriously injured four others, among whom was, Mr. Whitehouse, the cashier of the firm. The men killed were Thomas Harrison, a coal wheeler; David Middleton, a stoker; and Charles Jones, a boiler cleaner; and the first and last were married men with large families. The circumstances of Mr. Whitehouse's in- juries were peculiar. He was in the loading room which faces the boiler house on the opposite side of an men square. The shock of the explosion was so violent as to blow in the front of the loading room, and the broken glass and debris falling on the cashier cut one of his ears off, and he further sustained several scalp and other wounds, and was besides badly scalded all over his lacicly by the escaping steam. His condition left little hope of his recover, and he succumbed late on Sunday, An engine driver named Rowley was very badly scalded, and two other men were seriously injured by portions of the falling brickwork.' The boiler was inspected last week by an officer of a Manchester company in which it was insured, and it is said was being worked under the nominal pressure. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE : A PNINPUL STORY.—A story was told ,by a young Italian lady at the Liver pool Police Court on Tuesday well calculated to excite sympathy and sorrow. Elvira Petit°, who had been brought up on the charge of, httempting to commit suicide by taking vermin poison. stated, -through an in- terpreter, that she had been a pupil at the College of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, in Padua. After leaving this in- stitution she went to complete her education in Venice, where she becamai acquainted with a young Italian gentleman. Friendship ripened into love, and ultimately she was induced to leave school and take a position in the house of a titled lady. Subsequently she went to live with her lover, and a child was horn. The infant was -taken from her almost immediatekt by the father and placed at nurse. From then until now she had nevet seen it. She afterwards bebame a waitress at a café in tVenice, and while there her lover left for England and came directly to 'Liverpool, where he stayed for some ,time in order to learn the language and gain some -,knowledge of business. He wrote continuaily to her, and ultimately induced her to come to him at Liverpool, .but the treatment she received here was very different 'to what she expected, and she became so tired of her life that she took the poison. The magistrate gave the ac- • cused up to Mr. W. G. Clrossi, who acted as interpreter, on the condition that he would communicate with the Italian Consul, who would send her to the home for ,distressed Italians in London. . .

IMPENDING STRIKE IN THE COAL TEADE.—The crisis in the coal trade is every day becoming more acute, and a strike on an extensive scale would seem to be inevit- able. A conference of the Yorkshire miners' delegates was held on Thursday at Barnsley, at which it was strongly urged by Mr. B Pickard, M.P., and others, that the improved state of the coal trade justified the men in their demand. A resolution was passed to the effect that the men should give in their notices next week if the owners still refused to give the advance of 10 .per cent, in wages, and 40,000 notices were dis- tributed at the close of the conference.

THE CHURCH CONGRESS.—SpeciaI sermons were preached in Manchester Cathedral, St. Anne's Church, ,and Sacred Trinity Church, Salford, on Mon- day, in connection with the Church Congress, which -commenced its sittings in Manchester on Tuesday. The Church Army held a convention in the Gentlemen's Concert Hall, on Monday afternoon, under the presidency of the Bishop of Sodor and Man. Arch- deacon Farrar was also one of the speakers. A collec- tion during the meeting realized several hundreds of pounds in cash and promises. The Bishop of Manches- ter presided at the inaugural meeting of the Church Congress at Manchester on Tuesday, and delivered an address on the necessity for the existence of the Con- gress. At the afternoon sectional meetings, discussions took place on the Welsh Church, the duty of the Church towards seamen, and parochial evangelising work. At the Town Hall the subject for discussion was "Gambling and betting "on which several papers were read. At the Concer:t Hall a paper was contributed by Mr. Balfour on "The inadequacy of Positivism .to meet the highest needs of man. He declared that a philosophy of belief had yet to be constructed, nor were the founda- tions of such a philosophy likely to be laid by Positivist thinkers. Mr. Balfour aisb spoke at a workingmen's meeting on "The needs Of human nature, and their i supply n Christianity." On Wednesday morning the general assembly at the Free Trade Hall was concerned with the subject of "Foreign Missions." The afternoon I subject was "Philosophic Doubts." The Concert Hall section had before it "The Disposal of the Dead" in the afternoon, and "Social Purity" in the evening. At the Town Hall the sectional subjects were " Temperance " aod "The Sunday School System." A large meeting for i , working men was held n the evening at the Free ' Trade Hall, to consider the hindrances to Church work sind progress. NOTES BY THE WAY. The annual meeting of the Lancashire County Rugby Union was held on Friday evening at the Grand Hotel, Manchester, Mr. Rodger Walker presiding, and the principal Lancashire clubs were represented, including Liverpool, Manchester, Broughton, Broughton Rangers, Swinton, Free Wanderers, Wigan, South-east Lanca- shire Union, Barrow, Warrington, Liverpool Old Boys, Tyldesley-, &c., The balance sheet ;showed there was only a balance-of LM, though they stared with £234. One hundred pounds had, however, been given to Man- chester and Liverpool charities, the turnover being £554.—A discussion on the appointment of referees was raised by Mr. Warren (Warrington), who suggested that the county should take up the appointment of referees, atid settle their fees ; and after some discussion it was resolved, an the motion of Mr. Payne, seconded by Mr. Warren, that the following rules on the ques- tion be agreed to That every club being a member of the Conn. y Club shall, prior to the Ist of September every year, submit to the secretary of the county the names of one or more persons up to three who are willing to act as referees in any match in which a club member of the County Club shall be engaged. The per- sons whose names are so submitted shall elect a court, such court to consist of four such persons and the secre- tary of the County Club, with power to add to their number. The Referee Committee shall send a referee to each match in which a club which is St member of the county is engaged on receiving 10 days' notice from any- body applying fer a referee to be supplied. The County Club shall have power to deal with all questions having reference to the body of referees thus appointed." The clubs to send representatives to form the Lancashire Committee were elected as follows; Swinton, Manches- ter, Broughton Rangers, Liverpool, Free Wanderers, West Lancashire Union, Rochdale Hornets, Oldham, land Salford. The only alteration from last year's Com- mittee is the substitution of West Lancashire for r Barrow. . .

Warrington first and " A" teams still preserve their record inviolate. The first team met Carlisle on their own ground on Saturday and inflieted,a very decisive defeat on the visitors from the border city. The game was a pleasant and open one, and the home players laid themselves out for steady and consistent passing. To this more than to anything else is to be attributed their fine score, for almost every, try was the result of a series ' of well-judged passes. It does not appear, however, as if the" wire-pullers " are going to be any more success- ful than formerly in the matter of place kicking, though Barnes has done well so far with the places entrusted to him. The football match between the Maoris and fifteen of Surrey at Richmond, on Wednesday, was won by the Maoris, who obtained one goal and one try to one try by their opponents. .

Six ioa' ls to one! Thus reads the score that Runcorn piled on against its rival Cheshire Organisation, Sale,on Saturday, and that the enthusiastics followers of the wearers of the green were delighted, goes without saving. • 'Crompton was the terror of the visitors and he deserves a paragraph to himself. Although only 17 years of age his work in the second team last winter justified the' Committee in transferring him to the first team in the absence of Harry Speakman, and a right worthy successor to that sterling player has he proved himself. He plays with cool judgment, and is a capital dodger, and his performaKe of Saturday creates a record in football annals. The Chemicals on Saturday simewhat compensated for their defeat by Cleckheaton by vanquishing the visi- tors from Oldham. Considering the state of the Oen:loas the play was very open and iweresting, and if the local team could be induced to act wi Ii more com- bination they would be hard o beat. There seemed to be a mania for dropping goals in Runcorn on Saturday. The list is as follows :—Cromp- ton for Runcorn Ist v. Sale, 5; Harvey, for Sale v. Runcorn, 1; Woods, for Runcorn.. 2nd v. Tuebrook, 1; Houghton, for Runcorn Recreation v. Prodsham,l ; Darlington, for Frodsham v. Runcorn Recreation, 1; total, 9.

PENKETH TOWNSHIP MEETING. On Tuesday evening the half-yearly meeting of ther ratepayers of the township of Penketh was held at the Perry Inn. Mr. Thorpe, one of the overseers. pre— sided, and there were also present—Mr. R. Board- man, Mr. J. Johnson, Messrs. J. C. Routledge and Forster, overseers; and Mr. Thomas 11. Wilson. assistant overseen—Financial : The Chairman said it appeared that at the commencement of the half-year there was a balance' in the bank of £lB4 16s. 2d. A rate of is. in the £ was laid, which was estimated to raiser £357; the amount actually collected was £337 3s. 2d.; empties, &c., £l6 7s. 4d. • and a, balance of £3 9s. 6d. outstanding, pending appals. The expenditure had been £4OO 10s. 9d.-; leaving a balance in the hands of the overseers of £122 16s. 3d. The calls this half-year were heavy, the Union call being £36 more, and the Rural Sanitary special £l7 moft than the pre- ceding six months. On the motion of Mr. Rout- . ledge, seconded by Mr. Boardman, tte accounts were passed.—The New 4zt e : Mr. Routledge moved, and Mr. Forster seconded that a rate of is. 2d. , for the halt-year be levied, and this was agreed to.— The Friends' Schools: A discussion took place with regard to the action of the Assessment Committee respecting the rating of the Friends' School. The Chair- man took very strong exception to the statement of the Chairman of that Committee that the overseers of Penketh must have been influenced by some "personal feeling" in increasing the assessment of those schools. He said the overseers were actuated by no such feeling, but were merely carrying out the instructions given them by the ratepayers at a township meeting in March, 1887. He thought it very strange that when Mr. Owen, the surveyor, recommended that the assessment of the school should be reduced, the Committee could readily accept his advice ; but when Mr. Owen told them what the law was on the point, and that the assessment would have to be increased, they could entirely ignore his advice. Mr. Da,rbyshire had said that if the over- seers were dissatisfied, they should take the matter to the Quarter Sessions. He (the Chairman) believed the overseers had no power to take the case to the Quarter Sessions. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Forster said the Chair- man's statement in that particular was correct. If it were taken to the Quarter Sessions it would have to be by a ratepayer, and not by the overseers. He (the speaker) challenged the Chairman of the 'Assessment Committee to find in tile whole of the Union another similar institution dealt with in the exceptional way in which these schools were. He thought it was a strange thing for Mr. Darbyshire to vacate the chair at one of the Assessment Committee's meetings, when the subject • was under discussion, dud then from the floor advocate his own cause. Most gentlemen, he (the speaker) thought, would have abstained from taking part in a matter in which they were personally interested. (Hear, hear.) As that was the first opportunity the overseers had had of publicly and officially commenting on the aspersion cast upon them by the Chairman of the Assess- ment Committee in stating that they were influenced in their official duties by personal feeling, he would move that their Chairman (Mr. Thorpe) write a letter to the Chairman of the Assessment Committee repudiating the aspersion cast on the overseers by him in his statement that they were actuated by personal feeling in their dealing with the Friends' School case, and enclose there- with a copy of the resolution passed at the township meeting in March, 1887--Mr. Johnson having seconded the resolution it was carried unanhnously.—The meet- then terminated.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- man Harrison, and Councillor John Pierpoint. DRUNKENNESS.—The following cases of drunkenness were disposed Of :—Mary Hanson, in Hill-st., on Saturday evening, fined ss. including costs; George Brown, in Church-st., on Saturday evening, fined ss. including costs ; Brian Flaherty and John Conroy, in Buttermarket- st., on Saturday evening, each sent to hard labour for seven days ; Thomas Gormon, in Winwick-st., on Satur- day, fined ss. and costs; John Coulson, in Church-st., on Saturday, fined ss. including costs; Michael Duffy, in Percival's fold, on Sunday, fined ss. and costs ; Alice Blagg, in Bridge-st.' on Sunday, fined ss. and costs; iffiam Astley, in Eldon-st., on the 22nd ult., fined 2s. 6d. including costs. FURIOUS Daiviso.—Richard Holcroft. butcher, Apple- ton, was fined 10s. and cetsts for furiously driving a horse an trap in Bridge-street, on the 25th ult. Mr. A. BrowAe appeared for the defence. . _

DISTIMBIN.C; THE PicacE.—For this offence Frederick Pridden, Lord Nelson-st., was bound over to be of good behaviour, and two young men, named Thomas Caine and John Molyneaux, for having been disorderly in Buttermarket-st. were similarly dealt with.

BAD LANGUAGE.—WiIIiam Patten, Appleton-st,. was fined ss. and eosts for having on the 22nd. ult., used bad language in Howley-fields. Scnoot Cum.—The following cases were brought under the Elementary Education Act, Mr. George Riley prosecuting on behalf of the School Attendance Com- mittee :—Thomas Strettle, file-cutter, Mersey-view. The defendant in this case produced a certificate from the late schoolmaster of St. James'. which purported that the lad had passed Standard IV. Mr. Riley said the certificate was incorrectly made out, as the boy had failed in both standards 111 and IV.; and in support of his contention he produced the examination schedules for the years 1886,4887. The parent having been satis- fied of the error, Mr. Riley did not press the case, which was accordingly adjourned for U month.—Henry Sher- ' wood, labourer, Tilley-st. The defendant's son was proved to be an incorrigible truant, and the Bench made an order for him to be sent to the training ship Clio.— 'Thomas Gavin, forgeman. Silver-square, fined 55.; Henry Heesom, 33 Brick-st., fined 55.; John Watson, tanner, Church-st., fined 55.; William Bate, wiredrawer, Manchester-lane, fined ss; James Whitfield, carter, york.st. fined ss; Thomas Pemberton, forgeman, Warburton-st.. fined 55.; William Flatteley, forgemao, Beswick-st. In the latter case Mr. Riley proved to tlie satisfaction of the Bench that the lad was beyond parental control; the boy being a Roman Catholic he was sent to Father Nugent's Industrial School, Liverpool. A warrant was ordered to issue for the apprehension of Michael Flynn, Refuge-square, who failed to appear; but its execution was suspended until the following day to see whether the defendant would answer to. his summons.
TUESDAY.—Before Coun. Francomb and Mr. E. J. Guest.

A TROUBLESOME BM—James Quinn, a boy whose parents live in Widnes, was brought up for sleeping in a bread van at Bridge-foot. He has several times before been charged with similar offences, but appears to be incorrigible. He was ordered to be taken to the Work- house.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley, Mr. John Fairclough,'and Mr. R. Garnett. JAMES QUINN AGAIN.—The lad Quinn who was dealt with on the previous day for sleeping out was again brought up. He was charged with stealing a pair of boots, and, as he pleaded guilty, he was sent to prisoa for fourteen days, to be followed by detention for five years in a reformatory. TRAVELLING WyrnouT TICKET.—John William Hough- ton, a young man from Barnsley, was fined 10s._ and costs for having journeyed from Liverpool to Warrington, on the Cheshire Lines railway, without having pur- chased a ticket. The alternative of payment was four- teen days' imprisonment. THLIRSDAY.—Before Major Litton. CAUTIONED.—Mary Healey was charged with having been drunk in St. James-st., Latchford, on the previous night. P.C. Monoglian said that her husband when he c,eipie home from work found prisoner drunk. She had a child two months old, and there was no food in the house for the five other children. In consideration of this, the magistrate discharged her with a caution. NRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison and Webster, and Dr. Gornall.

ALLEGED DESERTION—Henry Scroggins. a young man, was remanded on a charge of having deserted from her Majesty's ship Penelope. ALLEGED THEFT OF A SHAWL.—Mary McCean,a middle- aged woman, was charged with having stolen a shawl value Bs. 6d., from the shop of Thomas Greaves, the Tower, Bridge-street. She Was dismissed with a caution.l xtog AN UNHAPPY MARRI§GE.—Thomas Waldren was sum- moned by his wife, Mary Waldren, who charged him with having deserted her on the 18th August. Mr Browne appeared for the defence. The complainant said that she had been married to the defendant five years. A fewmonths after marriage he seemed to get tired of her, and had since been very unkind. An arrangement was come to by which defendant agreed to pay his wife ss. a week. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE.—Michael Flynn, forgeman, Refuge-square, was summoned for not sending his child Matthew regularly to school. It was his tenth appearance for this offence. The magistrates made an order for the boy to be sent to Father Nugent's School at Liverpool. OVERCROWDING.—Catherine Mortnn was summoned for taking lodgers without having her house registered. On the 30th ult Inspector Powell visited the defendant's blouse, and found sleeping there eight persons in one foom, and four in another. Seven of the persons were lodgers, and the house, which was very dirty, was only adapted for five persons. The case was adjourned until Monday on defendant promising to get rid of her lodgers.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY, SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. F. Gooch, and Mr. Ziba Armitage. DRUNICENNESS.—For this offenc,e at Burtonwood on the 28th September, Patrick Garvin, farm labourer was fined ss. and costs.--Jno. Woodhouse, puddler, for hav- ing been drunk and disorderly at Sankey Bridges on the 29th September, was fined a similar sum.—Thomas Lanigan, for having been drunk and incapable, at Penketh, on the 23rd September, was fined ss. and costs. DISORDERLY CONDUCT ON THE HlGHWAT.—Margaret Woodhouse and Mary Cooney were each bound over in a SIM of £5 to keep the peace fof three months.

QUARRELSOME NAVVIES.—Thomas Jones and George Astall, navvies, were summoned for having disturbed the peace by fighting at Rixton on the 15th Septem- ber, and were each ordered to find a surety of £5 for their good behaviour during the next three months. CARTERS FINED.—For haying been asleep in their carts on the highway the following were fined :—John Davies, at Sankey on the 27th September, 25.. 6d. and costs ; James Joyce, at Sankey. on the 29th September, 2s. 6d. and costs; Thomas Hankinson, at Woolston, on the 22nd September, ss. and costs; Jno. Lythgoe, at Poulton on the 21st September, ss. and costs. No NAME ON CART.—James Sexton, grocer Winwick- road, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing one of his carts to be used, without having his name on it, PROTECTING A WIFE.--James Ashton, a platelayer, Rixton was summoned for having assaulted Margaret Jones al Rixon on the 30th September.—The evidence showed that defendant struck Jones a slight blow, because the latter had insulted his wife.—A fine of ss. and costs was inflicted.

SATURDAY. OCTOBER 6. 1888.

LOCAL Administration in the United States and in the United Kingdom is the title of a 13amphlet published by the Cobden Club which has an especial value, at the present time, when we are about to enter upon a new phase of local self- fgovernment. The writer is MR. F. C. MONTAGUE, !1/42d he has brought together a mass of informs,. on which enables the reader to realise, in some degree, the faults alike of the American system and,of our own. In a great country such as the LTnitPd States, and with the large powers which 'Vlong to each State, the forms of administration are numerous. But they resolve themselves Practically into three—the township system, the . ee'lln.„ity system, and a compromise system, which, as me name suggests, has something of the fea- tures of the other two. With regard to State government, MR. MONTAGUE remarks :—"A State of the American Union is in theory, and to some in fact, what its name indicates, a complete ty politic. The States' made the Union, and '1 State retains every attribute of sovereignity it those which have been expressly delega- 4. That is somethinglike ' Il'ovision. Would it not be better, by-the-by, if 4:ll)rae of the land which has been " nobbled " by ‘4le Church in this country were applied td the Zdowment of education ? THE Wurrington Town Council, speaking of it as a whole, is evidently not katisfied with the way in which Mr. DINWIDDIE is being discharged from the post of manager of the Longford Works; and we cannot think the ratepayers will be satisfied when they read the report of the discussion on the subject. It may be that Mr. Dzifwinras is not the best man that can be had for the post, and it may be, too, that he has not spent as much time at the works as the Sanitary Committee had a right to expect. We express no opinion upon these points, because they are as yet matters in dispute ; but it is just because they are in dispute that the voting on the question is unsatisfactory. It is true that the resolution was carried which discharges the manager as a servant of the Cor- poration; but there was undoubtedly great mis- giving on the subject, for seven only out of the score of members present voted against the amendment by Councillor MONKS, which proposed to defer the confirmation of the minute of dis- missal. It is true too, thatfive only voted for the amendment, and we are therefore confronted with the extraordinary fact that no less than, eight members voted neither one way nor the other, when the amendment was submitted to the meeting. To say that it is unsatisfatory is there- fore the least that can be said. It cannot be agreeable either to Alderman BURGESS; as Chair- man of the Sanitary Committee, or to Mr. DIN- WIDDIE ; but it shows either that half of the members who attended the meeting on Tuesday have not the courage of their convictions, or that they were not in a position to,have a conviction on the question at issue. We accept the latter hypothesis, but, unfortunately this leads us to the conclusion that the matter was one which required further inquiry and further discussion. And if it did, how isit we are not to have it? The amend- ment by Councillor Monks pointed in that direc- tion; and it is due to that gentleman, and to those who supported him, to point out that they studiously avoided saying anything that would make it difficuleof acceptance on the part of the Sanitary Committee. To judge from the discussion, it would appear as if the amendment was regarded ' as suited to the occasion. Councillor William Tinsley, who was amongst those who did not vote, suggested that Mr. Dinwiddie had not had justice done to him; and he asked—" Had he been allowed to go before his committee, or had the statements against him been made behind his back ?" This question—a most important one— was not,so far as we are aware,accorded an answer. Aldefman Harrison was amongst those who, at the previous meeting of the Council, had, as he confessed, voted in favour of Mr. Dinwiddie being asked to send in his resignation ; but, he said, " there were several things that wanted clearing up; The Council, he justly urged, ought to have more light upon statements, made by Mr. Din- widdie, which " very seriously conflicted with the statements made by Alderman Burgess." He there- fore hoped Alderman Burgess would adopt the suggestion which had been thrown out, and with- draw the resolution on the dismissal of Mr. Dinwiddie. It was a matter of course, after this, to expect that Alderman Harrison would vote for the amendment. But he did not ; nor did he, like some others, remain neutral. He executed that most difficult of all circus tricks ; he per- formed a double somersault by voting against the amendment. We believe Alderman HARRI- SON represented the opinion of the majority of the Council when he said there were several things that wanted clearing up; and, that being the case, he should have voted for an amendment which would have afforded an opportunity for the clearing up. It is suggestive that, while, as Alder- man BURGESS remarked, the Council at its pre- vious meeting passed a resolution on the subject "nearly unanimously," the Council, on Tuesday, was so far from unanimity that the highest vote was seven whilst the neutrals were eight. Look- part)

ing at the matter all round, it seems to us that Alderman BURGESS would have done well to consent to the question of dismissal being further deferred. He believes he has a solid case ; the statemehts he iinalies are certainly of a startling character; arid if they are correct Mr. DINWIDDIE ought to go. But are they correct? Or are they among the several things that want clearing up? That is what the ratepayers want to know, and that is what they have a right to know, before such an extreme step is taken as the dismissal of the head of an important department of the Corporate service. "Strike but heas " : and, again—" Let justice be done, though the heavens fall."

THE Commissioners of Newton would seem to be altogether too slow for 'the people they represent. They have been too slow at any rate in deciding whether they would accept the Jubilee offer of the Lord of the 'Manor of ten acres for a Public Park, or a plbt of land for a Public Hall in Tlliamson- Square, Earlestown, and MO towards the cost of its erection. It is not considered quite the thing to look £k gift horse in the mouth, but when one or two animals is offered, thero is some excuse for taking reasonable time to look their points over. But what is reasonable time? "There's the rub." The Commissioners have had the matter under consideration days, and weeks, and months. More than a year has, in fact, elapsed since the offer was first mule, and there are some who think that, if the Commissioners are left to themselves, the next Jubilee will be round before anything is done. But public opinion is stirring them up. Public opinion was at work ia the Earlestown Co- operative Hall, on Wednesday evening, and the result was an emphatic declaration that the Commissioners have been guilty of unaccountable delay ; that they have thereby treated Mr. LEGH badly; and that of the two things offered a Public Hall is much to be preferred to a Public Park. Mr. G. RATCLIFFE, one of the Commissioners, pleaded that he and his colleagues were about to call a meeting of ratepayers; but his observa- tions would have been "more germane to the matter if he had set about explaining why a meeting had not been called long ago. Of course if the action, or rather want of action, of the Commissioners is inexplicable to himself as to others, he must be excused for not explaining that which is not explainable. It is due to those who I spoke at the meeting to say that, while urging the desirability of buitiing a Public Hall, they are not particularly hopeful that it will be a profitable undertaking. But it is not suggested that a Park will be profitable, except in the way in which it I may contribute to the health and enjoyment of the inhabitants; and the question really is do the people of the district feel the need of a Park? They say they do not. There are as yet no densely crowded centres of population, nor are there likely to be for many years, whilst there is no denying that they are surrounded by park-like lands to which they have access. They do not feel they need a Public Park, but they feel the need of a Public: Hall; and when they are offered a site for one, and £5OO towards its erection, it cannot surely be a matter of surprise that they are ready to jump at the
"TOUCH AND GO." • Who could have thought it? Lord Hartington is to be welcomed, on his visit to Belfast, by the Orangemen of Ulster. Happy Hartington !

Another Liberal Unionist Secretary has come over to genuine Liberalism. This time it is Mr. Woodings, private secretary to Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, who has become converted. It is to be hoped Mr. Chamberlain likes it.

"The beautiful snow," is all very well in its place, but when it covers sheaves of corn it is rather out of season. "Like rosebuds filled with snow" has always been regarded as a far-fetched comparison, but is literally realised for once.

The Salt Syndicate has completed the ring • and it is not unlikely that the price of salt will be increased In consequence. But there is no need for alarm; it will not get behind ordinary reach; and it will not be taxed by the Government as it is in India.

A young lady of Detroit has just fallen a victim to tight-lacing. She was about to become a bride, and was dancing at a ball given in her honour when she suddenly cried out and fell to the ground. A blood vessel had burst, consequent, the doctor stated,upon exertion whilst tightly laced. Pitiful, and yet again pitiful.

Edward Banks, landlord of the Vine Inn, Widnes, was fined, on Thursday, for permitting drunkenness on the premises. The pohco are to be commended for taking action in such a case. There would be less drunkenneaS if the publican as well as the tippler was more frequently brought to book. The Magistrates expressed the opinion that Banks was not a fit person to keep a public- house, and yet, singular to say, they did not endorse his license.

"A Large Ratepayer" writes us on the question of the Mayoralty. but, as his letter reached us somewhat late, we hold it over until our next issue. He discusses, with a wide knowledge, the claims of Councillors Francomb, Platt, and Monks; and decides that the latter has the highest title to the post. Our Correspondent will see from our report that Councillor Monks, at a meeting held last evening, declined to allow his name to be brought forward; and that the present Mayor (Alderman Sutton) was unanimously invited to accept office for another year.

Some of our Tory contemporaries make a point of giving extracts from the Irish papers by way of showing what so-callerl "strong" language is used. But they need not go across St. George's Channel. Here are a few from the "Times" as applied to Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party :—" Nause- ous puerilities and transparent falsehoods," "mass of garbage," "whining poltroon," "subsidiary false statements," "colossal impudence," "grossest fabrications," "impudent, barefaced, and childish fabrications," "contemptible hypocrisy," and "gigantic impudence." Pretty good that for the orgax of "gentlemen."

The following "Impromptu at a theatre (by a victim of the prevailing fashion of feminine head- gear) " is from the pages of this week's "Punch" : This pile before me—l know not its nomen Hides all the actors, and half the flats. "The higher education of women," Applies not so much to their heads as their hats.

The following neat hit is from "A Church Con- gress Idyll" in the "Pall Mall Gazette." It is "suggested by Mr. Balfour's appearance amongst the Clerics" : A long, lank figure on the platform stands, And thumps the table with emphatic fist, • 'While cheery Churchmen clap their pious hands, • To tvelcome Balfour, the Evangelist. ' What though the cottar's home be made a wreck, Or Ireland echo with the peasant's groan? Go hang: a Bible round his blameless neck, For all the Bishops claim him as their own.

It is significant that some of the Tory papers are making a dead set against the Home Secretary. They blame him for laxity in police matters, and qicularly for not offering a reward as to the iiitechapel murders. But if Mr. Mathews is of opinion, as previous Home Secretaries aro said to have been, that the offer of large rewards leads to the manufacture rather than to the discovery of crime, why should he be blamed for acting as he believes for the best? Can it be that the Tories want to drive him out of the Cabinet to make room for Lord Randolph Churchill? It looks like it.

In the case of the child murder, at Haydock, the jury have not condemned the mother; their verdict is one of "death by drowning at the hands of some person or persons unknown." It seeing very extraordinary that two men should have taken the child from the woman and thrown it into the water; and on the other hand there is no reason to suppose that the mother wanted to get rid of her offspring—illegitimate though it was. It should be added that the police have not yet done with the case, which will be again before the magistrates to-day. At present it is another instance of murder and mystery.

Councillor Platt has importuned the Town Council of Warrington, on the question of the Intercepting Depots and their relation to the health and comfort of the inhabitants,until some- thing has come of it. The whole subject has to be gone into. Alderman Burgess thinks the character of the Committee is at stake ; and he shows that he is not afraid of carrying things to a logical issue when he says that "of all people in the world, it was not for the Sanitary Committee to commit a nuisance." He does not, of course, admit that there is a nuisance. That will be the point of the inquiry.

"A correspontlent whose letter appeared in Tuesday's 'Manchester Guardian,' calls attention to a curious fate which has befallen the monument erected in Every-st. burial ground to the memory of th/e hero of Peterloo. It has been taken down and sold as old stone. The monument, which was in the form of an obelisk about thirty feet high, was erected in 1842. The foundation stone was laid by Mr. Feargus O'Connor, M.P., in presence of about 15,000 people." Manchester Liberals cannot surely have been aware of what has been done, or they would not have suffered this dis- credit to the memory of brave Henry Hunt. ,

DAM AGM-N -C) TELEGRAEII WIREs.fAt Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, a boy named John Lee was summoned for having done damage to a telegraph wire at Bold, on the 17th of last month. From the evidence it appeared that a policeman saw the defendant thiowing stones at the telegraph wires. It was stated that considerable dainage was done to insulators between- Warrington and Bold, and last month men had in consequence to re-insu- late that portion of the lines. The magistrates ordered the defendant to pay a fine of 7s. 6d., with costs amounting to 12s. THE VOLUNTEERS.—Orders have been issued from the War Office for the whole of the rifles, and car- bines with bayonets, in the possession of tile Volunteers of St. Helens, Warrington. and other placeS, to be sent into the Royal Small Anne Factory at Birmingham, for the periodical examina- tion, repair, and browning and rebrowning. The entire armament is not tO be forwarded simultane- ously,but the commanding officers will be informed by the superintendent of the factory of the dates at which the weapons will be required. The arms of each corps are expected to be retained for about a month only, so as to interfere as little as possible with the drills, which are t.stimed in November for the Volunteer year opening on the Ist prox.

div.head: CRIMES OF VIOLENCE AT WIDNES.
div.p: CRIMES OF VIOLENCE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court on Monday, George Hunt, of 81 Church-st., was charged with causing grevious • bodily -harm to a man flamed Walter Davies by kicking him in the side., Dr. - Hutchinson said Davies had sustained serious injuries to the side of the chest, and was suffering from • pleurisy, of the left lung, consequent • upon these injuries. ' One of his ribs was also displaced. The man was pot in imminent danger but suffered severe pain. —Mr. Knowles appeared for the prisoner and alleged that the nien,had had a fight in a house of ill repute. He was prepared to !admit a common assault and take a verdict.—The prisoner was remanded for a week but was admitted to bail himself in £2O and two sureties of .£lO each.—Thomas Gibson, of 13 Peel-st., was charged with causing grevious bodily harm to an oil woman named Margaret Howard, of 15, Peel- at. The prosecutrix, whose face was almost hidden by plaster, stated that at the request of a woman named Roach she went into a house of a neighbour named Lancaster. "After a bit "the prisoner struck her oiethe face with something sharp, and she cried " Oh, my eye is out." The prisoner denied that he had anything in his hand, and said lie was likely to strike. her when she walked into his parlour, knocked the table over and smashed three shilling- worth of mugs and other things.—The prosecutrix denied this and prisoner was remanded for a week.

div.head: CONVERSAZIONE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: CONVERSAZIONE AT RUNCORN.

In connection with Bethesda Congregational Sun- day Schdol a Conversazione was held in the Lecture Hall, on Tuesday evening. Proceedings commenced in the early evening with a tea, and afterwards there was provided much to instruct and amuse the numerous visitors that filled the room. The pleasure of the audience was enhanced by a musical enter- tainment. The programme opened with a piano- forte duet entitled "Waves of the ocean," by Miss E. Littler and Miss Callister, who displayed brilliant execution. "Gates of the West" was sweetly sung by Miss Howard, who was also associated with Miss Hampson in the pleasing duet "Home to our mountains." For his rendering of " Simon the Cellarer " Mr. Clegg was encored, and responded with a humourous speech on Africa. "The broken pitcher" was capitally rendered -by Miss Ains- worth. The song "Doll's Revenge" was rendered in a pleasing manner by Miss Hampson. Miss Jones executed a pianoforte solo in finished style. and Mr. Horace Handley extracted sweet music from a peal of bell tubes, lent by Messrs. Lewis, of Ranelagh-st., Liverpool. A quartett by Messrs. Pilgrim, Edwards, Pennington and Fox, concluded the programme. Miss F. Handley ably fulfilled the duties of accom- panist. 'The company separated about half-past ten, having spent an enjoyable evening.
WIDNES REVISION COURT.
WEDNESDAY.

Mr. J. T. Font revising barrister, opened a court at Widnes Police Station on Wednesday morning for the purpose of revising the voters lists for the townships of Widnes, Cronton and Ditton. Mr. H. B. Shores represented the Liberal party and Mr. W. B. Woodnorth appeared for the Conservatives.. Mr. Goff and Mr. Houghton, assistant overseers, were present to render assistance. ADVICE TO A CARERTAKER.—Mr. William ThOMAS, of 20 Widnes-road, was objected to by the Liberals. Mr. Thomas was formerly caretaker at West Bank Board School and removed into his present dwelling on the 6th February, 1888. He had a vote for the school ; and was now objected to because there was a miss in the suc- cession —Mr Thomas asked if this was a valid objec- tion.—The Revising Barrister replied that it was. Every time he had removed during the qualifying year, 15th July to 15th July, he must make a declaration or claim or send a notice that he had removed so that the alteration might he made on the list, and thus carry his vote from one house to another. The taw required him to make a declaration.—Vote disallowed,

IMPORTANT TO POLICEMEN. —P. C. Almond, of 29, Birchfield road, entered the box and said he had been objected, to by the Radical party from having a vote. (Laughter.) It was proved by Mr. Shores that the applicant had occupied three dwellings during the qualifying period and that mention of one residence had been omitted from the list—The Barrister said if this was a mistake he would rectify it.— Mr. Goff said he knew that the constable had lived in two houses, but he wa.s not aware that he had occupied a third.—The Barrister said this was not a mistake, but an omission. He did not think be could call an omission a mistake
Mr. Shores: Clearly not, or else it is no use making an objection at all.—The Revising Barrister said the Con- stable in this case would have to come off.

THURSDAY. The revision was resumed on Thursday, at the• Public Offices. Mr. H. B. Shores (Widnes) again appeared on behalf of the Liberal and Nationalist parties, and Mr. W. B. Woodnorth represented the Conservatives. STATISTICS :—The business of the court included— Cronton : Owners' claims, 2; owners' objections, 2. Ditton : Owners' claims, 7 ; occupiers' claims, 10; owners' objections, 7; and occupiers' objections, 2. Widnes (North) : Owners' claims, 57 ; occupiers' claims, 138 ; reclaims, 3 ; county government claims, 3; objec- tions to register, 10. Widnes (South) : Owners' claims, 52 ; occupiers' claims, 221 ; and county electors (women), 28. Tne Liberals made 21 statutory declarations, every one being supported ; while the Conservatives made two, and were successful.

CLAIMS AMMNDETO f —Objection was taken by the Liberals to the name of Thomas Whittaker, Stanley Arms, Lugsdate-road, Widnes,' who claimed for a free- hold in respect of a house and shop in Ball-lane, Ditton. He now said that the property was leasehold, and Mr. Woodnorth asked the. revising barrister to amend. His Honour did so, though reluctantly, and the claim was allowed.—The Tories obfected to John Hicks, of 83, High-street, Wavertree, who made a claim in respect of. a freehold house and land, called Brook Farm, Smithy- Cmnton. It was shown that the claimant had a hatlNhare in the property, and Mr. Shore requested the revising barrister to amend, which was done, and the claim accordingly allowed. ,

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

FRUIT BANQUET AT WIDNES.-011 Tuesday evening a fruit banquet was held at the Wesleyan Chapel, Albert- road, Widnes, presided over by the Rev. T. Law. The choir sang selections of music at stated intervals, and the meeting was of an enjoyable character. Fruit was distributed during the evening, and everyone expressed their high appreciation of the manner in which the affair was carried out. The chapel, more especially near the rostrarn, was elaborately decorated with, fruit and flowers. _ _

SEDDEN DEATH AT RITNCORN.—Op Thursday, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquestat the Anchor Inn. in the body of John CotterilL a retired shoemaker, aged ' 64 years, who lived at 6, Rol:eft-street. It appeared that the deceased went into the coalvard of William Balcer on Wednesday for the purpose of watching the vehicles pass along Halton-road to Warrington. He complained of.spasms, and three-quarters of an hour later fell down dead. Dr. Mangan deposed that death, was the result of heart disease. Verdict accordingly. "Tae JoirN Bum," Boor, twelve months' wear gueran- terd. Usually sold at 13/6, our price, 10/6.—Uaynes', Horse- market-st., Warrington.—Adrt. ALLEGED ROBBERY AT RllNCORN.—Yesterday. before Major Ha.zlehurst and Mr. A. Thomas, Joseph Hoffland was charged with having stolen 15s. belonging to John Hoffland, of Norton. The prisoner had been staying at Norton a few days. Mrs. Hoffland being his aunt. On the night of the Ist inst: the money was safe in the , drawer of the sewing machine, and the pdsoner was alone in the room aVhen the other metnbers of he family had retired to rest. Next morning, after the pri- soner had left,the money was missed. The prisoner was remanded. ST. MARY' N PARISH CHURCH, WIDNES. —On Thursday evening the harvest festival was commenced at St. Mary's Parish Church, when the sacred edifice was , very tastefully decorated. The service was largely attended. The vicar reached an able and eloquent sermon appro- priate to the occasion. The prayers were intoned by the Vicar and the Curate (the Rev. John Connell, 8.A.), and Mr. I.N. Wharton read the ,lessons. Special harvest hymns and psalms were used. The offertory, which realised £2 19s. 3d., was devoted to the fund for the reslating of the roof. _ _

THE DRUNKARD'S DEATH AT RUNCORN.—At the Anchor

Inn, Brunswick-st., Mr. J. E. Worsley, the•coroner, held an inquest on the body of John Joseph Cunningham,' dock labourer, aged 34, who lived in Alcock-st. The deceased, it was stated, was a nun who drank very , heavily, and neglected his food.—Dr. Mangan said he had made a post mortem examination of the body.. The cause of death was syncope, accelerated by acute con- gestion of the liver and kidneys.. The stomach was inflamed, and contained a large amorint of alcoholic liquor, and the spleen was enlarged and congested. A verdict in accordance with the ,medical evidence was returned. • _

SIMMS-CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CIIAPEL,. WIDNES. —Harvest thanksgiving services were conducted in this chapel on Sunday, morning and evening, by Mr. R. F. Whiteside, of Liverpool. In the afternoon the Rev. C. Finch, of Runcorn, delivered an address to the scholap and friends. At each service the choir rendered appro- priate pieces of music, and collections were taken in aid of the funds of the chapel. On Monday evening a fruit ! banquet was held, and there was a capital audience. The musical part of the programme was ably sustained bV the Allerton Glee Union, and the proceedings were highly successful. Mr. Edward Warham occupied the chair. The building was very handsomely decorated with fruits and flowers, and, at the conclusion of the service, thke were distributed. INQUEST ,ON AN INFANT.—AR inquest was held at the Anchor Inn, Brunswick-street, on Thursday, touching he death of the infant son of Mr. Isaac Stubbs, mineral water manufacturer, Lowlands-road. The child was born on Monday, and next morniog was found lying ! dead in bed, resting upon its mother's arm.—Mr. A. ! Fletcher. of NorthvHch, appeared for Mr. Stubbs, and I said he thought the ince.test was unnecessary, and there were two doctors (Drs. Robinscn and McDougall) present to give the fullest information.—The Coroner said had ! he heard Mr. Fletclierls statement, and the statements of! ! the doctors, before the jury was summoned, he should have given a certificate.—A verdict in accordance with the evidence was returned, the Coroner remarking that there was not the slightest blame attached to Mr. or Mrs. Stubbs. , HAYNES% HAITI/SEWN WAtIIRTDIRT NAVVIES' HOOTS, from 12/6 to 15/-. 42 and 44. EforsomarketAit.. Warrlngton.—Adrt. MARRIADE AT WIDNES.—At half-past nine on Wednes- day morning, at Victoria-rd. Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. J. Bryant, assisted by the 'Rev. T. Law, Mr. Charles William Cooper, manager of the Widnes-rd. Boot of the London oot Repairing Company, was married to Miss Emily, second daughter of Mr. Thomas.; Sadler, joiner and builder, Widnes-rd. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a rich dress of blue satin, with hat to match. Her maids,. Miss Catherine ! Corker, of Lostock Graham, near Nortliwich, and Migs ! H. M. Mitchell, wore dresses of blue cashmere. The bridegroom was supported by Mr, James Haynes, jun., and Mr. Thomas Sadler, jun. After the nuptial knot had been tied, breakfast was partaken of a Vine Cottage, when there were present, in addition to tlfose named above. Mrs. Sadler, Mr. and Mrs. Willi am Sadler, ! Mrs. Law, Mrs. Bryant, Mr. J. Haynes, senior, (of ! Warrington, the "London Boot Repairing Company"). Mr. and Mrs. E. Peover, Mr. Alfred Cooper (Crewe), ! Mist"; Pryer (Northwich), Miss M. Corker (Lostock Gralam). and Master Fred Sadler. In the afternoon he , newly-married couple proceeded to Southport, where , they are spending the honeymoon. The bride received many beautiful presents. TmE RUNCORN BURIAL FEES.—A meeting of ratepayers was called for Thursday evening in Bethesda School- room, to consider fully the resolution passed by the Burial Board on the 12th September "That the charges and fees of the Burial Board, with the exception of those relating to the purchase and re-opening of graves, be the same for the inhabitant a of the townships of Weston and Halton as they are for the inhabitants of Ruhcorn." Mr. E. unison presided, and there were present Messrs. Rogerson, eloleburn, and Coleburn (members of the Board), Salkeld (secretary), Sutton (assistant overseer), and W. Jones.—Mr. Rogerson moved the resolution and pointed out that they would be doing a kind and friendly action to poor people if the motion was carried. The reduced fees would only mean a loss of £l5 a year to the ratepayers of Runcorn.—There was no seconder to the resolution, and the Chairman observed that it was clear the ratepayers did not take any interest in the matter ; otherwise there would have been a larger attendance.—Mr. Coleburn opposed the resolution, and said it would be unfair to the ratepayers of Runcorn if any alteration were made .—The proceedings concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman

ACTION AGAINST A RUNCORN CAPTAIN. At the Runcorn County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, John Heath, of Princess-street, Widnes; Joseph ralin. Sunnyside, Northwich ; and William Postles, of Witton, Northwich, sued Edward : Wilkinson mariner, Collier-street, Runcorn, for £l7 10s. 6d., balance of money had and received; and money paid. The defendant filed, a counter claim for £7 damages for the plaintiffs having converted to their own use certain goods belonging to him, including a pair of opera glasses, two charts, a parallel ruler, a clock, and other sundries, used in his business as a mariner. Mr. T. J. Peters, solicitor, Widnes, appeared for the plaintiffs. and Mr. Burton, solicitor, Runcorn, for defendant. Mr. Peters said the plaintiffs were the joint owners of the schooner" Sarah Jane," of which defend- ant was captain, and the claim was for the plaintiffs share of freight. After evidence had been given for the plaintiffs, the defendant was called, but he was unable tO refute the evidence of the plaintiff as to the amount due for freight. The articles left by him on board the schooner, he said, which plaintiff (Hea.th) rafused to allow him to remove,were worth the sum mentioned in his counterclaim. His Honor' after looking through plain- tiffs book, said he thought the amount claimed was due, and he ordered defendant to pay .£1 a month. On the counterclaim he gave judgment for defendant for £5, to be paid at £1 a month.

The woman was domestic servant at the Manchester Beerhouse, Wellington-st., and on- Monday afternoon was in charge of the bar during the absence of her mis- tress, Mrs, Pilkington. Warrington.—Advt, SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A WIDNES CAPTAIN.— On Wednesday afternoon, an inquest was held at Whitehaven on the body of Captain Owen Jones, of Widnes, who threw himself-in front of a passenger train at Whitehaven, on Tuesday, and who waa 1 shockingly mutilated. Deceased arrived from Liverpool on Tuesday morning with his steamboat Reginald, of Runcorn. After partaking of break- fast with the mate, he went to a shipbroker's With books and papers. Leaving these at the broker's without any message, he .went into the town, and afterwards proceeded to Corkickle railway station. Fie passed two porters without speaking. and, going to the end of the platform. waited until the Furness passenger train was within a few yards from him,. when he threw himself off the platform on to the metals. He WAS Inarried, and had two daughters. Latterly he had appeared &pressed. The jury returned a verdict to the effect flip he had com— mitted suicide, but there was nothing to show his state of mind at the time. div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical 01licer of Health reported that during the past month 26 deaths were registered, showing an average death rate of 17.6 per 1,000 of the eatr mated population. Exclusive of an inquest case, the death rate was 16-12. There was reason to fear that there was considerable overcrowding in several. parts of the town and especially with reference to houses where lodgers were admitted. The want of personal cleanliness and other sanitary conditions in th; houses and their surroundin 4s were calculated to bring about disease that in some instances assamed a virulent and fatal type. Surprise visits should be tnad'e to those houses, and anyone found offending against the directions of the Authority• should be dealt with ri4rously.---The Surveyor stated that there were 33 (reatlis in the correspon- ding period last year.
_ THE SHIP CANAL AND THE SPRINCIL-THE PROPOSED IMPROVEMENTS.

The Highway. and Building Committee recom- mended that the Surveyor be instructed to take steps to find the old Culvert at the Sprinch ; also that he be empowered to take the necessary steps to enable him to secure a copy of the tracing or plan of the said culvert supposed to be in existence.—ln reply to Mr. Mellor, Mr. Barker said he had taken steps to • obtain a plan.—The Chairman said he had received a letter from the Ship Canal Company, which had better now he considered.--The Secretary then read the letter, which referred to an application that the Commissioners would remove from their books a few yards of streetag,e at the Sprinch. The Company would be glad to know that the Commissioners had been pleased to accede to the request. • The small portion of street was a cul-de-sac, in which no one was interested hut the Company; all the land beyond, and on either side, was the property of the Company, and the one firm tenanting . a portion was subject to a month's notice at any time. The Commissioners had paid nothing for the street. The pavement, &c., had been paid for by the Company, and the ques- tion was thus not put to the Commissioners until the Company had removed every difficulty which they could imagine might stand in the way of the Board's doing what was asked.—The Chairman said the Board did not wish to put any obstacles in the way of the Company. There was, however, the difficulty of the culvert under the canal that stood in the way.—Mr. Meadowcroft asked was Mr. Barker in a position to inform the Board that when he found the culvert it could be used as a sewer, or what advantage it would be.—The Chairman explained that the culvert was one through which flowed the stream which formerly supplied the fountain opposite the Police Station. Mr. Timmins, who appeared to know all about it. wfts of opinion that, the culvert would be sufficient to meet the requirements of that part of the town without making a new sewer. If so, it was very essential that it should be found out.— Mr. Nleadowcraft said that the Company had no , information as to the reason why this concession was withheld. —The Chairman said that in the opinion of the High way Committee it Was necessary that the Board should have communication under the Canal. and, they must either find this culvert, or they would have to put other culverts under the Canal. The Board wished to avoid, as much as pos- sible, interfering with the traffic or with the Canal. It was only right that the Board should have some understanding from the Company about going under the• Canal, as at a future time there might be a difficulty in the Board getting what they required. --After further discussion, the subject dropped.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to £390 15s 3d. and accounts amounting to .£361 2s. 10d. were passed for payment.—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Itnison THB PUBLIC BATHS QLIESTION. Mr. Smith moved "That a Committee be appointed to consider the desirability (or cther- wise) of establishing public baths, and the probable cost of construction and maintenance." He believed th

lat if a vote of the ratepayers were taken. it would he found that two thirds would be in favour of baths. He proposed that the committee be com- posed of Messrs. Imison, Hankinson, Timmins. Dobson, Grice, Lightburn, the Chairman, and him- self.—Mr. P. Speakman seconded the motion. It was hard lines that the youths of the town should have, to walk over the, Bridge to Widnes to have a bath. He quite agreed that there should be a public bath.—Mr. Meadowcroft suggested that there should he added to the motion "That the Com- mittee be instructed to make inquiries as to the cost of maintenance from other authorities posses- sing baths."—Mr. Smith agreed.—The mbtion was :carried unanimously.

..ClO FOR A DONKEY BITE AT RUNCORN. On Tuesday at the Runcorn County Court, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes and a jury, Peter Ince, baker and greengrocer, of Bonk-st., Widnes, brought anaction against John Carter, cattle dealer, &c., of Frodsham, to recover .£5O damages alleged to have been sustained by plaintiff from injuries to the plaintiff's son and servant, Henry Thee, caused on the 7th May, 1888, by the defendant keeping an ass of a mischievous and ferocious nature, well know- ing the animal to ,be of that nature, whereby the said son was atacked, bitten, thrown down, and injured by the ass on Frodshana Marsh.—Mr. T. Swift, barrister (instructed by Mr. J. W. Knowles) appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. T. Shepherd Little,. barrister (instructed by Mr. Burton) was for the defendant. It appeared that the boy with a companion was walking home from ITrodsham across the Marsh, when the defendant's donkey pursued them. The boys ran as quickly as possible but the animal caught Ince, and seizing hold of him with his teeth. lifted him from the ground and shook him. The animal then dropped the boy to the ground, knelt upon him, and severely bit him. Fortunately two men appeared on the.scene and drove off the savage animal. Blood issued profusely from the boy's mouth, and he was so , injured that it was with great difficulty that the boy, arrived at Widnes. He had since been under the care of Dr. Hincninicon and was not completely recovered from his injuries The father said the boy assisted him in his business, and his services were worth 15s to 20s per week. It was proved that a few days previously the donkey had attacked a man named Maddock, and that the defendant bad been informed of the fact and was quite aware that the animal was of a ferocious nature.— The defence was a denial of such kowledge on the defendant's part, and evidence was given to show that the donkey was of a playful nature, and mu after men and boys for scraps of bread, &c.—The jury awarded the plaintiff'MO and costs.

THE REVIVON COURT.—Mr. Burke Wood, revising barrister, on Saturday commenced the revision of the voters' lists. sof the Eddisbury division of Cheshire at Dunham-o'th'-Hill. The business here was quickly transacted, and the Court was transferred to the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsha,m, where the lists for the Frodsham and Kingsley districts were gone through. Mr. W. Handley, of Runcorn, appeared for the Liberals, and Mr. Richard Humphrey Owen, of Tarporley, was for the Conserve. ives . Claims were made for a number of police officers, but the Revising Barris- ter decided that they could only be placed on division two as Parliamentary voters. Constables in the division are therefore disqualified from yoting for members of the County Council under the new Local Government Act. During the inquiry it was elicited that there are several hundred duplicate voters on the Eddisbury register, and the Revising Barrister pointed out that it was very desirable he reduce them to one entry, but before doing so notice must be given to the parties, so that they might select which qualification they would retain. An important pointto political agents was raised Mr. Owen, on behalf of the Conservatives, objected to a number of occupation claims because they had not been signed by the claimants themselves. It was proved that they had been signed by the Liberal agent with the authority of the claimant, and the Revisit*. Barrister held that this was quite sufficient. A number of other cases were adjourned for the production of the rent books, because the names did not appear on the rate book, Mr. Handley elicited from the assistant overseer that this was owing to the compounding clause being enforced, and the landlords had not reported the names of their tenants.
