div.head: -THE MAYOR EXPLAINS.
div.p: -THE MAYOR EXPLAINS.

The MAYOR said that before proceeding with the minutes he just wished to make an explanation. It was this: His attention had been called by one or two members of the Council to the statement he made at the last meeting of the Council, on the occasion of the retire- ment of some members, to the effect that he had often heard the same gentlemen make remarks quite as bad as the one made by Alderman Burgess; and ho just wished to say that, in making such remarks, he did aot refer to any particular gentleman who was then leaving the room, but that it was intended to be a general remark. His own opinion of the remark of Alderman Burgess was that it was not of so serious a character that it need be noticed, and in saying what he (the Mayor) did—he might have been wrong but he certainly thought he was not wrong—he meant that he had often heard remarks, not only by the gentlemen leaving the room but by nearly every member of the Council, which were, perhaps, not so serious as that of Alderman Burgess but were still of such a character and said in such a way that the members of the Council had gener- ally laughed at them and let them pass. That was what his impression was of what Alderman Burgess said, and, therefore, he did not think it wise on his part to rule that he was out of order, or that the remark was of such a serious character that it should be noticed. He hoped they should be able to conduct their proceedings in future in a* good spirit, and that they should all be friendly towards each other. They should, he was sure. get on a good deal better by conducting their proceed- ings in a calm way, instead of getting into wrangles such as they had been in the habit of doing of late. (Hear, hear.)
LETTER FROM MRS._ WARRINOTON WOOD.

The MAYOR read a letter from Mrs. Warrington Wood thanking the Mayor and Council for flleir very kind decision with regard to bringing certain works of the late Mr. Warrington Wood to Warrington. She could not express what a very great comfort it was to find that, through their kind permission, the memory of her beloved husband's genius in these works would find a borne in his native town. WATCH COMMITTEE.—THE POLICE OF LATCHFORD. The minutes of this Committee contained a report of the Chief Constable stating tha , his attention having been called to the undesirability of conveying prisoners in chatins through the streets of Liverpool on the way to jail, he had arranged with the Cheshire Lines Committee for certain trains to be stopped at Warrington for the purpose of conveying prisoners to Aintree. The MAYOR moved that the minutes of the Committee be adopted. Referring to the minute given above he said there was no doubt it was rather an unseemly pro- ceeding to convey a large number of prisoners through the streets of Liverpool in chains, but, unfortunately, the police officers had no alternative, having no prison van or conveyance at their disposal. He was glad, therefore, to find that the Chief Constable had made the arrangement with the Cheshire Lines Committee. Alderman HARRISON seconded the proposal. Councillor TINSLEY said he had a suggestion to make to the Committee with regard to the police arrangenients at Latchford. They were there a long way from the police station, and, although they had there a large community of very respectable people, still he was sorry to say they had some of another sort. He wanted to recommend, therefore, that they should have some sort of station for the police at Latchford. They cer- tainly ercpected to have something better than they hiir at present, and he thought they had a right to ask for it. They had had several robberies in the district, and flower gardens had been broken into. Alderman HARRISON was sorry to say that the peace- able inhabitants of Latchferd were often disturbed by broils, and he thought, therefore, it would be an advan- tage if they could have a re-distribution of the police force. _

_The MAYOR said there was at present an application in tilt 1004 9t ttlg 119111.0 Secretary for sanction to increase the police and it is expeeed the4lial4Ctipn would be given at the end of the year. When that was :,!fn:le they would be in a position to grant more officers to Latch- kV_ rounciuor FA. ROBERTS said there was a necessity for a police station, or something of that nature at Latchford. It was almost impossible to ask a police officer to bring such men as they had there now all the way to the Bridewell. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HARRISON thought Mr. Tinsley's object was to procure some temporary provision pending the increase of the police force. They were in a compara- tively unprotected state now. Councillor E. GREENALL said that, particularly on Sundays when the police were not about, it was hardly safe to leave women in country houses by them- selves just now. He did not say it was the navvies Who were to blame for this, but thfre were people loafing about. Atderman WEBSTER said the WAch Committee had done all they possibly could a present. The Home Secretary had virtually consented to an increase of the police force, so that a re-arrangement of the police force would be necessary, and he had no doubt that Latch- ford, as oGII as other parts of the 'town, would receive attention. Latchford certainly required special atten- tion. Alderman BURGESS said it was not so much an increase of the police force that was wanted at Latchford as that accommodation there should be provided for the officers. From what he knew of the length of time needed to get any arrangements carried through an office in London, a' good deal of mischief might. bo dou in the meantime. tHear, bear.) What was wanted was such provision that it would not be necessary to bring one of these very powerful men all the way from Latchford to Warriiigton bridewell. The MAYOR said he would promise that the matter was brought before the next meeting of ' the Watch Com- mittee. and as far as he could assist them he would do so. (Hear, hear.) The minutes of the Committee were then confirmed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIMITING COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the plans of the following buildings be approved :—Bakehouse in Wash- lane for Mr. F. T. Carlisle; .hree cottages in Thelwall- lane for Mr. Edward Rogers, conditionally; addition of cOLlSldting room to dwelling house, 3, Bewsey-rd., for Dr. Adams. Councillor Purr, in moving the confirmation of these , minutes, said they had not yet heard from the London and North-Western Railway Company as to whether they were inclined. to renew their offer of the land for the proposed new street. Until they got that reply, the Committee could not move further. Alderman WEBSTER called attention to the naming of the streets, and remarked that in many cases, the names were illegible. Councillor GRF.ENALL suggested that the street names be put on the lamps so that they could be read at nights. Councillor rurr said the Committee would look into the matter with regard to the naming of the streets, and he thought Councillor Greenall's suggestion, more especially as regarded the main streets of the town, was worth consideration, and it should be brought before the Committee at its next meeting. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were confirmed. FINANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the sum of thirty guineas be paid to the Borough Auditors for auditing the Treasurer's accounts for the year ending 25th March, 1888. On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER the minutes were passed. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—THE DISMISSAL OF MR. • DINWIDDIE i LIVELY DISCUSSION. The minutes of the Sanitary Committee contained the • , following items :-4. That the Town Clerk be instructed to negotiate with Mr. Robert Pierpoint for ihe purchase of a plot of land behind the Infectious Diseases Hospital. Mr. Dinwiddie not having sent in his resignation as required by the resolution of the Council of the last meeting; Resolution, that M. Dinwiddie be dismissed from his office of manager of the Longford Works." Alderman Burgess, in moving the confirmation of these minutes, referred to the minute with regard to the • purchase of land behind the Infectious Diseases Hospital, don said that brought him to the question of the hospital; and the condition of the town. At the last meeting of the Council he said that the Committee should not hesitate, if the necessity came for urgent, immediate, and decided action. They had all their arrangements complete, and they could extend their hospital, he supposed,the next &.y if the requirement came. He was glad to say, however, from information he had received from the Medical Officer of Health since he came into the room, that there was a diminution, though not a large one, of the number of patients in the hospital. (Hear, hear.) So far as the piece of land belonging to Mr. R. Pierpoint was concerned, they were already in posses- , sion of it, and they had the tent on the ground so that if absolutely required they should be prepared, in about twelve hours, with hospital accomodation for at least a dozen small-pox patients who would be separated . entirely from the other infectious wards. Before the piece of land was purchased, they should have th come to the Council for confirmation, but they wished to be prepared, while at the same time they tried as far as they could, to study the public purse. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the resolution with respect to Mr. Dinwiddie, Alderman Burgess said the Sanitary Comnaittee,with the resolution of the Council a.sking Mr. Dinwiddie to resign in their hands, had allowed a reasonable time to elapse, and then they passed that resolution on their miqutes. He did not propose to go into that question any further than he did on a former occasion. He told them then that the reasons for requiring Mr. Dinwiddie's resignation were that the time he made at the works was unsatis- factory ; that the shortening of the time of the men at their work, and their having the same wages paid to them, was unsatisfactory; that the shortening

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1888.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday night he Mayor (Alder- inan Sutton) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Burgess, Harrison, Webster; Councillors Barker, J. Pierpoint, Percival, Tinsley, J. Shaw Green, J. Platt, Greenall, H.Roberts, F. A. Roberts, Monks, Wright, Dixon, J. V. Taylor, Francomb, Heaton, Bolton, Hutchinson, J. Taylor, Fleming; Messrs. Brook (town clerk) ; Whittle (deputy town clerk); Dr. Gornall (medical officer); Longdin (borough surveyor); Chorley (borough treasurer.)

of the time the machines were expected to work, and thac without consulting the Committee or anybody else, was unsatisfactory ; that the quantity of coals and gas consumed was very unsa isfactory ; and that, in fact, there was a generally extravagant and inattentive con- diton of things on the pan of the manager. He did not propose to add anything to that; he would allow i, to stand where it is. He might, however, say, that since the last meeting of the Council, they had had three or four weeks' working of the machinery at Longford, and he was very glad to tell them that the results were very much more satisfactory. It would be within their remembrance that, on a recent occasion, he took the opportunity of saying what he then believed to be absolutely true, and what he was now more and more convinced was true, that was, that the machinery a, Longford did its work as well as it. could do, and that, when they did not get the quantity of material they knew they were entitled to, the fault was not in- the machines but in the management. Since the last meet- ing the works had been in other bands, Mr. Dinwiddie having been invited to take a month's holiday—and he (Alderman Burgess) hoped he had been enjoyinv,, himself if he had been away—and he might tell the Council that the results of the working of the machines during Mr. Dinwiddie's absence fully confirmed the statement he made in that Council. He had in his hand Mr. Din- widdie's returns for the first week in January last year and ,he last week in December, giving a resul of 6 tons , 12i cwts. as the average week's return of the material sent to Longford, and he had had 14.4 WM) of crude material wherewith to make that product. The figures as to raw material were slightly wrong, as he could not have had quite that quantity, but it was of little impor- tance, it was so small. The crude m aerial may be said to be pretty much what it was at the end of January last year, but now they had, as the result of the working! since Mr. Dinwiddie left, a return, not of 6 tons 12i-cwts'. but of 9 tons 2cwts. out of the same material, making a difference of 2 tonsibewts. each week. if they took the trouble to ascertain what that came to they would find that it amounted in the year to a very large figure, taking it at £6 a ten. In addition to that there had been a, lessened consumption of coal to the extent of from 35 to 40 per cent as compared with the correspon- ding month of last year. If they took the increased pro- duct out of the same material, the lessened consump- tion of coal, and that there was no wages being paid during that period, they would find that if the same thing was carried through an entire year-it would mean a saving of not less than £l,OOO to the orough. He might be asked how that difference c,airle about? He would say that that was the difference which came of careful observation and strict attention to what was going on in the place. If those minutes were confirmed that night, and inasmuch as they had got to a pro- duct of over 9 tons per week, they were not very far from that period which he spoke to them about not long ago when he told them that their crude material had in it llf tons weekly, and that he should not be con- tent with less than a 10 tons return. CAuncillor MONKS : Will Mr. Burgess be kind enough, when he is making his statement, to give the percentage of moisture in the manure now made,and the percentage of moisture in that mat:lp during the last twelve months? Alderman BURGESS : The percentage of moisture in the thanure now made is less than it was,in the manure made when we were getting 6 tons 12cwts. Conncillor WRIGHT seconded the proposal for the, adoption of the minutes Ntithout comment. Alderman WEBSTER said he thought that to dismiss I Mr. Dinwiddie would be a very drastic proceeding indeed. No doubt, judging from the statement by Alderman Burgess, the request that he should no longer be manager at Longford Works was a reasonable one, hut he (Alderman Webster) did not think that the Committee should proceed with such a serious step as to dismiss him. _ .

The MAYOR said that the Corporation were legally bound to give Mr. Dinwiddie three months'notice. Alderman WEnsTsm said he thought the appearance of the word" dismiss" implied some offence, and cast a stigma upon a man. He had no -doubt that Mr. Dim:riddle was a straightforward man, but he appeared not to be equal to the management of the works. When he read thelninutes of the 'Committee, he thought the step proposed was rather more serious than the case demanded. If it was simply that Mr. Di nwiddie was to have notice to leave at a given tjtne he had not a word to say. He thought the word fi " should be erased. Councillor MoNtri said that he was very glad to notice the altered tone of the discussion of that question. He thought that by-and-bye they would solve the difficulty, for it was a diffiult question to solve, and he believed that it would be solved financially in a satisfactory way. Alderman 13VAGESS (interrupting) asked to be allowed to make a forthee statement. He should have said, but it escaped pis memory, that, with the concurrence of the committee, he felt that, under the altered state of things, the time was come when the Council should go, with the committee, most minutely into the interior working of the whole of the Longford works—that they should have, not by a report from a committee, or any statement made in that Chamber, an enquiry of the most exhaustive character into everything eettnected with the works, beginning at the foundation and going on to the finish. The Council as a body might make the enquiry, or depute certain members not connected with the committee to do so on their behalf. The com- mittee had nothing, they never had anything, to con- ceal. They had had a difficulty to contend with, and they did not keep it a secret from the Council. That difficulty was that while they were quith satisfied with the mechanism, they were not getting the results that they were entitled to at Longford. He believed that now it would satisfy not only the Council, but the public mind, to have an enquiry by.a deputation or by the whole Council. He desired a most exhaustive enquiry; and he was persuaded that the time would not be long ' when they should arrive at a correct conclusion for the future. Councillor Momm said that he was very glad indeed to find that thd Sanitary Committee, and the Chairman of that Committee, had got to a point where they would receive suggestions from other people. He must say, in justice to many members who had been in the Council for a long time past, that it had been very difficult, in the view of many people, to obtain information regarding Longford. He thought that if the openness now expressed had been practised during the last two Or three years, a great deal of the bitterness and the pain that had been caused would have been entirely avoided. He himself had never seen what the Sanitary Committee could gain bywithholdinganyinforrnation whatever, and he ventured to say that if the policy of not giving inform- ation had been persisted in the Committee would not al'eveM tha goal to which Alderman Burgess had referred AO easily as they would by having the advantage of tto experience, and the thought, of other members of the Council, who might not be directly asociated with the Committee. During the initial stages of the work, when the first manager was there, both Mr. Barker and himself gained a good deal of practical useful informa- tion. He had been through the worki during the last week and he was sorry to say that The did not find that improvement in the method of manufacture that he should have expected after five years' experience, and the duplication of the machinery. He said this in all good feeling, because he thought that Alderman Burgess. since the last meeting, must have felt that he made a mistake in attribnting what he (Mr. Monks) called unworthy motives, to any members of the Council in the course that they chose to take on this question. He would refer to the question of the management, and the dismissal of Mr. Didwiddie, because he thought that, while perhaps many of the members would agree with the ultimate object, he thought many would entirely disagree with the way in which it had been done. He could not at that time help giving expression to a very wide-spread feeling that the relations between the Chairman and the Manager had been such as they should have been glad if they could have been avoided. He was prepared to move that the minutes be passed, with the exoeption of the one dis- missing Mr. Dinwiddie, in the hope that all the good things of which the Aldermarr had spoken might be proved to be facts. Those who had anything to do with the management of the works knew very well that there was nothing more illusory and deceptive than to compare a week's or a fortnights working with the average for a year, and to set one as against the other. When, some years ago, it was decided to make an extension, results were at the time obtained which the management had been entirely unable to verify over a year's experience, and he was afraid, from what he had seen himself when in the works, that there was some deception, or some mistake, with reference to the,moisture in the manure that he saw being dealt with at Longford. He should doubt very much himself whether there was not a very great deal more moisture in the manure than the Alderman thought. He thpught that the time for discussing the whole question Ytould arrive before long. He should like to be satisfied in his own mind more than he was that night that they were taking the right step before they dismissed Mr. Din- widdie. With regard to the use of coals, if what he saw last Thursday was the practice at Longford. they would not only use coals this year, but they would use a very large quantity. He was not saying that this was the fault of he manager, because this consumption of :coal might depend upon causes entirely beyond the control of the manager. In his mind there was a suspicion that the two or three weeks were being used as a test time, and the working results for the year would not come out in anything like the same proportion. If such results as the Chairman had given were not maintained for the year it would throw a very serious responsibility upon , him and the Committee. He himself should much pre- fer that the matter should stand over for a month or so, until the new committee had had time to consider the whole matter, and deal with it. If the new com- mittee, which would be elected in November, came to the Council and said that, all things considered they be- lieved that the interests of the Corporation would be served if Mr. Dinwiddie's services were dispensed with, and there might be many reasons why he was not a suitable man, then he thought that it would be a very,hard thing for any member of the Council to gain- say it. He thought that the step proposed should not, in common justice to Mr. Dinwiddie, be taken that night, and he proposed as an amendment 'that the minutes of the Sanitary Committee be confirmed with the exception of the one of the 26th September, requir- ing the dismissal of Mr. Dinwiddie from his office of manager of the Longford works.

Councillor Dutow seconded the amendment, and re- ferred to a visit that he and Councillor W. Pierpoint had made to Longford. He could, he said, endorse what had been said by Councillor Monks in regard to the naoisture. In going into one section of the works, and there were many sections, he saw a large quantity of liquor run- ning away from it. He had his attention called to it by Councillor W. Pierpoint. Having referred to the expen- sive plant at Longford, Councillor Dixon said that he could understand that the returns might prove what the Chairman had said, and that, during the last month or six weeks, with very great care and attention, they might get the results he had mentioned. Of all the plants he had seen, there was nct another so defective, there was not another that would cost so much money to work, and there was not another works in such an unsatisfactory condition as the works at Longford. He should like the whole question brought up, so that section by section could be discoased.

F. --:"ci--- Councillor .A. BMUS said that he felt very much in sympathy with Alderman Webster. If it was possible in any way to lessen the force of the resolution as regarded Mr. Dinwiddie, he should be very glad if the Sanitary Committee would do so. The charge practic- ally implied by Alderman Burgess's remarks accentuated the dismissal to a large degree. The deduction that they must draw from the fact that Mr. Dinwiddie had been Oven a month's holiday, that the management had been given to a second man, and the statement that some- thing like- £l,OOO a year might be saved, was that Mr. Dinwidde had really cost the town £l,OOO a year during his management, as well as his salary of £2OO a year. He suggested to the Committee that, pending a thorough investigation into the management as well as the machinery, they should postpone the matter of Mr. Dinwiddie's dismissal. There was undoubtedly some fault, but still it was possible that the blame was not on-the part of Mr. Dinwiddie, but on the part of the Committee for .having appointed him to the post. The.Mayon said that he thought, in justice to the Com- mittee, that it should not be forgot that in thefirst place Mr. Dinwiddie was called upon to send in his resignation, and, although the resolution of the Committee was con- firmed at the last Council meeting', Mr. Dinwiddie did not think fit to send in his resignation, and therefore it was necessary to pass a resolution pf the sort in question. Mr. Dinwiddie having been appointed by the Council, the Committee did not feel themselves competent to dis- miss him without the sanction of the Council. The mere working of the resolution was formal. Of course, it did not mean that Dr. Dinwiddie was to be dismissed with- out notice. He would, of course, be entitled to receive the Ikal notice. . _ _

Alderman WEBSTER thought it would have been better if the words used had been—" that notice be given to Mr. Dinwiddie to terminate his engagement." In all probability Mr. Dinwiddie would have to seek another situation, and the fact of having been " dismissed ' might go against him. He thought that it would only be fair to Mr. Dinwiade to withdraw the resolution.

Councillor TINSLEY having spoken, Councglor PLATT said that Alderman Burgess had cer- tainly made out a good case, and one which, no doubt, he believed to be true. At the same time it might be the case that for two or three weeks the manu- facture could be carried on in such a waythat it was not possible for it to be carried on war ,a year's time. He did not think the Committee ,were free from blame in having accepted Mr. Pinvsiddia's services for five years, and then finding oat ilat he was losing £l,OOO a year. They should havc found that out before the lapse of five years. He did not think there would be any harm in allowing the matter to stand over for a month to hear the explanation on the other side, if there was one.

I Councillor MONKS said that this was the only way in which they could bring the matter before the Council with the object of fully elucidating all the circum- stances. Alderman HARRISON said that he sincerely hoped that Alderman Burgess would be able to see his way to with- draw the portion of the minutes having reference to the dismissal of Mr. Difiwiddie. At the last meeting the Council voted for the minutes which contained a resolu- tion that Mr. Dinwiddie be requested to send in his resignation. How they were to vote against the Committee that night without stultifying themselves he did not know. If the resolution was withdrawn, it would release them from the difficulty. It would also be giving Mr. Dinwiddie fair play. A letter Mr. Dinwiddie had written very seriously conflicted with the statement macW by Mr. Burgess at the last meeting of the Council. He theuint that they should have more light upon the subject. It was a remarkable thing that Alder- man Burgess only a short time ago moved that Mr. Dinwiddie's salary be advanced from £l5O to £2OO a year. It was certainly remarkable that Mr. Dinwiddie'il incompetence was not discovered before that resolution I was moved. If it was not discovered it must be assumed that at that time he was worth his £2OO a year. Whether he had become less competent or not since then he thought was open to an explanation. He should be glad if Alderman Burgess would withdraw the resolution for thel)resent, in order that it might be subsequently considered, after a most careful test had been applied to the operations which had recently taken place. Councillor HENRI( ROBERTS said that he welcomed mOst cordially the change of tone which had come into the debate. In regard to the, discovenes made by Councillor Dixon, he might quote the Scripture, which said " These things have been hid from the wise and prudent, and revealed onlyto—(laughter.) He would not complete the quotation. (Laughter.) Councillor MONKS asked if that was not importing an unfriendly feeling into the debate? Councillor HENRY ROBERTS said he thought they were all in a good humour that evening; he certainly had no intention of wounding either the feelings of Coun. Dixon or the susceptibilities of Councillor Monks. He agreed that the resolution might have been framed in a manner which would not have been so harsh as it seemed to be, and he believed the Chairman would not I object to alter its wording. But he was sorry to say that he could not go with those members of the Council who asked that the matter might be postponed; and for the reason that he had not heard a good argument that night in favour of a postponement. After the statement which had been made by the Chairman in regard to the practical failings of Mr. Dinwiddie, surely they could not expect the committee to retejn his services. He , therefore felt bound to support the action of the com- mittee in that matter, at the same time agreeing with, the suggestion that the wording of tl'e; minutes be , altered so as to mate the reeolution less hard. The MAYOR, in the course of further remarks, said that it appeared to him, speaking as a sub-chairman of the Committee, that in Councillor Monks attributing to the Chairman that night the same impure motives which he himself complained of Alderman Burgess giving utterance to at the last meeting, that the imputation he now put upon the Chairman for doing what he had done to get rid of Mr. Dinwiddie was not altogether just. , Councillor MONKS: I put no imputation on the Chair- man. The MAYOR: I think you attributed to the Chairman— Councillor MONIES : What did I say? The MAYOR: You said you thought the Chairman was getting rid of Mr. Dinwiddie not because he was incompetent, but for personal reasons. Councillor MONKS: No; I call you to order, sir. I never said anything of the sort. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR: Well, I understood you to say so. At all events, I think it would be very wrong indeed to ask the Committee to continue on Mr. Dinwiddie under all 'the circumstances. _ _

Councillor Mo:gas said that Alderman Burgess and he had differed on the subject of Longford; it was practically the only difference which had risen between them, and he was extremely sorry that Alderman Bur- gess had made it a personal question. He had met the Alderman again and again in the street, and although they had known one another a very long time, they did not even speak to each other. Notwithstand- ing that, he said publicly there was not another man in this town who recognized more than he did the services of Alderman Burgess and the disinterestedness with which he perfotmed his duties as a member of the Cor- a oration; and he ventured to say that if the suggestion which he made to Alderman Burgess when first they started the machinery at Longford—a suggestion that he should get a man who should be present when the machinery was put together, and who should study it as far as he could, with the view that he should become the manager and take charge of the works—had been listened to and acted upon it would have saved them a great deal of trouble. Alderman BURGESS, in reply, said that he did not know whether the members had theiaght of the result, but it was quite right he should call attention to the fact that the condition of things would be exceedingly strained if Mr. Dinwiddie was retained in his position as manager, even for a month. He (the speaker) did not think Mr. Dinwddle had anything to complain of at the hands of the Committee, but he did think that if Mr. Dinwiddie had been left to himself the contention that evening would not have come up. They belived Mr. Dinwiddie had not done for the Committee what he ought to have done, and that they were right in getting the confirma- tion of the Council to the minute asking for his dismissal. Mr. Dinwidgie had sent a letter to the Town Clerk's office saying that he was taking time to C.Q nsider the matter. He understood, he said, he was in the hands of his friends—that he was not acting exactly, on his own idea, but in conformity to the wishes of his friends, as he called them. Well, he thought that was a mistake, and he did not see how any good could come by retaining Mr. Dinwiddie's services, even for a short period. He said this in the most serious manner possible, that he felt the most humiliating part of his public life in connection with the Council Was that he had been instilimental as largely as he had been in introducing Mr. Din*iddie into •the employ of the Corporation. It was a mistake, it was the gravest error he could charge himself with, and he I was very desirous indeed that the matter should be set right. So far as the.jaotice was concerned, he was pre- pared to do whatever could be done legally. He was prepared, under the guidance of the Town Clerk, to move that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the one which said that Mr. Dinwiddie be dismissed from his office of manager of the Longford works, and in lieu of that to substitute the words "That notice be given to Mr. Dinwiddie to determine his engagement with the Corporation as manager of the Longford works." That, he added, in answer to a question, would be subject to three months' notice.
'W

After further discussion Councillor MONKS said that he wished his amendment to go to the .vote. For the amendment there voted :—Councillors Monks, Dixon, John Pierpoint, Platt, and Barker; and against it Alder- men Burgess, Webster, and Harrison. Councillors Wright, Francomb, and H. Roberts, and the Mayor. The amend- ment was thus defeated by seven votes to five. A number of members did not vote.

• Councillor PLATT/ said he wished emphatically to bring under the notice of the Sanitary Committee the very grave and serious nuisance caused in the town by the intercepting depots. The nuisance arising from these works was spreading wide-spread alarm in their neigh- bourhood, and there was a great deal of sickness in the districts where they were,though whether that was due to the depots or not was a medical question. The inhabi- tants of the neighbourhood ofthe depots were strongly of opinion that it was. He should be glad to let that matter rest for the present if it, as well as the other matters referred to, was to be left to a Committee df the whole Council, to take evidence on the matter and decide what has to be done. He ventured to think that course might suit ties Sanitary Committe who knew that they had made a great mistake in putting down those depots, as very likely it might provide them with a retreat,if the Council determined the depots should be discontinued which they had not got the backbone to do themselves. Alderman BURGBSS, in replying,referred to the question of Alderman Harrison as to the raising of Mr. Dinwiddie's salary to £2OO, and said that when Mr. Dinwiddie was appointed it was promised him that the question of an increase should be brought up at some future period. He hoped that would be satisfactory. Alderman HARRISON : I think it will not. , The Maxon thought they had better not interfere with that matter shy further. Alderman Bunoess said with regard to CoUncillor Platt's remarks, it was not for the Sanitary. Committee to create a nuisance. ("They do.") He did not care how long or how severely Mr. Platt dealt with that question as long as he believed it to be a nuisance. He (Alderman Burgess) had never said it was not ; he had never made any admission of any kind, and he was going to be very careful how he made admissions. (Laughter) What he wanted was an examination into the working of the whole of the Sanitary system from beginning to end, and he did not care how soon it came I—the sooner the better.

The MAYOR said if the Council was to be brought to consult with the committee the whole thing would be gone into then. ' Alderman Bunorss said he should demand that for their own sake ; he should not be content with anything else.
The minutes of the Committee as amended were then passed.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE.

In the minutes of this committee the following resolutions rere recorded :—That the sewers be con- tinued in Orford Avenue,Conie's.Corner, and Stephenson- street to receive the sewage from the houses recently erected in those streets; that the footpath on the West side of BattersbytLane be continued from Sharp-street to Conie's Corner • that the Town Clerk be instructed to recover the following apportionment of the cost of forniing and paving part of Museum-st. between Parker- st. and Arpley-st :—Andrew Rathbone £42 9s. 10d. ; Thomas Fletcher £llO 15s. 3d.; Lord Wimmarleigh £75 6s. 9d.; The Queen's Benefit Building Society £67 18s. Pd.; the County of Lancaster £156 Us. lid. • total £453 2s. td. That the Town Clerk be instructed to serve the necessary notices, and take the necessary pro- ceedings, for the due execution of the work of forming and paving Dixon.-st„ and the recovery of the expenses in the event of the owners being in default. On the motion of Councillor WRIGHT, seconded by Councillor FRANCOMB, the minutes were confirmed.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained the following : The Inspector's report, from which it appeared that 85 cues had been enquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 61 cases for 127 children. That 20 cases had been taken before the magistrates, and fines inflicted in 19 cases, and one boy sent to the ship "Clio." 37 cases were, brought before the Gom- rnittee and dealt with. The average attendance at the Public Elementary SChools during the month bf August was 7,459; corresponding period last year, 7,513 ; de- crease 54.
On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Councilor J. SHAW GREEN, these minutes were con- firmed.

MUSEITM, LIBRARY AND ARTS COMMITTER. The return for August of thiL Committee showed as follows :—Visitors to museum ,043, decrease 2 per cent. as compared with August, 1887; books issued in reading room 1,628, decrease 20 per cent. ; books issued in lending department 2,049 increise 36 per cent. Re- port of the curator of the following gifts, for which the thanks of the Committee were ordered to be sent to the donors :—Partridge eggs (21) and doves' eggs (4), from the Town Hall Committee; ancient spur, from Mr. S. Norbury ; double nest: fly-catcher's inside thrush's, from-Mr. R. Garnett, J.P. ; "catalogue of the India Office Library," vol. 1., from the Secretary of State ; two n'llillemotS and razorbill, from the yacht " Ane- mono."

Alderman WEnsrEn moved, and Councillor BOLTON seconded, the confirmatlisfi of these minutes. In answer to Councillor 'Platt, Alderman WEBSTER said that the new scheme with ngard to the lending of books was, so far as numbers were concerned, working very well; but whether it would be financially satisfactory they could not tell till the end of the year.—The minutes were adopted.

TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The bath-keeper reported to the Committee that the income from the Baths during the past four weeks was £lO is. 2d., and for the corresponding period last year I-212 16s. Bd. The Committee had passed the following resolution, that Councillors J. Pierpoint, Jolley, and Bolton be appointed to consider and report upon the best mode of improving the entrance into the gardens from Kendrick-street, and also as to the laying out of the land in front of the Town Hall. Also, that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to have the band stand repaired. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman HARRISON seconded the adoption of these minutes, which was agreed to. MARKETS COMMITTEE. The total income of this Committee from all Sources during the past two weeks was £262 15s. 6d. On the motion of Councillor TnistitY, seconded by Councillor J. SHAW GREEN, these minutes were con- firmed.
FOO TBALL. (RUGBY.) PARR V. HALTON.—Played at Halton on Saturday. Final result: Parr, 1 goal, 1 try,, 3 minors; Halton, 2 minors.
Therm HEILTH v. FsnarwonTn.--These teams met at Grange Park, and a pleasant and evenly contested game resulted in a draw.
WIDNES v OLDRAm (A TEAms).—This match was played on Saturday at Oldham. Result: Widnes, two goals and eight minors; Oldham, one goal, two tries, three minors.

LATCHFORD TRUE BLUES V. SUTTON.—Played at Sutton on Saturday. Half-time result: Sutton, 1 try; Latchford True Blues, 6 minors. Final result: Sutton, 1 try ;Latchford True Blues, 7 minors. RUNCORN RECREATION V. FRODSHAM, (2nd Teams).— Played at Frodsham on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the Recreation. Score :—Runcorn Recreation, one try and four minors; Frodsham, two minors. • Rtmconx RECREATION V. FRODSHAM.—This match was played at Runcorn on Saturday. Frodsham won the toss. G. H. Jones kicked off for the Recreation with a light wind in his favour. A feeble return being made, the Recreation rushed in the visitors' quarter, where Way rested for a long time. The Reci were the first to score, registering a dead ball, and shortly afterwards S. Houghton dropped a splendid goal from a pass by G. H. Jones. This roused Frodsham up, who came away with a rush, Tudor kicking the ball over the bar, whereupon the Frodsham captain claimed for a punted goal, which was disallowed, much to the chagrin of the Frodsham umpire, who expressed his opinion in rather a forcible manner. The Recreation scorea another minor, bring- ing on half time. On changing ends play was of a very even nature, Frodsham having the wind in their favour scored several minors from long kicks. Just before the call of time Darlington, of Frodsham, dropped a grand goal from opposite the 25 flag, leaving thelame drawn. Score :—Runcorn Recreation, one dropped goal and two minors • Frodsham, one dropped goal and five minors. For Frodsham Webb and Brooks, forwards, and T. Rogers, back, played a good game, while the best on the Recreation side were G. H. Jones, forward, and Fondle- bury and Houghton, backs. .

SiLE V. Sr.—A splendidly contest in game between the second team of the Sale and the first team of the Sankey Club was played on the ground of the former, on Saturday afternoon. In the first half, Lings for the home team secured a try, which was converted into a goal, but was disputed by the umpire owing to a mistake having been made in bringing the ball out. Hostilities had no sooner been resumed, than thrdugh the pressing of the home team, Sankey were compelled to concede a touch down, which was the principal feature in the first half of the play. On changing ends, the good play of the Sankey forwards kept the game in the home 25. Here Stephens got possession, and made a brilliant run, tackling all who meant opposition, and secured a try, which he failed to convert into a goal. The game ended as follows : Sale, two tries and two minors; Sankey, one Iry and four minors. The teams were as follows :—Sale : J. Jones, F Latham, A. Step- liens, J. Wood, A. Drinkwater, H. De Rome, H. Lings (captain), W. Rae, R. G. Boot. B. Walton, J. E. David- son, W. Reid, T. Robinson, S. F. Green, and R. Holt. Sankey: J. Beery, A. Dakin, J, • Brady; W. Cartwright, D. 11toon, J. Jefferson (captain), J. Pemberton, W. Pemberton, W. O'Neil, A, Worral, J. Beddle, T. Cooper, W. Townley, and J. Dakin.

TURBROOR v. RUNCORN A TRAM,--Tuebrook played 1 their first home fixture on Satitrday, their engagement being with Runcorn A team. Both sides were well' represented. The home captain won the toss, and Runcorn kicking off, the Brook quarters were at once the scene of operations. A series of well-contested scrimmages resulted in Wood getting possession and dropping a grand goal. Re-starting, the visitors' backs were again busy, and after A. Vickers effecting a relief, Lunt, receiving a smart pass from Wood, cleverly eluded all opposition, and grounded the oval over the home line. Wood was called upon to take the place, but the major point was not achieved. From the drop out the visitors again succeeded in placing the home team on the defensive, the backs being especially called into requisition. On the ball rclling ever the line, a minor point was conceded to ease the pressure. The home team now showed up`to greater advantage, Bayley and Vickers being especially prominent in their attempts to break through the visitors' defence. The interval shortly arrived, with Runcorn leading by one goal one try and one minor. After the re-start, Tuebrook pressed their opponents severely, andseerried like scoring, but their effors were frustrated by Booth conceding a minor point. After the kick-out the home' team still ° pressed, and kept the ball within the Runcorn half, it eventually rolling into touch close to the visitors' line. Lining out, Bleasdale pouncing the oval into play, got over, but Ellis Pearson failed to improve the point. From now to the finish of the game the ball travelled quickly from end to end, neither side being able to add to their score. the result stood—Runcorn A, one goal, one try, and two minors; Tuebrook, one try and one minor. Teams:— Runcorn: Booth. back; Cawley, Woods, and Lunt, three-quarter backs; Evans and Winyates, half backs; Gatley, Halewood, Abrams, Shaw, Bowyer, Barker. Rigby, Lea, and Dutton, forwards. Tuebrook: Bayley, back; Eccles, Mitchell, and A. Vickers, three-quarter , backs; L. Vickers, and Bleasedale, half backs; Hollo- way, A. Pearson, E. Pearson, Wylie, Western; Grundy, Dunn, and WoOtOn, forwards. • WIDNES v. 'OLDHAM.—These two teams met on Saturday afternoon, on the Lowerhouse-lane ground, Widnes. The ground was wet and slippery, but never- theless a good game was the result. This was the first time a contest has been decided between the two teems for the past three years, and considerable interest was evinced in the game, about 2,000 persons putting in an appearance. Oldham won the toss, and Widnes kicked off, by Plumpton, against a strong breeze. The ball was worked gradually to the visitors' quarters, and Kiddie dribbled over the line, but Broadhurst kicked dead. In a skort time an appeal was made by Johnson, of Widnes, for a try, but was subsequently disallowed. Plumpton made a fine run from the centre, and after a bit of good dodging- was secured. Barlow secured the leather, and when Clarke was charging put in a fine kick, which turned matters to the Widnes 25. W. Lees obtained a free kick from a Widnes forward, after which Mallalieu kicked dead. Mills got possession, and passed to Logan, who ran with the ball to the Widnes line, and not until some good dodging was he secured. The play assumed a more even aharacter, a lot of lying on continuing for some time. Barlow made a splendid run from the centre of the field, and on slipping near the Widnes quarter flag was prevented from carrying his attempt into execution. After a bit of open play Barlow tried another rush, but the leather was driven into touch. When free again, Kiddie passed to Clarke, when a lot of close passing took place in the visitors' 25, with the result of another minor. Play continued in a give and take fashion until half time followed, when the teams stood—Widnes, two minors: Oldham, three minors. After the change matters assumed a more vigoroualook. The ball was adeptly dribbled to the Oldham 25, from which Holt secured a try no goal resulting from Plumpton's kick. After bringing out, a I few long kicks were witnessed, and Plumpton returned in a neat manner. Another try was secured by Barber, but Kiddie failed at the place. For some time after the Wid nesians had a hard struggle, and the game terminated thus :—Widnes: two tries, seven minors; Oldham, four minors. Teams :—Widnes: Back, S.. Bingham ; three- quarter backs Plumpton (captain), -Parkinson, and Clarke ; half backs, Farrell and Wilkinson • forwards, Smith, Kiddie, Gandy, Barber, Pennington, Holt, Williams, J. Johnson, and Gordon. Oldham : Broadbent, back; Barlow, Moseley' and Logan, three-quarter backs ; Mill (captain) and Holden, half backs; forwards, Armstrong, Hankinson, T. Lees, W. Lees, Ingham. Whitehead, Bromley, Mallalieu, andanother. RuNconx v. SALE.—At Runcorn, in unfavourable weather, Hughes started the ball, and Crompton kicked well, and soon Sale kicked dead. Fast forward play enforced the game. A dribble by Rooker got to Run- corn half. Crompton saved, and some passing was indulged in by Davies, Hughes, Wainwright, and Riley, thelatter being well held by Harvey near the Sale line. As the result of a judicious kick by Drinkwater, the home quarter was visited, where Riley touched down Sale continued on the aggressive until P. Riley made a good run and finished with a pass to Wainwright, the ' latter making a bold bid for a try, but Tomlinson safely tackled him on the line. H. Hughes got an opening, and ed pass out to G i ayter, who ran n, Crompton scoring a goal from .the place. Crompton afterwards, after an excellent dodgy run, dropped a goal in the coolest fashion. Afterwards Drinkwater passed out to E. Har- vey, who dropped a good goal, bringing about half-time, with the score as follows :—Runcorn two goals and two minors, Sale one goal and one minor. The forwards on , both sides in the second half worked with great energy, until Runcorn got a firm footing in the Sale half, where play located, when Crompton enlivened the scene by dropping his second goal in the easiest manner possible. An onslaught was made on the Sale line, but the defence was good. The dribbling and running of the home 1 team was neutralized by the safe defence of the Sale backs, who saved and tackled fearlessly. Davies and Riley made efforts to geOn, but were held on the line, when the ball was thdown to Crompton, who dropped his third goal, dispensing with the formality of a ,try. Another rush by the home front rank got the ball under the bar, when, to the intenstedelight of the Runcornians, Crompton, from beneath the bar, coolly sent the ball over again for the fourth time. The Sale men under this heavy fire played hard, until young Crompton again stirred them up, and had another shot, which again was only too well meant, and by a splendid drop sent the ball flying over the bar for the fifth time. The game was at this point most exciting, the spectators cheering lustily, but Crompton, who kept cool, had the hardest luck in not bringing off his sixth goal, when the announcement of "No side" relieved Sale from a heavier score than was piled on :—Runcorn, six goals, five minors; Sale, one goal, one minor. Teams :—Run- corn: J. Brazendale, back ;T. H. Davies; 3. H Cromp- ton, and W. A. Riley, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes and J. Hollingworth, half-backs; W. Hughes, G. T. Wainwright, W. Faulkner, F. Hancack, R. Dolan, P. Riley, 3. Gayter, A. Hampson, and E. Andrews, for- wards. Sale: R. Tomlinson, back; W. Stephens, F. Drinkwater, and E. Harvey, three-quarter backs; A. Walters and W. Price,half-backs ' • T. Lings, E. W. Hunt, H. A. Howes, P.R. Rooker, C. Chapman, W. Whitehead, H. Walton, H. Harvey, and S. Green, forwards.

WARRINGTON A" Thera v BLIINDBLLSAND6 18T.—The above teams met at Blundellsands on Saturday, in raffia dull weather. The Warrington captain wen the toss and thirty-fives being the time agreed upon to play, the home captain kicked off at 3.40, the ball going into touch. Lawless broke away, but a wide pass on the part of Bibby let in the home team, Jolley stopping them from becoming dangerous. Warrington worked the ball into the home half, but Clarke getting possession from a loose scrimmage ran the ball back, being brought down by Samson. A free kick by Jolley caused play to be located in the Blundellsands' 25, but the home team worked the ball to centre, where some neat passing be- tween Lawless, Rowe, and Daniels took place, the latter player kicking into touch at the home quarter flag. From the line out Adamson passed to Sanson, who dropped at goal, a minor point resulting. Clarke dropped out, and no return being made play rested in the Warrington half. Norris here put in a long kick, and Jolley returning with a very lofty, punt, Alty got pos- session and made a grand run, gaining a try near the posts which Clarke converted into a goal. Isherwood restarted, ARS,' running the ball back to centre: The visiting fowards now played with great dash, and took the oval into the home half, but a well-judged kick by Clarke again took play to midfield. Warrington, how- ever, again pressed, and Bibby getting possession in the home 25 made a splendid run and gained a try. Jolley took the place kick, but failed at goal. Clarke restarted Sanson returning to Norris, who was collared by Adam- son. Lawless next crossed the the home line, but the point was disallowed. Blundellsands tranVerred play to centre, where Unsworth came away with a dribble, and being joined by Bate, Rowe, and Lawless, the ball was rushed over the line, a maul taking place, a try being ultimately given in to Lawless. The kick at goal again failed. Half time was called with the score standing— Warrington, 2 tries and 1 minor; Blundellsands, 1 goal. On change of ends Isherwood restarted for Warrington, play resting in the home half. A combined aribble of the Warrington forwards placed the home team on the defensive, and Lawless securing the ball from a scrim- mage near the line dashed over, and gained his second try. Isherwood this time tried at goal, but failed, the ball going just wide. Samson returned the drop out, into touch, the visite. s again having \tcl touch down. Unsworth next put in a good run, which, was neutralized by' Norris and Freeman, then Daniels was conspicuous with,a beautiful dribble to the home full back, whom he collared before any return could be made. Holmes, Lawless, and Adamson now broke away splendidly, taking the ball over the line, the latter player grounding the oval. Isherwood again took the place kick, but failed to land a goal. Warrington pressed severely, but Clarke by a dodgy run transferred to centre, where he was stopped by Jolley. Time was called with the score standing :—Warrington, 4 tries and 3 minor points; Blundellsands, 1 goal. Teams :—Warrington. Full back, T. Jolley; three-quarter backs, Daniels, Bibby, and Sanson; half backs, Lawless and Rowe; forwards, Adamson (captain), Eyes, Donohue, Isherwood, Holmes, Lloyd, Unsworth, F. Bate, and Beard. Blundellsands : Full back, A. Parr; three-quarter backs, Norris, Clarke, and Alt3r ; half backs, Roughley (captain) and Wright; forwards, Hiddleston, Carr, E Devnold, D. Devnold, Bradshaw, Freeman, Jones, Brainwood, and Davenhill.

WARRINGIrON V. CARLISLE. These two teams met for the first time en Saturday on the ground of the former, in the presence of a very large concourse of spectators. Both teams were well represented, though Jollley was absent from the War- rington contingent through indisposition., The weather was not altogether favourable as a pretty smart wind was blowing along the field, and in the second half there was a sharp downpour of rain. Turner for Warrington kicked off against the wind, Creaghan preventing a reply. The game was taken to the Carlisle line, and a smart pass from Evans to Massey almost enabled the latter to score ; however, Hodgkinson came to the rescue of his sideefor a free kick being allowed him, he was enabled to relieve the pressure. Povey came through a pack in marvellous fashion, drib- bling past his opponents with precision, finally transfer- lug the game from his own 25 to the visitor's line. Tinkler was hereabonts cheered for his efforts to save his side, but a combined rush by Turner and Ashton was taken up by Povey to the line. Quick work by Fair. Turnef gave Evans a chance, and the later gained a brilliane try, Fair. Turner making a good bid for goal. Hodgkinson dropped out, the game settling in mid-field. Wilson got away from a pack, and was the means of placing the home team on the defensive. This was only momentary, for Evans, interceptinva pass of Dodgson's, transferred to the visitors' quarters. Barnes passed neatly to Evans, and headway was made by a well- judged kick. From a pack near the line, Antrobus, Speakman, Evans, and Massey each indulged in trans- fers, with the result that the last-named scored at the corner flag, no goal resulting. Despite this rapid scoring the visitors played up to a man, and, urged on by the cheers of the excited spectator*, Dodgson dropped out. They could not break through the home defence, Barnes coining in for a fair share of applause for some neat play. After Evans and Barnes had passed and repassed to each other, Evans got over, but unfortunately in his last endeavour to gather possession he had the ill-luck to make the ball dead. A scrimmage was ordered at the quarter flag, and Scott replied to a grand punt of Massey's. Povey was again to the fore by one of his well-timed dribbles, and after Telford had threatened the home citadel Speakman intercepted liome passing of the Carlisle backs, and extinguished whatever chance they had of scoring a major point. Massey and Ashton now shone with some pretty work, and after Appleton, Barnes, Black, and Dodgson had exchanged kicks, Barnes became prominent by a smart save A grand drop at goal by Dodgson nearly had the desired effect, a minor resulting. Appleton became conspicuous soon after the drop out, and after Scott had been allowed a free kick Speakman with a smart pass to Massey neutralized the advantage gained. The home forwards now went away with a dash, and although Dodgson and Wilson responded gallantly, they could only add a minor point to their score, half time being called with the score reading Warrington two tries to Carlisle two minors. .The wind had now subsided, and p, slow drizzling rain had set in, rendering the oval very greasy and sadly against accurate passing. From the kick off Wilson almost got in, Appleton pushing him into touch a yard from the line. By good eginhined play of the Warrington forwards, conspicuous amongst o hers being Turner and Littlewood, the game was taken to the Carlisle quarter flag, where after a series of pretty exchanges Evans secured possession and, dodging his opponents splendidly, gained his second try, Fair. Turner again failing at the place. Massey replied to the drop out, a touch in goal resulting.. Antrobus and Barnes showed up now for the Warrmgtonians, and Scott was compelled to relieve his side by conceding a minor. Although the odds were greatly against the visitors they played up with renewed vigour. They elicited cheers for a splendid dribble, and although Dodg- son had a clear course, the fleetness of Massey averted any danger. Turner responded in brilliant styletand went down the field at a terrific rate, the bval being taken I over, Littlewood grounding, but through some infringe. ' ment the ball was ruled back. However, fortune still favoured the home club, for after a futile drop at goal by Evans, Bandies was in attendance and grounded near the posts, Barnes adding a goal. The restart from centre found the Warringtonians on the visitors' line, and a mull byScott allowed Nevins to gain a try, the kick at raai failing. Massey made a good run from the drop out, and almost got in. The interest in the match had somewhat subsided, and scrambling play was now seen until the whistle sounded for "No wide" with the score as follows :—Warrington, one goal', four tries, four minors ; Carlisle, two minors. EGThe game was an eminently satisfactory one from a spectator's point of view, as both teams seemed bent upon keeping it open, and anything in the nature of roughness or " off-sidedness" were conspicuously absent. Though the fates were unfavourable to the Cumbrians 1 from the beginning, the latter never showed the slightest discouragement, and played their level best up to the finish. The home team played finely and systematically rall through, and almost every try they scored was the result of unselfish and well-wdged passing. Evans made a splendid centre,and he was well supported by the two wing men. A word •of praise is also due to the half-backs who played a thoroughly unselfish game. With regard to the forwards, Povey's praises were on everybody's lips for his repeated fine dribbles from the pack and his efforts were capitally backed by W. Dillon, pack, Ashton, and Creagan. Of the visitors' pack Wilson, Dodgson, Hodgkinson, and Black were worthy of notice. Teams :—Warrington: Apple- ton, back • Massey, Evans, and Barnes, three-quarter backs; Antrobus and Speakman, half-backs; Dillon (captain.), -Fair. Turner, Ashton, Povey, Littlewood, Nevins, Bandies, E. Dillon, Creaghan, forwards. Car- lisle: Scott, back; Dodgson (captain), Telford, and Hodgkinson, three-quarter backs: Wilson and Tinkler, half-backs; Burgess, Davies, Brown, Black, Bell, Metcalf, Ballinger, S. Edwards, and yipond, forwards. Referee: Mr, Roger Wilcock, West Lancashire Union.

The Gas Committee reported that the average illumin- ating power of the gas during the past four weeksfwas equal to 17.80 candles at both works. The Committee also recommended that the tender Of Messrs. John Scow- croft and Co., Limited, to supply 1,000 tons of coal, be accep ed ; and, that the sum of thirty guineas be voted to the Somugh Auditors for their services in auditing the accounts of this department for the past year. Adopted on the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Alderman HARRISON.

WARRINGTON &ED THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT. The General Purposes Committee recommended that the report of the Parliamentary Sub-Committee (assisted by Messrs. Platt, Francomb, and Wright) as to the division of the borough into three county electoral divisions be adopted. The report Ltated that the population of the borough and of the several wards as ascertained by the poll taken on the 12th of May last is as follows :—ln the North-West Ward, 16,241; in the North-East Ward, 15,689; in the South-West Ward, 2,935; in the South-East Ward, 7.436; in the Latchford Warti, 5,024: total, 47,325. That the number of burgesses in each ward is as fol- lows:—In the North-West Ward, 2,489; in the North- East Ward, 2,404; in the South-East Ward, 1,209; in the South-West Ward, p 11; in the Latchford Ward, 763. The Sub-Committee therefore beg to recommend that the borough be divided as follows :—Electoral Division No. 1 to consist of and be coterminous with the North. West Ward ; electoral division No. 2 to consist of and be coterminous with the North-East Watfd ; electoral divi- sion No. 3 to consist of and be coterminous with the South-East, South-West, and Latchfbrd Wards. Adopted on the motion of the MAYOR. A FAREWELL.

The Queen and Royal suite will leave, Balmoral for Windsor Castle on Wednesday, November 14th, and travelling during'the night, will reach the Royal borough on the morning of the 15th, shortly before nine o'clock. CONGRESS Os' RAILWAY SERVANTS.-011 Tuesday, at the Preston Piiblic Hall, the annual congress of railway servants of England, Ireland, Scotland, and Wales was commenced. After the reading of a letter by the secretary from Mr. P. Stewart Macliver, stating his inability to be present, 'Mr. Harold Lewis, of Bath, who wastappointed president,' addressed the conference. He complimented them on the growth of the society, it having increased its numbers by the addition of 1,864 members in the past year, being the largest growth since the year 1874. Referring to the question of overtime, he said men often worked sixty-eight hours a week, and it had been stipulated that a man could not have over- time unless he worked 144 hours a fortnight. They had 'moved rapidly during the last few years, and the voice of the many would now be listened to.—The Secretary's report showed that the society at present consists of 194 branches, and the total number of members on June 30th last was 11,630. The gross income during the year 1887 amounted to f 22,883. On Wednesday the Congress considered that to each gang of platelayers there should be attached a man to give warning of approaching trains. Resolutions were also adopted in favour of the amendment of the Employers' Liability Bill.

div.head: ALLEGED CHILD MURDER AT
div.p: THE ALLEGED CHILD MURDER AT
HAYDOCK.

The single young woman, named Hannah Harri- son, of Chipsley-row, Ilaydock, who had been re- naanded on a charge of causing the death of her illegitimate son, George Albert, three years of age, by drowning him in Queen Pit reservoir. Haydock, on the previous Sunday night, was again brought up at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday. The magistrates on the Bench were Mr. R. Hough- ton (chairman), and Messrs. F. J. Gillespie and W. F. Gooch. Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, ap- peared on behalf of the prisoner.—Superintendent Heywood stated that the prisoner was apprehended on the previous Monday, and was on the following day brought up at Warrington and remanded to that Court until the inquest on the body could be held. The inquest was summoned for the Wednes- day, but it was adjourned until Monday. He had, therefore, to ask that the prisoner might be re- manded to some convenient day after the day of the inquest.—Mr. Riley said he did not oppose the remand, and after some conversation it was decided

that the prisoner should be ,remanded for a and to be then brought up at the Warrington Co Police Court. - 4 INQUEST AND VERDICT. On Monday, at the Waggon and Horses Hotel, dock, Mr. Brighouse, coroner, resumed his inquiry, the circumstances attending the death of the boYiu Albert Harrison, whose mother was in custody charge of causing his death. Mr. H. L. Riley wal the proceedings for the accused, and Superintei Heywood and other police officers were present. A of the locality showing the road to Ashton and the voir at Queen Pit, in which it was inferred the rhlh been drowned, was produced.—Mary Cross said sill the wife of John Cross, of Clipsley-row, Har Hannah Harrison, her daughter., was a single wn aged twenty-four, and her son, George Albert, los im years of a. On Sunday afternoon, tlfe 23rd 111'_ ~ daughter 'i'ook the child and went to Ashton. eleven o'clock,ths same night she saw her daught the back of Twenty-eight row, in Haydock-lane. le-agedwomannamedMaryAnnTianowwski, ler the title of "Madame" Kanowwski, is ied to attending markets in the capacity of Affst,-was brought before the Warrington I Magistrates on Monday morning on a of having stolen from the platform of the I Station, on Saturday night, two leather cases hug six medicine bottles, three hookas, a a mahogany case, a box of surgical instru- , and a napthita lamp,together of the value of 4., the property of William Cunningham, a st from Byrom-street,Deansgate, Manchester. ..os evidence it appeared that Kanowwski, who is a and who lives at Widnes, had on Saturday been selling her wares in the Market, where the n. had also been carrying on his business. In prosecutor went to the Central Station in 'n Proceed by train to Manchester, taking with ' articles in question. He placed them on the 1,41119 and, with another person, went into efradiment room. Prisoner in the meantime the platform, and, as she was drunk and rather )Us, she was ordered to leave the station pre- She said "Let me have my things, then," and Up the articles produced—those alleged to' have stolen. Shortly afterwards the prosecutor came out ' refreshment room, and Missed his luggage. He 'tied the matter to Constable Lambert, who is a policeman, and that person remembered the r having left the station with the luggage. - was made for her, but she could not be found eleven o'clock, when she returned to the station to ,rain for Widnes. Prisoner had no luggage with . nen, and on being questioned as-to the missing pro- '3' she denied all knowledge of it. She was given ',custody, and on the following morning P.O Chant- "lnd the missing property at the British Workman * House in Horsemarket-St., where the prisoner left tween nine and ten on Saturday evening. In reply 3 charge, prisoner said "The two cases and the are mine ; the others I know nothing about." In -ie of his evidence Constable Lambert said that -isoner was ordered off the station she was 'le drunk." What he meant by that term, he fled, was that she tried to make herself appear "when she could,scarcely walk. After the evidence ta concluded prisoner said that she remembered 'about the matter, and the prosecutor said that mown her for twenty years, and had never heard of her doing anything dishonest. The crates imposed a fine of 20. s and costS, or, in It of payment, fourteen days' imprisonment, and a charge of drunkenness against the prisoner was ,wn.

Continuing his evidence, witness said thO last time he was in the house was in May, and then he was not in for a minute.—Sarah Brookes (recalled) said it was true that Mrs. Hurdsfield, immediately after she came hack from the doctor's or from some other errand had told her that in the mean- while she had asked he deceased if it was true that she had taken anything, and she said "No, it's a lie." She could not say whether it was directly she came in, but in the course of the morning, before deceased died. After hearing Mrs. Hurdsfield say this, she saw the deceased again, and said to her, "Emily, will you tell Mrs. Hurdsfield what you told me on Saturday ?" and she said "It's too late."—By the Coroner': She had seen Cunningham and the deceased woman together :At Buckley's, but she had never seen Cunningham in deceased's house. Since she had kept such company, she had little to do with her. The Coroner said he though- it would be better to have a post- mortem before they proceeded any further. They could not do without it. It was necessary on Cunningham's account, and for the cause of justice.— A juryman asked if it would not be as well to have the postman called who took the round.—The Coroner said he might say that the postman could not remember leaving anything at Mrs. Buckley's, but if they liked they could call him at the next hearing, as well as the son of ,he deceased.—The inquiry was then adjourned until Thursday. The adjourned inquest was held at Knutsford on Thursday, when Dr. Garstang said he had made a post mortent and found no trace of poison. The deceased died from hemorrhage. The coroner saki there was no case against the man implicated, and the jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical evidence.
BEWSEY-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL HARVEST THANKSGIVING.

- • Special thanksgiving services for the safe gather- ing in of the harvest were held at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, on Sunday. The sacred edifice was decorated for the. occasion in an elegant if not profuse manner. The reading desk presented a picturesque appearance, being fringed with clusters of oats, the panels being embossed with beautiful clusters of white asters, relieved by a background of dark green ivy. On the centre panel of the rostrum was suspended a remarkably fine cluster of white grapes with a bunch of dark ones as a centre, while the side panels were decorated with a beautiful lattice of oath. The rails were wreathed with long stems of clinging ivy, while the same plant, with branches of fir, studded- with dahlias, was wound round the communion table. The space inside these was filled with vegetables, fruit, and a number of choice plants, a prominent place at the foot of the communion table being , occupied by a large cottage loaf. The table itself was entirely hidden beneath a tasteful arrangement of moss, upoit which were laid several baskets of flowers and fruit. The front of the choir stalls was embellished ;with a trellis- work and edging of corn and flowers. All the windows were occupied by hothouse plant i; surrounded with cut flowers. The pillars were adorned in a tasteful manner by fringes of oats and ivy, varied with flowers of various colours, and the standards, &c., were decorated in a similar manner. The bulk of the decoration was done by Mrs. Brookes, Mrs. J. Shaw Green, Mrs. Furness, Mrs. John Hayward, M. Isaac Hayward, Mrs. Beaman, Mrs. Place, Mrs. Price Edelsten, Miss Emily Benne-, Miss L. Horton, Miss Birchen, and Miss Jones. Gifts of material were sent from many friends both inside and out of the congregation. The principal contributors,how. ever, were: Mr. John Bennett (Bewsey Hall), Mr. Join Taylor (Sankey Hall). Mr. John Hindley (Rixton), Mr. J. Shaw Green, Mr. Isaac Warbur.on, Mr. George Nack- hurst, Mr. Jchn Hayward, Mr. Isaac Hayward, Mr. Parkinson, Mr. John Houghton, and Mr. Buck. The morning service was taken by the Rev. E. H. Jackson, who preached an excellent sermon from the text, "For hOu presentest him with the blessing of goodness." (Psalm xxi. 3) ; while in the evening the Rev. William Brookes delivered an eminently practical address, based upon the words, "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matt. VI. II.) There were large attendances at both services. Special anthems were sung by the choir, Mr. James presiding at the organ.

TEMPERANCE MEETING AT WIDNES.

Under the auspices of the United Temperance Demonstration Committee, a public meeting and entertainment were held at the Volunteer Hall, on Monday evening. Mr. Benjamin Brown occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. T. Lai, Messrs. Shaw (Earn orth ), S. Stringer, T. Reay, J. Thompson, &c. In opening the proceedings, the Chairman said he was glad to take part in the develop- ment of those principles which were so sound in them- ' selves. (Hear, hear.) The result of 40 or 50 years' -labour in the Bands of Hope and other' temperance or- ganizations was to sun in the higher moral tone that prevailed in many departments of life, and especially in reference to the drinking customs. He trusted that the work would still go on, and leaven this nation until we should see far better times through the res-riction if not the total prohibition of the sale of intoxicating drinks. (Applause.)—The Rev. T. Law announced that he Was a " life teetotaller," and he was there to publicly declare his colours as soon as pos- sible. (Applause.) He moved "That this meeting con- siders the sale of intoxicating liquor on the Lord's Day to be unfair, and,ifijurious • and demands for Etigland the same prohibition of theraffic in intoxicating liquors during the whole of the Lord's day, as in other parts of the United Kingdom and many of our Colonies, which has been attended with most beneficial results."—Mr. Fox seconded the resolution, which was dipported by the Chairman, who said he was Satisfied that a higher and healthier moral tone would pervade Widnes if it were not for Sunday work and the Sunday opening of public-houses. The publican ought not to have a privilege over the other tradesmen, and a privilege that was used to the degradation of our fellow beings. Con- sidering the present state of trade in Widnes and the action taken by certain manufacturers, he thought that nine tenths Of the, Sunday. work in Widnes could be abolished now. (Hear, hear.) The abolition og Sunday labour would be a grand thing for the men, for their house. 4, and for their employers. (Applause.) The resolution was passed unanimously and was ordered to be forwarded to the Prime Minister, to Mr. Edward Moss, M.P., and to Mr. Stevenson. The entertainment consisted of selections of music rendered by a choir of 250 children from the various bands of hope in the town. Under the leadership of Mr. S. Lamb, the Choir gave much satisfaction. An interesting feature was a recitation contest. Among those over ten years of age th'ere competed :—Betsv Kenrick, Mary Ellen Farmer, Francis Lamb, Maggie Harrison, Saralr Hollins, Esther Hambrook, and Albert Lees. The prizes were awarded to Esther Handbrook, 1 ; Maggie Harrison, 2; Mary Ellen Farmer, 3. In the competition for children under ten only three competed, and they were placed as follows 1, llarry Taylor ; 2, Phoebe Seincolls ; 3, Willie Buckley. , A speaking contest caused much interest. Mr. Henry Wright obtained the first prize, and Mr. John Thompson the second, Mr. T. Reav was the only other competitor. —The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

• SNOW STORMS.—On Thursday in many parts of the country the cold was intense, and from the Isle of Man and Scotland come reports of severe snowstorms. At Kirkwall, in Orkney, the gale was fierce, snow fell throughout the day and at night there was a tremen- dous storm of hail—of square lumps of ice and big hail- stones."
