- . Ittttrs to tin Obitor. _ THE RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION AND ITS CANDIDATES. Sir,—As I see that the Ratepayers' Association is think- ing of bringing candidates forward for the Town Council ?this November, might I smggest that its nominees be men who can vote. One scmetimes hears it said contemp- tuously of certain members of Parliament that they can vote, and that is all they are good for. Ent" there's a sea below the sea," andthere are deeper depths of inanity than have been reached by members of Parliament even. These can always be relied upon to vote at the bidding of the "whip," but the Warrington Ratepayers'. Association has representatives in the Council so helplessly invertebrate that they cannot even vote "aye" or " nay. ' Let us hope that the new nominees of the Association will have the courage of their opinions, and that they will be able to assume the perpendicular when these opinions are to be asserted. Yours &c., MOTOR. Oct. 3,168 a.

ST. PETER'S PARISH, WARRINGTON. Sir,—l shall be grateful if you will permit me through your columns to call the attention of Churchmen to the pressing need of a church in St. Peters' Parish. It is just 14 years since St. Peter's was endowed and gazetted as a 'separate Peel Distukt, but as yet there is no church for the parishioners-to worship in. although efforts have been made from time totime to build one. The great difficulty which stood in the way of this work being carried out, was the impossibility of procuring a suitable site in the district as then arranged. This difficulty has at last been overcome, as the boundaries have been altered so as to include a site offered by Mr. William Sharp. The living is in public patronage it/the alternate gift of the Rector of Warrington and the vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington, the next appointment being the Rector's. The nominal endoWment is £248, the net receipt £l5O. The population of the parish is now nearly 7,000, almost entirely composed of the working class of society, and to accommodate this formidable number and to minister to their moral and spiritual interests, there is at present one schoolroom, capable of seating at the outside 200 persons. This building is also used alternately as a Sunday school, day school. night school, for tea parties, band practises, public meetings, and even for parliamentary and municipal voting The services of the Church are thus most objectionably interfered with by the trivial and rougher incidents of secular life. It is now proposed to build a Church to seat 700 persons at a cost not to exceed £3,000, and plans which have been prepared by Mr. Med- - land Taylor, of Manchester, have been approved by the Committee for this purpose. The church to be erected will be entirely free and unappropriated. Ido most earnestly hope that all Churchmen in this neighbourhood will help forward this most needed and valuable work. The build- ing of a Church in this very poor parish must depend on the good will of those outside the parish, as he inhabit- ants of the district are quite unable by themselves to accomplish this object. I therefore appeal to all who, daily pray" Thy kingdom come," to show in a practical form that they mean what they say, by joining in this work for the spreading of that kingdom in this poverty- stricken district. The small sum of £lOOO only is needed in order to enable this work to be at once taken in hand. —I remain, &c., 16, Salisbury-st.

div.head: GEORGE DANIEL WRAY.
div.p: GEORGE DANIEL WRAY.
LONGFORD DEPOT.-LETTER FROM THE MANAGER.

...... &r,—l regret theoremarks of Alderman Burgess at the last meeting of the Town Council compel me again tO take up my pen. He says, "I hold in my hand Mr. Dinwiddie's return for each week for the year, com- mencing the first week in January and ending the last week in December, in which he gives 6 tons 12 cwts. 1 qr. as his average week's return of the material worked through at Longford ;" and again, "We have the result of the working since Mr. 111 inwiddie left ; return, not of 6 tons 12 cwt. 1 qr., but of 9 tons 2 cwts., out of the same material, each week." And still again, "the percentage of moisture is less than when we were getting a return of 6 tons 12 cwts. 1 qr." Now, Sir, the average of 6 tons 12 cwts. 1 qr. per week that I made was perfectly finished manure, ready for the grinding mill. The 9 tons 2 cwt., is not finished and ready for the grinding mill, but is simply an estimated quantity from a larger quantity of wet material produced; and if next week they were to finish it fit for grinding, similar to the 6 ton 12 cwt. 1 qr., they could not pro- duce more than another 2 tons—so that if the 9 tons 2 cwt. and the further 2 tons be averaged for the two weeks it would just be over 5 tons per week. This is a serious matter. Who is telling the truth ? The Coun- cil and Committee should try and learn this as soon as possible, for if a system of deception is being practised upon them they will be landed in far greater trouble and difficulties than they have had yet to encounter. There is just another matter I wish to notice and then I have finished. The Chairman says, "If Mr. Dinwiddie had been left to himself‘ the contention that evening would not have come up. He wished Mr. Diriwiddie had been less interfered with and they would not then have experienced such a difficulty." These statements are altogether incorrect. I have acted throughout in this matter, wisely or unwisely, entirely on my own responsibility, and have not been in the ;lightest degree interfered with by anyone. The Chairman again says, "Mr. Dinwiddie had sent a letter to the Town Clerk's office saying that he was taking time to consider the matter. He understood, he said he was in the hands of his friends—that he was not acting exactly on his own idea in ---' •• ' • --0 his friends, as _1 Winorrnity to tun wlsnes . Ile called them." This is on a par with his othell gate- I ments, the letter I wrote can, I have no doubt, be seen at the Town Clerk's office by any member of the Com- mittee or Council, and they will see that I have not said that I was not acting exactly on my own idea, and that I never mention my friends in it. The letter was simply an acknowledgment of the receipt of a copy of a resolution asking me to resign, and that I would consider the matter and write them further on the subject. I was pleased to read that a full enquiry into the whole scheme and management has shortly to take place. I think that ultimately, and at no distant day, the truth will prevail.—l am, sir, yours respectfully, THOMAS DINWIDDIE. [lf, as our correspondent insists, the Sanitary Committee are comparing unfinished with finished manure, they are doing Mr. Dinwiddie a gross injustice. The point is an important one, and ought to be determined without delay—ED. E.r.j

CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES PUBLICAN. On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Edward Banks, landlord of the Vine Inn,Waterloo-road, was summoned for having permitted drunkenness on his premises on the 15th of last mouth. John Howard and Sebastian Kenrick were also sum- moned for having been drunk•on the premises. Mr. Rideal appeared for the defence. Evidence was en by P.C. Maitland to the effect that at about ten o'clock on the night in question he, in company with Constable Holbrook, visited the house of the defendant Banks. They found eight persons in the parlour, and one of them, the defendant Howard, was drunk. Passing through the bar, they went into the kitchen, and there found three persons. One of them, the defendant Kenrick, was lying on the floor. He was drunk, and on the floor near him was a broken glass. The constable drew the land- lord's attention to the matter, and he (the landlord) thereupon commenced to abuse the officers. In Corroboration, evidence was given by P.C. Hol- brook, who said that the defendant Kenrick was so drunk as to be unable to rise from the kitchen floor without assistance. For the defence, Mr. Rides] , submitted that there was no evidence to show that the men Howard and Kenrick had been served with drink in the house kept by Banks. He also con- tended that Howard was not drunk, and, while admitting that Kenrick was somewhat under the influence of liquor, he accounted for the fact of his being found on the floor by stating that someone had pulled his chair away, and caused him to fall. After hearing evidence for the defence, the Bench fined defendant Banks .C 2 with 198. costs. The licence would not be endorsed, but the magistrates were of opinion that Banks was not a fit person to keep a public house. For having been drunk on the premises John Howard was fined 10s. and costs, and Sebastian Kenrick was fined ss. and costs. The case occupied the attention of the court for a couple of hours.

VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT
ItUNCORN.

SPEECH BY THE VICA_R. The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connection with the F. and G. companies (Runcorn) of the 2nd C.V.R was held in the Drill Hall, Green- way-road; and as usual proved a very successful function. A capital audience assembled, and had the pleasure of listening to an admirable musical , entertainment. Songs were given by Miss Amy R.l Giles, (of Chester) and Miss Clara Taylor, and Messrs. E. S. Giles, (Chester) Lewis (Widnes), J. H. Harrison, 1 B. ' Morris A. Fox, and T. Whinyats. Miss B. Hankin- son skilfully performed a pianoforte solo. The, duties of accompanists were fulfilled by Mr. W. "i 3 Kay and Mr. J. Ravenscroft. The Rev. A. Maitl'and. Wood presided over the proceedings, and at the com- mencement delivered a speech, in which he reterred to the great progress the volunteers had ina4le in efficiency and numbers since they,' were established ; and said when they c,onsidered that this country was at this Vane prac- tically defended by not more than eighty thousand regular troops, and that tha popularity of the militia was by no means increasing, we ought to pay every regard and attention to the con- dition and welfare of the Volunteers of this country. (Hear, hear.) Speaking in advocacy of the Volunteer movement, the Vicar said that in no place in the world could the qualities of esprit de corps and the qualities of good fellowship be better learned than amongst the Volunteers. (Applause.) One of the things most wanted by English young men of s.ll classes was to learn that obedience which they could learn from being drilled. He hoped that we should never have a conscription, but he did wish that our young men when at the age of a hobbledehoy, would put themselves under the guidance of Sergeant Player, and be trained to behave themselves and to be useful members of the community. (Applause.) Captain •Jolliffe said in past years they had been in the habit of grumbling at the way in which Government had treated the Volunteers, but he was glad to say that matters were mending in this respect. (Hear, hear.) That the recognition of the Government had been well appreciated during the past year was evinced by the fact that the drilling of the Runcorn Companies had been better and the shooting both in class firing and in ' private practice had shown a very marked improvement —5 points per man better than last year. (Applause.) The detachment under his command now numbered 168 men and only one of these was non-efficient. They had been to camp and there had behaved splendidly and had passed a very satisfactory inspection. The detach- ment sent the usual number of men to Wimbledon, and they had not come back altogether barren, because Captain Timmins, who was one of "their best shots, brought back the Martin's cup. (Applause.) No less than £5O had been contributed towards the prize fund, and they were deeply grateful to the people of Runcorn for their support. (Applause.) Mrs. Walter Wigg then presented the volunteers with their prizes, and she was afterwards cordially thanked for her kindness. The following is a complete list :

WARRINGTONIA.NS IN AMERICA. • INTERVIEW WITH MR. W. PORTER. This week we give further particulars of the interview of one of our representatives with Mr. W. Porter, who is on a visit to Warrington, from Van- couver, British North America.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
FATAL ACCIDENT AT WARBURTON.

An accident which has unfortunately been attended with fatal consequences, happened to a boy named Thomas Deganes, who lives at Hollins Green, and was employed on the Warburton section. Be was " spra.g- ging " wagons—that is to say stopping them with pieces of wood—on a high bank, next to the Warrington road at Rixton, when he was knocked down by the tipping engine and severely crushed. He was removed to the hospital at Latchford, and his injuries were attended to by Dr. Burne, but he soon afterwards succumbed. MOORE TO STOCKTON HEATH. . _ _

The severe weather has made the work very hard for the navvies. At Moore a navvy has sustained a slight breakdown, and is.being, repaired. At Morley Common the men are cutting through the rock rapidly, in spite of the cold and .wet. At Stockton Heath the large American navvy employed removing George's Bank has finished a second breadth. The new road Is also pro- gressing at a satisfactory rate. LATCFIFORD TO WARBURTON..

_ At this section two American navvies at the head of the cutting have cut through what was an oat-field, and are now within ten yards of the cottages opposite Cedar Lawn, the late residence of Alderman Pickmere. The new road between Thelwall-lane and Knutsford-road is now open, and is in the best condition for traffic. Mr. T. A. Walker, the contractor, visited the section on Wednes- day, accompanied by Mr. W. W. Topham. IRLAM. Ddiring the past week there has been a further exten- sion of the Ship Canal works on the Irlam section. and excavations are now being made in the meadows at Lower Irlam lying between the Irwell and the tollbar on the Manchester and Warrington turnpike road. The track or ballast line which has been constructed from Irlam station, on the Cheshire Lines, to Irlam Boat, on the Flixton side of the river, has been extended along the valley of the Irwell beyond Salamanca locks, in the direction of Hulme's Bridge, Flixton, where it will join ,hat rnnning from Barton. At Boat Lane, Flixton, quite a young colony is being established. There are about 20 workmen's huts being erected, in addition to a hos- pital, the contractor's stores and offices, and engine sheds. Although a cart road has been made across the river, connecting Flixton with Irlam, for the use of navvies and the contractor's vehicles, visitors are stiil compelled to cross the river by boat. A large cutting of the canal has been made between Boat Lane and the river, which has now reached a depth of 25ft , and the excavations are being tipped in the meadows lying in the direc ion of Partington. and a very high embank- ment is being raised towards the Cheshire Lines Rail- way, which will be diverted and raised in order to allow ocean-going steamers to sail underneath the arch of the railway. Navvies are still engaged in the cutting on the westerly side of the Cheshire Lines at Partington, which is to divert the Mersey into the Irwell. On the Irlam section there are about nine locomotives at work, and three more are to follow to-day.

div.head: BARTON.
div.p: BARTON.

The progress of the Barton section has been so satis- factory that night shifts have been dispensed with, and a number of men discharged and sent to the Salford section, where night work has been commenced, and whither the French and German steam navvies from Barton section have been sent. The formation of the trackway underneath the southern arches of the aque- duct and Barton ' Bridge is nearly completed, and ledges have had to be cut into the solid rock on the southern bank of the river. Between New Barnes, Sal- ford, and the Hollins Green boathouse no less than twelve track bridges for ballast lines have been made across the river. TELEPHONEIC COMMUNICATION.

A telephone is now erected along the whole line of the Canal and communication is open from Manchester to Eastham. The switch exclian,e is at Thelwall, where the telephone clerks are kept busy attending to the numerous messages passed up and down, A WEAK BRIDGE. The temporary bridge erected by Mr. Walker from Statham across the river to Rixton Ley has again shown symptoms of weakness. The insecurity of the founda- tions is probably accounted for by the fact that the whole island is quicksand. Orders have been given to repair it with all possible speed. jtiff; AdellAistrr TO THE SCOTCH

div.head: EXPRESS AT WINWICK.
div.p: EXPRESS AT WINWICK.

" Zinco," who writes the London letter for the "Sheffield Weekly Telegraph," made reference in Saturday's issue of that journal to the recent mis- hap to the Scotch Express near Winwick Junction, in the following terms :—" The Race of Death, as the speed competition between the rival " expresses" has been called, has justified its title. Already the catastrophe is a nine days' wonder, and when memory is a little blunted the race may begin again. There is money in it—sufficient excuse for official blindness. The point I wish to note in connection with this past event is one which ought to appeal to the latent chivalry I believe to exist in every true British heart, The V.C. is given to the heroes of strife, to those who either successfully strew the battle-field, or who, from another aspect secure the liberties of their country. It is con- fined alone to winners in the game of war; but as great heroes—greater, perhaps--are to be found in the unconsidered ways of life, wherever there are danger and iisk, some helpless wait to rescue, something to do in the interests of pure humanity, unattended by any crown of laurels, or sound of popular applause. In one of my recent letters I spoke of the gallant Fire Brigade, who often at a moments notice, in cool blood, not in the exciting and inspiring rush of battle, do deeds that stand level with that of the famous Light Brigs ie. "Theirs not to make reply— Theirs not to reason why; Theirs but to do and die. Into the Valley of Death Ride the brave firemen." Not a fireman, scoring many lives plucked from the burning, ever won the Victoria Cross. And not a pointsman whose cool action at a critical moment has saved as many lives as a V.C. has taken, has even an order of merit awarded him. When the Scotch express was flying through a deep cutting at sixty miles an hour, a signalman noticed that "something was wrong"—" someone had blun- dered." He put up his signal to call the driver's attention to the state of affairs. He also telegraphed for the man next door to do likewise, and by this means the driver was enabled to pull up much quicker than he would otherwise have done. Meanwhile, however, the train had been tearing up the line for a long distance. Some state that this occurred for a distance of a mile, and when the train drew up it was found that three of the car- riages were greatly damaged; but the brake had considerably slackened the speed of the train, and so rapidly was the stoppage effected that neither the .engine nor the brake van left the rails or was in any way injured, nor was the permanent way damaged except for a few yards. When it became known what had occurred and how narrow had been their escape, there was naturally great excitement amongst the passengers ; but, except in the car- riages nearest to the disabled van, few passengers travelling by the train were aware that anything had gone wrong until informed of the fact after the halt. And this prevention of a great "slaughter," was due to the quickness and promptness of the signalman, who will probably not even be com-

div.head: TOURNEY TO VANCOUVER.
div.p: THE TOURNEY TO VANCOUVER.

"When I went to Vancouver," Mr. Porter said, "I went by way of Quebec, and right overland from that town to my destination. On landing at Quebec, Englishman-like, I felt as though I should like to see the citadel, a place famous for its connection with the great General Wolfe. I consequently went there with my wife, and, seeing a sentry walking in front, we told him we wanted to go through the citadel, but he walked on and took no notice. We repeated what we thad said, and just at that moment a soldier—evidently a corporal-- walked out of the massive gateway, and we told him what we had told the sentry, but he, like the other, said not a word and walked away. We stood awhile when an officer came out, and after telling him what we wanted he replied " all right," and told a man to show us through the place. With the exception of these few words, we did not hear another syllable of the Queen's language in the citadel—even the drill instructor who was drilling the Artillery spoke in the trench language. In Quebec itself, you scarcely ever hear the English language ; and when my wife went, into the markets she had to have an interpreter .with her. From Quebec we went on to Ottawa. a very nice place, and just as well situated as a capital city could be. The Parliament houses here are situated on a kind of mount overlooking the city, and the view from them is very fine. we stayed a few days with friends in Ottawa, and found that there, as in Quebec, the French language is predominant, and that the French Canadians seem to have a vetoing power oval. everything. From Ottawa we went right on to Winnipeg, the great centre of the Manitoba wheat- growing district. Although at the present time it is pretty dull, Winnipeg undoubtedly has a great future before it, and will in course of time be to Canada what Chicago is to the States. The wheat of Manitoba is poured into Winnipeg by rail, water, and every possible means of conveyance. The rail- way journey from Winnipeg to Vancouver was unbroken, and for a day and a half we travelled over a rolling prairie which remined one of nothing so much as the sea. In America they are far in advance of England in the matter of railway travelling. You may walk from one end of. the train to the other, and at night you can sleep with as much ease and repose as if you were in your own private house.

div.head: VANCOUVER AS A FIELD OF EMPLOYMENT. _. .
div.p: VANCOUVER AS A FIELD OF EMPLOYMENT. _. .

With regard to wages the man who, I think, does best at Vancouver is the engineer, as he can almost demand his own figure. After him comes, perhaps, the plumber, and then the mason and bricklayer. The mason gets about six dollars a day, and the bricklayer five dollars. The painter gets about three dollars a day, the carpenter—if there are no joiners—from two and a half to three, and the common labourer from two to two and a half. The style of living of workpeople there is much superior to what it is in England. Take the case of a brick- layer. or even a common labourer. He goes to his work in the morning and at twelve o'clock knocks off for dinner. He takes off his working clothes— or deshabilles as they call them—which he wears above a good suit and then goes to his hotel, for nearly all men live at hotels. He sits down at the table, his employer perhaps sitting at the same table, and has a dinner of four or five courses, fruit, fish, flesh and soon. After dinner, or lunch as they call it, he will put on his deshabilles and go back to his work, and so on day after day. His meals will cost him about seventy-five cents a day, and his bed at night about twenty-five cents or in all about a dollar a day. After his day's work "Jack is as good as his master," and the workman does not consider himself in any way inferior to his employer. As amusements they have their theatre and other places of resort, and games, including the national game of lacrosse. In fact they enjoy themselves pretty much as you do in England.

div.head: NOBLE SAVAGE.
div.p: THE NOBLE SAVAGE.

We have a number of Indians who are most peaceable, and the quietest class of people I ever met with. They are Christians and very religious, and I believe most conscientious in everything they do. I was going to say that I would tooner trust an Indian than a white man at all events you can trust them with anything, they are so truthful and honest. They live chiefly by fishing. The dog-fish is not a fish which The Canadians eat, but it is very profitable for the oil that is obtained from its liver. The Indians catch these fishes, take the livers out and put them in a barrel, where they dissolve them- selves into oil, and this oil is sold for use at the saw-mills round about, and is worth in English money about half-a-crown a gallon. The Indians are very sober, and in Act saloon keepers are not allowed to supply them with liquor under a penalty of two hundred dollars. They consequently never taste liquor except when a little smuggling takes places, and then those who are guilty are made an example of, if they are caught.

div.head: ME. WINSTANLEY AT SALEM.
div.p: ME. WINSTANLEY AT SALEM.

In answer to a question as to Mr. Winstanley, who left Warrington recently with his family for America, and who now lives at Salem, Oregon, Mr. Porter said: "Salem is between 300 and 400 miles from Vancouver, and is the capital of the State of Oregon, although by no means the largest town in that State. It is situate on the Williamette river.l I made a journey to see Mr. Winstanley, and spent' three or four days with him. When I got on to the' platform at Salem Station, who should I see but Mr. Winstanley himself, although he was not expecting me, but I can tell you he was right glad to see me. If I were to describe Salem I should say it was like Knowsley Park, with white houses studded about it, and a main street running right 1 through it. But Knowsley Park is not near so grand, for there you have not got gigantic moun- tains, peaked with snow away in the background as they have at Salem, nor have you the beautiful green foliage, leading right up the Mountains, almost till your eye strikes the snoW.eap. As soon as Mr. Winstanley got to Salem he got work at 31 dollar a day, and he bought a piece of land of about forty acres, which is, I should say, worth nearly twice as much as he paid for it. While I was staying at Salem, Mr. and Mrs. Winstanley and I called apt the house of a fellow workman of Mr. Winstanley—a large house standing in its own grounds, and led up to by an avenue, bordered on both sides with fine peach trees; and whilst there we had placed before us plates of peaches of a most remarkable size, and SO rich that they seemed to melt in \MUT mouth The climate is delightful, and the Williamette Valley is one of the finest growing Idistricts I know of. A POLITICAL FORECAST. With regard to Canada as a colony, it is not worth two straws to England. It sticks to England simply because of the benefits derived from the connection. I believe the time is not far distant when Canada will be independent, or connected with the States. Is is only a question of a few years. In conclusion, Mr. Porter said that his present intentions were to stay in England till the 31st October, when he would sail by an Inman line steamer. He was in England partly for pleasure and partly to transact some business in connection a gold and silver mine, near to Vancouver, in which he has a fourth interest. While here he would be glad to give any information he could with regard to Canada, and he would not consider he was being troubled by any one who applied to him for such information.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A FARM LABOURER.—A farm-labourer named Patrick Kirby, employed by Mr. Warburton, farmer, Bold, on Wednesday morn- ing was brought to the Warrington Infirmary suffering from a broken leg, a.nd internal injuries. He had been run over by a horse and trap belonging to Mr. Warburton. The injuries were fatal, and he succumbed to them yesterday morning at about 12 o'clock. An inquest will be held. div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. W. Deacon.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. W. Deacon.

DRUNKENNESS.—For thi-s—o-fi;Ce a fine of 5s and costs was imposed upon the folloning :—Eliza Hankey, no residence ; Thomas Jones, Po4l-lane, Runcorn ; Daniel Cramley, St. Helens; Henry Brassington,Lugsdale-road ; John Bradshaw, Liverpool ; Mary Jane Doyle, Water- st. ; and Daniel Tobin, Charlotte-st. Patrick Burns, a militiaman, of Warrington, was fined 10s. and costs. REMANDED CASES.—Wm. Byers, of Water-st. was re- manded for a week, on the charge of having on Satur- day night stolen a shawl belonging to Alfred Walker, a stallholder in the Market Hall'. The prisoner is "wanted" on other charges. Ellen Byers, his wife was also re- manded on a charge of 'stealing three shawls, a frock, and other articles,' also the property of Alfred Walker. The prisoner alleged that she was " pricing" the articles and the boy at the stall did not give her time to pay for them.

div.head: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.

THURSDAY,—Before Mr. E, K, Muspratt and Mr. G. Pilkington, DatrNIMNESS.—The following pArSons were dealt with for this offence :—William Beasley-, fined ss. and costs; Thomas Hayes, lined ss. and costs; Ellen Roach, fintd ss. and costs; and Thomas Rosvere, fined ss. and costs. DISTURBING TER PEACE.—Thomas Allen, a middle-aged man, was summoned for having committed a breach of the peace on the 23rd ult. The constable who proved the case said that defendant createda great disturbance, and broke the furniture in his house. He was ordered to be bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, himself in £lO, and one surety in £5, or, in default, to go to prison for seven days.—James Malone was similarly dealt with for having committed a breach of the peace on the 22nd ult.—Annie Twambley, for having disturbed the peace on the 22nd ult., by shouting, and fighting with Bridget Carlon, was also ordered to enter into recognisances. and find one surety of £5, to be of good behaviour for three months. Bridget Carlon was similarly dealt with. DOG AT LARGE.—John R. Lee was fined 2s 6d and costs for having allowed his dog to be at large. MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—Thomas Kennedy was ordered to contribute a shilling per week towards the support of his mother, who is in receipt of relief from the Guardians. —Thomas Howard was ordered to contribute Is 61 per week towards the support of his mother.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS..
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS..
MONDAY.—Before Mr. James Handley, and Mr. G. L. Davies. _

LICENSING MATTER-S.—Ann Atherton, was granted the transfer of the license of the Waterman's Arms, Queen- street, formerly occupied by her husband, deceased. James Woods was granted temporary authority to sell at the Bridge Hotel, lately occupied by John Bobbing- ton; and similar permission was granted to Thomas Lana,han, at th. Rose and Shamrock, Mersey-street, and Jessie McGuifog at the Shamrock Tavern, Regent-street. Funious DRIVING.--John Moores, 22 Trinity-street, was charged with having on the evening of the 19th ult. in Greenway-road, furiously driven a pony and cart.— P.C. Breeze said the man was driving at a rate of from 12 to 14 miles an hour past the Cemetery Bridge, and two men fell from the back of the cart. The defendant could not draw up the pony for 150 yards.--Defendant said his pony was not the size of a big donkey," and having been heavily worked on the day in question, the animal could not go at any more than a trot. He called two witnesses in corrobation.—Superintendent Rolling- worth said furious driving was very prevalent, and if the practice were not stopped some serious accident would occur.-J-The Bench imposed a fine of ss. and costs 10s. 6d•

DRUNK AND DISORDERLEY.—John Feeney pleaded guilty to being drunk and disorderly, in Cooper-st., anq he was fined ss. and costs. For using obscene and profane language in Fryer-st. Kate Carroll was fined ss. and costs 9s. 6d.—A fine of ss. and costs 6s. Bd. was imposed upon John Kelly, labourer, for being drunk and dis- orderly in Church-street on Saturday night and similar fines were imposed upon Michael Rogers, a stranger; Mary Fairhurst a stranger ; Alice Hampson, 14th appear- ance; John Coleman, a labourer; John Barnes, a young man ; and Elizabeth Williams an old woman. Fines of 10s. and costs were imposed upon Rose Scott, an old woman ; and David Ankers, of Widnes. A FAMILY SQUABBLE —James Gregory, a young man, was summoned for assaulting Alfred Harrison. Com- plainant stated that about eleven o'clock on the 22nd ult. he was having a drink in the Lion Hotel, Greenway- road, when 'the defendant entered seized him by the throat and threatened to dash his brains out. He dragged him out into the road and struck him three times causing him a black eye. Charles Wilson gave similar evidence.—The defendant alleged that complaint ant was drunk and he (defendant) paid for him a pint of ale. They had married sisters and the complainant

called his mother-in-law a foul name. In consequence he pushed him into the road but never struck him.—James Littlenvore, and Martha Kilgress, the 'no her-in-law, 'gave evidence for the defendant, who was dismissed.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. •
div.p: LATEST NEWS. •

At the Thames Police Court, on Friday, Richard Bartlett was committed for trial for murdering his wife with a hammer at Poplar. The miners at Butterlev Colliery, Ripley, Derby, have determined to support the decision of the Manchester Conference for an advance.

Thomas Moodie, watchmaker, and two other men, were remanded at Edinburgh on Friday charged with stealing Lady Londondefry's jewels on Thursday. All the jewels were recovered from the prisoners. A Berlin correspondent says the Empress Frederick has abandoned her intention of going to Scotland on a visit to the Queen, and will return to Berlin from Kiel, to take up her winter residence in her own palace. GALES IN THE NORTH SEA.—The smack Ruth arrived in Yarmouth Harbour on Friday morning, having lost three of her crew—the owner's son and two of the hands. They were washed overboard, and drowned.—The Shade of the Evening smack has also arrived with the loss of one hand—the owner's son.

DEATH IN A BALLnoom.—The county ball at Hamilton was brought abruptly to a close on Friday Morning by a sad occurrence. While engaged dancing Colonel Aikman, V.C., fell on the floor and died almost immediately. The deceased received the Victoria Cross for meritorious conduct in India. Heart disease is supposed to have been the cause of death.

SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A FORGE—About nine o'clock on Friday morning a man named Alexander Pope, employed at the Bolton Iron and Steel Works, met his death in a fearful manner. He was assisting in the removal of a heavy shaft, when it accidentally fell upon him, crushing in his chest, and opening his head. The injured man was taken to the Infirmary, where he died in a snort time.

THE WESTMINSTER MURDER : SUPPOSED CLUE.—Police- inspector Marshall went to Guildford, on Friday, to bring to London the leg of a woman which was recently found near the railway line there, and which was stated to have been boiled. The limb will be compared by Dr. Bond with the trunk lately found at Whitehall. It is believed that some very important information has been obtained, which will shortly lead to the identification of the murdered woman and to an arrest.

, ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE. Elizabeth Bloxham, age 24, wife of a mechanic at 48. Gew:giana-street, Camden Town, on Thursday night took oxalic acid, and administered some to her four-year-old boy. She died, but the boy survives. The motive of the crime is unknown. THE BLACK MOUNTAIN EXPEDITION. It is stated from Simla that the third column of General M‘Queen's expedition, while advancing on Friday morning upon Surmulbutspur, on the Black Mountain, had a skirmish with the enemy, in which six men of the Sussex Regiment and two Sepoys were wounded.

div.head: WHITECHAPEL MURDERS.
div.p: THE WHITECHAPEL MURDERS.

The man arrested at Bishop Stortford on suspicion of being concerned in the Whitechapel murders was set at liberty yesterday afternoon, the police having ascertained that the account he gave of himself was correct. No fur- ther arrests have been made, and no persons are now in custody. The fac similes of the letter and postcard addressed to the Central News, and signed Jack the Ripper, have now been posted up at each Police Station in the Metropolis. It will be remembered that in the posh ard, which was posted on Sunday afternoon, the writer stated that "num- ber one (the Berner-st. victim) squeale,d a bit." Until yesterday it had been assumed that, as in the case of the other victims, the cutting of the throat caused instan- taneous death, but in his evidence before the Coroner yesterday, Dr. Phillips expressed the opinion that, in this instance, the victim did have time to scream.

_ The funeral of Kate Eddowes, the Mitre-square victim, will take place on Monday afternoon in Ilford cemetery. Tho police have commenced a systematic search of unoccupied buildings in the Whitechar l district. They are on the look-out for a Malay, upon whom saspicion has fallen.

div.head: INQUEST ON THE BERNER STREET VICTIM.
div.p: INQUEST ON THE BERNER STREET VICTIM.

The inquest on the body of Elizabeth Stride, who was found murdered in Berner-street on Sunday morning last, was resumed yesterday afternoon at the Vestry Hall, St. George's-in-the-East. Dr. Phillips, divisional police sur- geon, said, from the position of the body, he Was of opinion that deceased was seized by the shoulders, placed on the ground, and that the perpetrator of the deed was on her right side when he inflicted the cut. The incision was from the left to the right. Deceased's assailant might have kept clear from blood stains. There was no perceptible trace of any narcotic.—The Clerk of the Swedish Church, Princes-square, gave evidence of identification. Deceased was a Swede, and born near Gottenburg. She married an Englishman named Stride, who was drowned in the Princess Alice disaster.. Wm. Marshall, labourer, said he saw deceased in Berner-street about quarter to twelve, Saturday night. She was talk- ing to a man who wore a short black coat, dark trousers, and a peaked cap.—A young mannamedJames Brown said he saw deceased in company with a man standing near the Board School, in Berner-st., at a quarter to one on Sunday morning. The man was wear- ing a long overcoat, which reached almost down to his heels.—P. C. • Smith stated that lie passed deceased in Berner-st., at twelve-thirty, on Saturday night. She was talking to a man who was carrying a parcel wrap- ped in a newspaper. It was about eighteen inches long, and five or six inches broad. He wore dark clothes, and a low felt hat.—Other evidence of a formal nature was given, and the inquiry adjourned until Tuesday fort- night.

ING CLUB. We give below the awards in the annual conapeti- tion of the vacation sketching club connected with the Warrington School of Art. The sketches of the members of the club have been on view during the week at the School otArt,and if not quite so nutner- ous as on some previous occasions they show pro- 1 gress both in the advanced and elementary sections, and particularly in the latter. The slight falling off I in the number of sketches may probably be entirely attributed to the unfavourable weather prevniling most part of the vacation, as the club has a longer list of members than formerly. The object of the club, it may be mentioned, is" first to encourage original study from nature; and, secondly, that of affording past students the opportunity to continue' their association with the instttution." The I adjudicators in the competition were Mr. H. D. Barkas (bead master); Mr. W. D. Schroder (art master,Chester); Mr. E. Renard (art master,Saltaire). The following is the list of the awards : Advanced section, Mr. G. Toft, (347 marks) ; Miss Holmes, (304) ; Miss M. Burgess, (300.)—Elementary section, Miss Walton (292 marks) ; Miss Shipton (286) ; Miss Brierley, (190.)—Special competition: Best study from life, prize (given by Mr. J. Best still life study, prize, (anonymous), Miss Calvert ; commended, Miss Chrimes.—Architectural sketches, prize, (anonymous), to Mr. H. A. Barkas. Set of three sketches on imperial sheet —to show applied principles—viz., linear perspective, ground work of colour, completion of study, prize, (anonymous,) Mr. J. ci.Dewhurst.—Best subject in the elementary section, prize, (anonymous), Miss Brierley.

THE PRESENTATION TO AIR. ThouAs BIRCIIALL. —We understand that the presentation, proposed to be made to Mr. Thomas Birchall in recognition of his services as president of the Warrington Co-operative Society for the past twenty one years, is to take place at the quarterly meeting of mem- bers of the Society, on Monday ovening, the 15th inst. The articles chosen are a silver urn, a secre- taire, and marble timepiece with side pieces, and are of the value of .£5O. They are to be shown to-day and for the ensuing week in the centre window of the Co-operative Stores. The presenta- tion is to be made by Councillor F. Monks.

OFFICERS SHOOTING COMPETITION.—On Thurs- day afternoon, at Altcar rifle range, a shooting competition took place between the officers of the Ist V.8.P.W.5.L.R., whose headquarters are at Warrington, for a challenge CUD, value £25, pre- sented by Mr. F. A. Roberts. The conditions were seven shots at 200, 500. and 600 yards. At the con- clusion of the firing at the three ranges it was found that a tie had occurred for the prize between Col. Bolton and Captain Buukton, and to settle the matter it was decided that each should fire seven shots at 600 yards. This contest resulted in favour of Captain Buckton, who beat his opponent by 10 points to nil.

BRITISII WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. Established 1866. Incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862. CAM OFFICES :, BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending April 300 h, 1888, Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Policies, and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. Cl. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to MI up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consen.ed to do, and I he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Polley in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18s Bd, being an increase of £21,926 us 9d. The total amount of payments was £163,018 14s Id, leaving a balance upon the year's accounts of £15,292 4s 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 19s Orls The amount paid in Claims during the year was £77,479, including £4,411 6s Surrender Claims. The total sum paid up to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 is 10d. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, \ was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 188 10d, showing a net increase of 39,070 Assurants, and £27,820 us 9d in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director. D. A. BECKETT, Secretary. DISTRICT OFFICE : • MARKET GATE CHAMBERS, WARRINGTON. S. GREEN, SUPERINTENDENT.

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. A BICYCLE "CRACK." Some stuff thersePs up wi' t' fawse notion They've nobbut to try,—to succeed, When t' fact is iv they tried a life-time, They'd not be mitch nar when they deed. 0' t' sooart, ther wur ne'er sitch a humbug As one mon co'd "Blether-brained Jack;" He'd jabber o'er nowt else but " wheelin'," Th' poor chap wur a bicycle "crack!" Aw've heeard as his fost meawnt o' th' saddle Wur on to t' " steom " wheelers at th' Fair; Hr spent three an' ninepence i' riding, Then swooar he'd mek Blegburners stare. Lien bad wi th' velocipede faver— Aw'm sure a foo' never wur woss ! He'd part wi' his brass free as watter, An' peyl hissel' just like a hoss. Heaw happy he wor while t' Fair lasted, An' then thee wur tears in his e'en, Till his mate bowt, among some odd lumber, An owd scithor-grindin' machine. He offered id Jack as a bargain, 'Twur just t' thing to practise his feet; Jack bowt id. an' kept t' troddle gooin' An heawr or two every neet. An' then, bi hard pinchin' an' scrapin', He bowt a velocipede chep, An' led id hooam, gentle as could be, smilin' face, red as a hep. He practised i' th' backyard a fortnit', Balanced up wi' two clooas lises Cu' t' prop; Then tawked abeawt lickin' o t' records, - Hand-running, fro' t' bottom to t' top. Wed twistin's an' twinin'a he went thro', Wed fo's, wi' sad damage to th' heyd, He geet, when he ventured th' oppen, An' cluttered on t' stooanes at full spreyd. Fooak axed wur his bicycle fuddled, For id wriggled abeawt like a worm But Jack only lafft duo' his plaisters, An' sed as he worn'd th' best form. At fleet, when he'd swallowed his "baggiu'," To ride on his "tit" he ne'er missed ; An t' lads used to pkrike eawt wi' laffin', Whenever owd England he kissed. 0 th' pleecemen believed he wur crazy; His ways wur suspiciously eyed, Bekose they felt sure as his antics Wur signs as he meant suicide I He kept geddin' bowder an' bowder, An' tried to do bits o' odd tricks, • But, just when he thowt he could manage, He'd drop, like a cartlooad a" bricks. One day, he wur rattlire off, deawn broo, An' lifted his feet up too soon, When he coonz remand his face wur lob-sided An' swelled like a ragmon's balloon. At last, when he'd missed bein' run o'er, fleleet i' misfortune a bit; Wi' speed up, he catched a stooan sideways, An' o'er he fell—souse in a pit! . Thad give him a dose o' t' rheumatic An' drooave a gret champion fro' t' track; But wait till he gets reawnd, an' gradely,— Yo'll Lear ov a "bicycle crack !" JACK 0' ANN'S.
